INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Fifty Fifth Repor t on the Action Taken by the 
Government on the recommendations/ observations of the Committee contained in its Three 
Hundred Thirty Ninth Report on Demands for Grants ( 2023-24) of Ministry of Civil 
Aviation. 
2. The Three Hundred Thirty Ninth Report  of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Cultur e was presented to the Parliament on 
the 13 th  March, 2023. 
3.  The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations  of the Committee contained in its 
Three Hundred Thirty Ninth Report were received fro m the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 
19 th  June, 2023. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 19 th  
September, 2023.

Aviation on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundred Thirty -
Ninth Report on Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of Ministry of Civil Aviation which  was

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Assessment of Demands for Grants (2023-24) and Annual Plan (2022-23) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the projected demand of the Ministry for B.E. 2023 -24 was 
Rs.3,532.13/- crore. The Ministry of Finance reduced it to Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore, which 
indicates a reduction of Rs. 418.77/ - crore. The Budget allocation for 2023 -24 is 66.75% 
lower than R.E. 2022-23. The Ministry also stated that the Ministry of Finance d id not assign 
any reasons for the reduction. However, the requirement of additional funds to meet the 
activities of the Ministry will be taken up at R.E. 2023-24 stage. 
 (Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The requirement of additional funds to meet the activities of the Ministry will be 
taken up at R.E. 2023-24 stage. 
 
Regional Connectivity Scheme – UdeDeshkaAamNagrik (RCS-UDAN) 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee was apprised of the R.E., Actual Expenditure and Actual/R.E. 
percentage since the introduction of the RCS Scheme. The Committee notes that the Ministry 
has been able to make utilization of the R.E. allocated to it with utilization figures as high as 
100% (2017 -18); 91.61% (2018 -19), 108.26% (2019 -20); 100% (2020 -21); and 98.62% 
(2021-22). The Committee was also informed that 53.67% of the R.E. allocation for 2022 -23 
has been utilized upto 31.01.2023. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The entire allocation of Rs 900.00 crore at RE 2022 -23 stage for the scheme RCS -
Udan has been fully utilised (100%). 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to utilize the funds allocated for 
B.E. 2023 -24 to the maximum extent possible, by removing the shortcoming and obstacles 
observed earlier and through bette r planning. The need for better planning in the RCS is the 
need of the hour, since a major allocation of Rs. 1,244.07/ - crore, accounting to 39.95% of 
the B.E. 2023-24 allocation of Rs. 3,113.36 has been made in the scheme. Besides, RCS is the 
second highe st expenditure of the Ministry for 2023 -24. This greatly illustrates the 

3 
 
importance the Government attaches to the Scheme. The Committee would like to highlight 
the fact that a major allocation of B.E. for the Ministry is towards AIAHL for disinvestment 
of Air India, which is not creating any asset for the Nation. Hence, the allocation for RCS 
assumes more significance as it creates permanent assets for the Nation and adds to its Gross 
Domestic Product. 
 (Para 26) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Recommendations of the committee have been  noted. All efforts would be made 
for utilization of funds allocated under B.E. 2023-24 for RCS to the maximum extent. 
 
Achievements in 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes that as per the Output Outcome Monit oring Framework for 
2022-23 (till 31.12.2022), the Ministry has not been able to achieve the targets in most cases, 
with achievements in the range of 40% to 67% only. Only in the case of passengers travelled 
in NER, it has achieved a percentage of 261.5%. The Committee notes the low performance 
of the Ministry on almost all the constituents of the RCS -UDAN Scheme, except one. The 
Committee hopes that with the increased allocation, the Ministry would do meticulous 
planning to ensure full utilization of funds and achievement of targets. 
 (Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Recommendations/observations of the Committee have been noted. 
 
Revival of Underserved and Unserved Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee during its earlier deliberations was informed that the reasons for the 
delay in operations of RCS projects, relate to delay in completing the work owing to land 
issues; delay in removing obstacles; and delay in regulatory clearances. Further, there were 
Airline related issues such as delay in  obtaining Scheduled Commuter Operators Permit by 
new entrant Airlines; non -availability of suitable aircraft; aircraft leasing issues; long lead 
time for delivery; maintenance issues of small aircraft; difficulties in procuring spares from 
abroad. Also, C OVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted domestic and international flight 
operations, due to suspension of scheduled commercial operations. Furthermore, reduced 
passenger demand, un-viability of flight operations, collapse of revenue streams coupled with 
high fixed costs resulted into liquidity crunch for airlines. The Committee notes that the 
delays are mostly due to operational issues or lack of compliance of agreements by the Select 
Airline Operators (SAOs) or issues such as land availability, pend ing with concerned State 
Governments. The Committee feels that such impediments should be removed at the earliest 

4 
 
to enable the Ministry to achieve its set targets. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
before allotment of RCS routes, the antecedents a nd past performance of SAOs may be 
thoroughly scrutinized, so that difficulties are not faced at a later stage. The defaulting SAOs 
should be held accountable for not meeting deadlines. The Committee also recommends close 
coordination with State Government s to remove bottlenecks, such as land availability issues 
in operationalization of RCS routes. 
(Para 35) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Recommendations/observations of the Committee have been noted. 
 
NER Schemes: Providing Air Connectivity and Aviation Infrastructure in NER 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee notes that out of the total B.E. 2023 -24 for NER Schemes amounting 
to Rs.230.01/ - crore (S. Nos. 1, 2, 3 & 4), Viability Gap Funding (VGF) amounts to Rs. 
190.01/- crore for Alliance Air; SAO ; and Alliance Air for Dornier Operations in NER. The 
Committee hopes that VGF will give a helping hand in improving air connectivity in NE 
Region, which has suffered due to the non -commercial viability of routes and uncertainty of 
operations due to weathe r conditions which led to non -operation of scheduled airlines. The 
Committee notes that out of the total Scheme allocation of Rs. 500/ - crore from 01.04.2021 to 
31.03.2024, Rs. 230.01/- crore has been allocated for B.E. 2023-24, accounting to 46% of the 
total budget allocation for the Scheme, while it was allocated Rs. 178.77/ - crore at R.E. 
20223-23 stage. This indicates the priority of the Government towards this Scheme. 
 (Para 41) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Recommendations/observation of the Committee have been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Members of the Committee during its earlier deliberations, repeatedly pointed 
out the remoteness of the NER and the need for adequate air connectivity in the Region. The 
Committee had taken up the issue of the development of Advanced Landing Grounds (ALGs) 
for the State of Arunachal Pradesh, specifically at Dirang, Daporijo and Anini, with the 
Ministry. Besides, the extension work at Dibrugarh Airport; direct flight for Itanagar; and 
modernisation work at  Dimapur Airport has also been highlighted by the Committee, since 
these are the main airports connecting the NE Region to the rest of the country. Besides, the 
Committee had also taken up the issue of high prices of air tickets for the NE flights. 
(Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Recommendations/observation of the Committee have been noted. 

5 
 
 
Surge in Air Fares and Rationalisation 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee takes note of the fact that after the repeal of the Air Corporations Act, 
1953, the airfare is market driven and depends on market fares, and is neither established 
nor regulated by the Government. It notes the DGCA’s comments that the airfares were 
regulated for a fixed period during the COVID pandemic in compliance with Aircraft Act , 
1934 and the regulation was withdrawn as the COVID pandemic abated and that airlines are 
free to fix reasonable tariffs under the Aircraft Rules, 1937, with regard to cost of operation, 
services, reasonable profit and generally prevailing tariff. 
 (Para 71) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Observation of the Committee has been noted. 
 
International Operations 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee notes the Ministry’s reply with regards to granting ‘Point of Call’ 
status to International Airports in the country. The Committee feels that parity should be 
maintained between the international and domestic carriers for operating passenger services 
in the country. The Committee recommends that Ministry should identify a balanced 
approach to liberalize the guid elines for granting of ‘Point of Call’ status to the Indian 
airports to ensure better air connectivity. The Committee opines that better connectivity to 
international airports in the country will give passengers more options to choose from and 
increase the  influx of international passengers. The enhanced number of international 
passengers/tourists will eventually boost the tourism prospects of the country and aid in 
economic development. 
 (Para 170) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 The Ministry has noted the Committee‟s observations. 
 
Sustainable Aviation 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee recommends that the Government should encourage the use of Bio -
ATF and formulate a policy in this regard. The Ministry should also assess the requirement 
of necessary technological innovations to ensure that the use of Bio -ATF is promoted. The 
Committee opines that the FUA will lead to optimal utilization of Indian airspace and result 
in reduction of flight time; fuel consumption; and carbon emission. 

6 
 
 (Para 175) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The Ministry has noted the Committee‟s observations. 
 
Promotion of Research and Development 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee notes the progress of Research and Development initiatives that the 
Ministry has introduced with respect to access control and security at airports. The 
Committee appreciates that the Ministry has switched to a biometric enabled system from the 
earlier paper -based permits for the movement of employees in Indian airports, ensuring a 
paperless environment. The Committee would like to know the details of the 48 airports 
which are planned to be covered under the Centralised Access Control System in the 1st 
phase. The Committee desires to know whether the Ministry plans to cover the remainin g 
airports in the subsequent phases and the details thereof. The Committee recommends that 
the Ministry should devise a foolproof mechanism to keep a check on the automated access 
control of employees and vehicles to ensure unauthorized intrusion in the airports. 
 (Para 203) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 The recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

7 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Assessment of Demands for Grants (2023-24) and Annual Plan (2022-23) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the B.E. allocation for 2023 -24 is Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore, 
which is by far the lowest of all the B.E. allocation in the last five years. In fact, th e B.E. 
allocation has been steadily decreasing from Rs. 6,602.86/ - crore (2018 -19), to Rs. 
4,500.00/- crore (2019-20), to Rs. 3,797.71/ - crore (2020-21), to Rs. 3,224.67/ - crore (2021-
22), barring the year 2022 -23 when the Ministry received a B.E. allocati on of Rs. 10,667/ - 
crore on account of disinvestment of Air India., and now the lowest at Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore 
for B.E. (2023 -24). These decreasing allocations have been made despite the increasing 
trend of inflation in the country, which implies that the effective allocations are ever lower. 
Even during allocations at R.E. stage, the fund allocation remained below the projected 
demand of the Ministry, other than the year 2021 -22, though the Ministry has shown a good 
capacity to absorb the funds allocated to it, with percentage expenditure as compared to R.E. 
allocations i.e., as high as 98.96% (2018 -19), 98.56% (2019 -20), 99.07% (2020 -21) and 
98.99% (2021 -22). For the year 2022 -23, the percentage expenditure was 86.14% as on 
31.01.2023. The Ministry assured the Committee in its Demands for Grants meeting that full 
utilization of the R.E. allocation would be achieved. 
 (Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The actual expenditure up to 31.03.2023 during the FY 2022 -23 is Rs 9321.06 crore 
which is 99.54% of RE allocation of Rs 9363.70 crore, hence the consistency of absorbing 
capacity of the funds allocated to the Ministry is maintained over the years. 
  
Safety of Air Transport Operations 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee is of the view that the projected demand of the Ministry reflects the 
expenditure on targets and objectives it seeks to achieve in that particular financial year.  The 
Committee is aware that the Civil Aviation Industry had suffered a major setback on account 
of Covid-19 pandemic and needs full budgetary support from the Government at this critical 
juncture, where it has to recover its losses and come up to its earlier level in the first instance 
and then grow at an even faster rate. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of 
Finance should favourably consider additional grant of funds to the Ministry at R.E. stage, to 
enable the Ministry to achieve its set targets and achieve the aim of the Indian Civil Aviation 
Industry. 

8 
 
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The recommendation o f the Committee has been noted for compliance.  Ministry of 
Civil Aviation will take the issue with the Ministry of Finance for provisioning of additional 
grant favourably at RE stage to enable the Ministry to achieve its set targets and achieve the 
aim of the Indian Civil Aviation Industry. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes that a major part of the B.E. allocation in the financial years 
2021-22, 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 consists of the budgetary allocation towards the 
disinvestment of Air India, which effectively did not create any asset for the Civil Aviation 
Sector in the long run. The Committee hopes that the trend would be reversed with the 
completion process of the disinvestment of Air India and more focus would be laid towards 
asset creation in the Civil Aviation Sector. 
(Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 During the process of disinvestment of Air India, calculation was done for 
requirement of funds for repayment of past Government borrowing, past Government 
guaranteed SLB Lease rentals and past dues/liabilities of Air India after the taking over of the 
debt of Rs. 15,300 crore by M/s Talace Pvt. Ltd. Accordingly, financial support was sought in 
FY 2021-22 for payment of remaining debt and liabilities.  
3.2 Accordingly, financial support of Rs. 61,130.96 crore was provided to Air India 
through AIAHL in the form of equity in FY 2021 -22 in respect of repayment of past govt. 
borrowing, past govt. guaranteed SLB Lease rentals and past dues/liabilities of AIL.  
3.3 In FY 2022-23, the BE allocation of Rs. 9,259.91 crore included   the provision of Rs.

Surge in Air Fares and Rationalisation 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee during its deliberations expressed concerns about the high fares 
charged by the private airlines in the domestic sector. The Committee also pointed out the 
wrong information published by the private airlines on t heir websites, regarding the number 
of seats left in the flight and the prices of the tickets. The level of misinformation can be 
gauged from the fact that even after the last tickets have been sold, the same number of seats 
show on the website, as indicated before the tickets sale. This indicates that airline operators 
are misguiding the public and forcing passengers to pay more. In view of the above, the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should formulate appropriate guidelines regarding 
rationalization of fares and publishing the correct information on the website of the airlines. 
 (Para 66) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Currently there is no provision under the obligation of which airlines are required to 
publish number of seats left in the flight on their website. The airlines are selling tickets as 
per their respective distribution system, which is in line with the practice followed 
worldwide. However, the observations of the Committee have been noted. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee also pointed that 'Predatory Pricing' is being restored to by the 
domestic airlines sector. A particular airline may sell its air tickets at such a low level, that 
other competitors cannot compete and are forced to exit the market. A company that does this 
will see initial losses, but eventually it benefits by driving competitions out of the market and 
raising its prices again. The Committee desired to know whether the DGCA had at any point 
of time, intervened to check the fares of air tickets. The Committe e also expressed concern at 
the fact that in the domestic sector, private airlines are charging different fares for same 
sector, route and same direction of flights. This is specifically so for the NE Region and Hilly 
areas including Jammu & Kashmir and La dakh, where the prices of domestic sector tickets 
are, sometimes even more than the international airline sector prices. 
 (Para 67) 

13 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Under the provision of Sub Rule (1) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, every air 
transport undertaking engaged in scheduled air services require to establish tariff having 
regard to all relevant factors, including cost of operation, characteristic of services, 
reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff. 
10.2 Government has laid down route dispersal  guidelines with a view to achieve better 
regulation of air transport services taking into account the need for air transport services of 
different regions of the country. It is, however, up to the airlines to provide air services to 
specific places depending upon the traffic demand and commercial viability. As such, the 
airlines are free to operate anywhere in the country subject to compliance of route dispersal 
guidelines issued by Government. 
10.3 The airlines are required to deploy adequ ate capacity in NE region, Jammu & 
Kashmir and Ladakh as per the provisions of the RDG (Copy of RDG is enclosed)  
Annexure-IV. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee is fully aware that the Indian domestic Aviation sector is growing in 
an open marke t and acknowledges that the private airline operators should be given a free 
hand to decide the air fares as they are governed by competition and depends on market 
fares. It also notes that there is a provision in the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which inter -alia has a 
provision for fixing the air fares after considering ‘reasonable profit and generally prevailing 
tariff’ amongst other factors. The Committee observes that presently the surge in air fares 
does not reflect any sort of mechanism on part of the Minist ry to control the fares, based on 
existing Aircraft Rules, 1937, as during surge in air fares the prices go beyond the acceptable 
or justifiable limits of 'reasonable profit and generally prevailing tariff'. 
 (Para 72) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1 Under the provision of the sub Rule (1) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, every 
air transport undertaking engaged in scheduled air services requires to establish tariff having 
regard to all relevant factors, including cost of operation, characteristic of serv ices, 
reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff. Airlines are free to charge reasonable air 
fares as per their operational viabilities subject to compliance to above said rule. The airline 
pricing system runs in multiple levels (buckets or RBDs ) which are in line with practice 
being followed globally. The prices are fixed by airlines keeping in mind the market, 
demand, seasonality and other market forces. The airfare increases with increas e in demand 
of seats as the lower fare buckets get sold o ut fast when bookings are offered by airlines. 
Some of the airlines have introduced Apex -90, in addition to existing advance purchase 
schemes of 60 days, 30 days, 14 days etc., in which highly discounted fares being offered 
which would entail travelling ev en during peak seasons on low fares. The fare structures 
stated above have been displayed by airlines on their websites. The airlines are compliant to 

14 
 
the prevailing regulation as long as fares charged by them are in line with fare displayed on 
their website. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee notes that while on one hand Government plans to make air transport 
affordable for the common man and the air capacity is being increased, on the other hand 
there is no commensurate expansion of the capacity to bring in aircrafts. This creates lack of 
airline tickets considering the high demand and leads to increase in the prices. The 
Committee recommends that there should be a mechanism with the Ministry such as capping 
of upper and lower prices to s top the practice of 'Predatory Pricing' or the sudden surge in 
prices. The Committee is of the firm opinion that a perfect balance has to be maintained 
between the commercial interest of the private airlines and the interest of the passengers so 
as to enab le the private airlines to grow and at the same time the interest of passengers 
should also be kept in mind, so that they are not fleeced in the garb of commercialization. 
The Committee feels that even though price buckets are being created as per internat ional 
aviation norms, a close watch has to be maintained by the DGCA & the Ministry and a 
mechanism should be devised to monitor the websites of various airlines to prevent them from 
misguiding passengers. And, in case the private airlines do not publish t he correct 
information regarding fares, they should be penalized for it. The Committee observes that the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation has a responsibility to the travelling public and the nation at large 
to ensure that predatory pricing mechanism are not ado pted by the airlines under the cloak 
of free market economy. The Committee recommends the Ministry should formulate a pricing 
mechanism for air fares to ensure that passengers are not charged exorbitant prices. The 
Committee also recommends that DGCA may b e empowered to regulate tariffs based on the 
data generated by their monitoring Department or otherwise. Further, the passengers may 
also be given an option to approach the said Department with their grievances. 
 (Para 73) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 DGCA has not been empowered with the economic regulation of civil aviation and air 
transport services under Section 5A of Aircraft Act, 1934. 
12.2 Also, Competition Commission of India has issued order dated 06/03/2013 that the 
Commission can neither go into th e issue of MRP i.e. what should be the MRP for any 
product or service and fix the MRP, nor the Commission can give direction to the 
Government of India that it should fix MRP of a service being provided by private 
entrepreneur. In fact, that will be contra ry to the spirit of competition law. At present, the 
forces of demand and supply govern the air fares. Whenever supply is more and demand is 
less, air fares fall and in lean season the airlines do decrease air fares. It is only when demand 
is more and supply is less that the airlines venture to increase the air fares (Copy of the  said 
order is enclosed) Annexure-IV(A).

Steps taken to rationalize Taxes on ATF 
Recommendation/Observation 
26. The Committee notes that the airlines in the country are spending a significant 
amount on Aviation Turbine Fuel and rationalization of VAT rates will be very crucial in 
reducing the operating cost which will improve the viability of the airlines. The Committee  
feels that lowered rates of VAT on ATF may result in reduced price of air tickets, enhanced 
air connectivity and fuel uplift. The Committee notes that airlines are picking up ATF from 
those States/UTs where VAT rates on ATF are lower. Also, the resultant increase in revenue 
from sale of aviation fuel may aid in the growth of tourism, better employment opportunities 
in the States/UTs. 
(Para 126) 
Recommendation/Observation 
27. The Committee notes that the pricing of Aviation Turbine Fuel is majorly influence d 
by the international product prices, depreciating value of Rupee and other market conditions. 
The Committee further observes the high ATF prices prevailing in the country which is 
further aggravated by high taxes such as customs duty, excise duty, sale/S tate tax, Value 
Added Tax (VAT) levied thereon. The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be 
made to lower the taxes being levied on the ATF. The Committee has been given to 
understand that the cost of ATF nearly accounts for approximately 40% of the total operating 
cost of airlines and impacts the financial viability of their operations and affects their 
competitiveness because Indian carriers are unable to compete against their global 
counterparts on account of the exorbitantly higher prices of ATF. 
(Para 127) 
Recommendation/Observation 
28. The Committee notes the efforts being made by the Ministry in coordination with the 
respective State/UT Governments, to bring down the State Tax/ VAT. The Committee notes 
that 18 States/UTs have lowered the tax levied on ATF while 6 States/UTs are still le vying 

23 
 
high rates of Tax. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should proactively follow -up 
with the remaining States/UTs especially Assam, Maharashtra, Delhi, Bihar, Tamil Nadu and 
West Bengal which are charging high VAT rates on ATF. The Committee a lso notes that 
despite ATF being an input fuel (similar to coal and gas), the issue to include ATF under the 
ambit of GST is a long pending issue and requires final resolution by the GST Council. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance with 
renewed efforts. 
(Para 128) 
Reply of the Ministry 
28.1 Government has consistently engaged in consultations with Airlines and OMCs on the 
issue of ATF pricing. Taking cognizance of the high value added tax (VAT) on ATF levied 
by States, the issue was taken up with the States/ Union Territories. As a result, VAT on ATF 
has been reduced by 19 States/ UTs viz. (i) Andaman & Nicobar Islands; (ii) Uttarakhand; 
(iii) Jammu & Kashmir; (iv) Ladakh; (v) Himachal Pradesh;(vi) Trip ura; (vii) Madhya 
Pradesh; (viii) Haryana; (ix) Uttar Pradesh; (x) Dadra and Nagar Haveli & Daman and Diu; 
(xi) Arunachal Pradesh; (xii) Manipur; (xiii) Jharkhand; (xiv) Mizoram; (xv) Gujarat; (xvi) 
Goa; (xvii) Karnataka; (xviii) Rajasthan; and (xix) Mahar ashtra. The issue has also been 
taken up with Hon‟ble Chief Ministers of Delhi, Assam and West Bengal. 
28.2 MoCA has also taken up the issue of inclusion of ATF under the ambit of GST with 
MoF on various levels. MoF has stated that Article 279 A (5) of the  Constitution prescribes 
that the GST Council shall recommend the date with effect from which the GST would be 
levied on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and ATF. As 
per the section 9(2) of the CGST Act, 2017, inclusio n of these products in GST will require 
recommendation of the GST Council. So far, the GST Council, in which the states are also 
represented, has not made any recommendation for inclusion of these goods under GST.

Sustainable Aviation 
Recommendation/Observation 
40. The Committee welcomes Ministry’s vision to develop a sustainable Indian Aviation 
Industry through energy conservation, the adoption of sustainable practices, and 
improvements in emission measurement. The Committee notes that the Ministry has decided 
not to participate in the voluntary phases of Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for 
International Aviation (CORSIA). The Committee would like to know the reasons for India’s 
non-participation in the voluntary phases of CORSIA and how it benefits the Indian 
scheduled carriers with international operations. The Committee also notes that the offsetting 
requirement f or Indian carriers under CORSIA  will start in 2027. The Committee may be 
apprised of the Ministry’s plans with regard to the issuance of necessary g uidelines to 
Airlines to motivate them to either use Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) or offset their 
emissions by purchasing carbon credits from ICAO approved scheme. 
 (Para 173) 
Reply of the Ministry 
40.1  Government has decided to participate in CORSIA scheme only from the mandatory 
phase i.e. 2027, so that the airlines of developing countries like India get time to grow more 
and do not face any financial consequences due to CORSIA by joining in voluntary p hase. 
Due to the COVID pandemic, there were  no offsetting requirements in the years 2019 -2020-
2021 as per ICAO. The Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Directorate General of Civil 
Aviation have held meetings with the Indian airlines to sensitize them regarding the impact of 

36 
 
CORSIA on them once the mandatory phase starts and the resultant need to be prepared for 
the same. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
41. The Committee notes that no funds have been allocated to the Ministry towards 
sustainable aviation and urg es the Ministry to furnish the reasons for it. The Committee 
would like to know the present status of the Ministry’s Report containing its views on the 
recommendations of the Bio -ATF Programme Committee. The Committee may also be 
apprised of the details of  the plan being formulated by the MoP&NG for production, supply 
and related issues of SAF for use in the aviation sector. 
 (Para 174) 
Reply of the Ministry 
41.1  CORSIA is applicable only to international flights originating from one country to 
another. The financial implications due to offsetting under CORSIA (on account of use of 
SAF or purchase of Carbon credits) will be borne by individual airlines depending upon their 
international operations as and when applicable. 
41.2 The Bio -ATF Programme Committee report has been circulated by M inistry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas (M oP&NG) to other relevant stakeholders on 19.12.2022. The 
comments on the same are awaited.  MoP&NG has notified the National Policy on Biofuels 
2018. The Government is adopting a multi-pronged approach to promote and encourage use 
of biofuels by focusing on advanced biofuels including bio -CNG, bio-methanol, Di-Methyl 
Ether (DME), bio-hydrogen, bio-jet fuel, etc. The scope of the Policy encompasses jet fuel as 
a 'drop in' fuel produced from Biomass, agri-residues, wastes such as Municipal Solid Wastes 
(MSW), Plastic wastes, Industrial wastes etc. which meets the Indian standards for Jet fuel, in 
pure or blended form. Oil Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) have identified Mangalore a nd 
Panipat for setting up Bio-ATF pants based on different technologies.

8.2      Basis of Enterprise Value adoption: 
 The Preliminary Information Memorandum (PIM) for strategic disinvestment of Air 
India Limited (AI) including AI‟s shareholding interest in Air India Express Limited 
(AIXL) and Air India SATS Airport Services Private Limited (AISATS), was issued 
on 27th January 2020.  
 As a part of the first process (PIM issued in Jan 2020), it was decided by GOI that at 
the time of closing of the Proposed Transaction, the debt to be retained in AI & AIXL 
(combined) would be INR 23,287 Cr (it was clarified that there would be no re-
allocation of debt & liabilities of AISATS) and the IBs had to submit their Financial 

54 
 
bid (at the RFP stage) considering that the debt of INR 23,287 Cr would have to be 
serviced by AI & AIXL (combined) post the strategic disinvestment exercise. 
 However, the strategic disinvestment exercise got adversely impacted by the outbreak 
of COVID-19 pandemic in India/world starting mid-March, 2020. Considering 
significant deterioration in operating environment for airlines (including AI) due to 
COVID, it was difficult for potential bidders and GOI to determine level of 
sustainable debt for AI + AIXL, upfront, at the EOI stage itself. COVID-19 resulted 
in a dynamic market situation which continued to be unpredictable and fast changing. 
It may be noted that final difference between the EOI submission date and RFP 
submission date was around 9 months and hence within long period of time any 
decision taken at the EOI stage would have been impacted by the dynamic situation 
that existed in the next 9 months. 
 Due to the effects of COVID, the operations of AI got significantly reduced and the 
amount of support needed from AI to run the reduced operations and meet the fixed 
costs, increased significantly. A snapshot of the key operating and financial 
parameters of AI in the first 4 months of FY21 (as provided by AI) is given below: 
Particulars (INR Cr) FY20 FY 21 (4 month actual) 
Revenue 27,284 2,260 
EBITDA (-)323 (-)1,366 
Cash loss (-) 3,323 (-)2,738 
ASKMs  (Mn) 63,200 3,348 
 
 It may be noted that the ASKM (Available Seat Kilometres) of AI have dropped by 
~85% in the first 4 months of FY21 and the cash loss in the first 4 months is nearly 
82% of the cash loss achieved in the whole of FY20.  
 Considering the above factors, GOI deliberated multiple alternate divestment options 
and decided that instead of pre-fixing debt level at EOI stage – bidders may be asked 
to quote combined debt + equity value (Enterprise Value) to GOI in their financial 
bid.  
 This Enterprise Value (EV) approach allowed for market price discovery based on 
real time assumptions at time of financial bid submission allowing for a better price 
discovery process which was not anchored to a “debt level” fixed at the time of EOI 
submission, which was almost – months earlier than the financial bid submission date. 
EV approach had also been suggested by some potential investors (written query 
received post PIM issuance but declined prior to commencement of COVID) and the 
same is also inter-alia used in a lot of private sector transactions. 
 It was considered that EV approach may expand the universe of bidders resulting in a 
more competitive bidding process and by extension may further result in better value 
realisation for GOI, on account of the following: 
i. All interested bidders (conservative as well as aggressive) may be able to submit bids, 
as each bidder would be free to work out the total EV which it was willing to service 
post privatisation; 
ii. Since there is no pre-determined debt level, no bidder would be dissuaded from 
submitting bids in case his bid was lower than the pre-determined debt level at the 
time of EOI. 

55 
 
iii. It would prevent a situation where the debt level determined at the time of the EOI, 
became a de-facto floor for the EV. 
iv. For GOI also, since Reserve Price is determined close to actual bid submission, GOI 
Reserve price will also better reflect the situation at the time of financial bid. GOI‟s 
interest continued to be protected as only that bidder would be selected as the 
successful bidder, whose bid is better than the Reserve Price.

Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) Services 
Recommendation/Observation 
14. The Committee notes that India is predicted to be a front runner among nations so far 
as Global Annual MRO demand, with an Annual Growth rate of 9.10% for the period 2021 -
2031. The Committee notes that MRO demand in India is also anticipated to grow at a much 
faster rate than the rest of the world, thereby entailing attractive investment opportunities for 
domestic as well as foreign investors, OEMs and leading MROs across the world. Therefore, 
the Ministry should avail the opp ortunity and make all out efforts to ensure various domestic 
and foreign investors invest in the MRO sector in India by way of alliance and collaboration 
and make detailed plans accordingly. The aforementioned statistics substantially validate the 
potential of India to become a significant regional MRO hub and gradually strive to establish 
its foothold in the global MRO supply chain. Further, rising demand, as shown in graphical 
predictions for the next decade, makes the Indian MRO industry an ideal destina tion for 
strategic investors, Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and global MRO players. 
 (Para 113) 
15.      The Committee commends the policy initiatives such as the MRO Policy 2021, 
National Civil Aviation Policy 2016, and fiscal policies such as r ationalisation of GST, 
removal of Gross Turnover Tax (GTO), etc. which reflect the vision of the Government to 
develop India as a global MRO hub. The Committee appreciates that a French company, 
Safran, has announced its intention to set up an MRO at Hyder abad, after 100% FDI was 
permitted, which implies that the change in policies are showing positive results. The 
Committee is of the view that the growth of the MRO sector will also depend on how 
efficiently it can address and remove the key challenges face d by MRO players in India. The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry will make all out efforts to implement the various fiscal 
measures at the ground level and also ensure proactive interaction with MRO industry to 
remove any bottlenecks that may arise. Since MRO services constitute 12% to 15% of overall 
expenditure of any airlines operator, setting up MRO services in the country would reduce 
the expenditure on MRO services and subsequently reduce the airfares in the domestic 
routes, which will consequently reduce the cost of air travel and benefit the passengers. 
 (Para 114) 
 

61 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1    Government seeks to facilitate setting up of aircraft MRO services in India through 
various policy, regulatory and other incentives and the Government has tak en various 
measures to create a conducive environment for the development of Aircraft Maintenance, 
Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services. 
15.2    With a view to incentivise the growth of MROs in the country and also contribute to 
the ease of doing business, M oCA has brought out the new MRO Guidelines in Sept. 2021. 
Salient features of the guidelines are as follows: 
a. Concession fee, in any manifestation including royalty, shall not be leviable on new/ 
renewal of existing contracts. 
b. Selection of agency and procedures for allotment of land/ space under rationalized 
land/ space rental for new MRO contracts and renewal of existing MRO contracts, 
shall be through e-tender by AAI. 
c. The renewal of the existing land leases/ space license of MRO service providers/ 
Aircraft Maintenance Organizations (AMOs) shall be on the basis of bidding wherein 
Right of First Refusal (RoFR) shall be given to the existing lessee/ licensee to match 
the first rank bid in terms of the Selection criteria provided its bid is within 15% of 
the most competitive bid received. 
d. The quoted/ accepted lease fee shall be escalated @15% after every 3rd year. 
e. The maximum period of contract, new or renewal, for allotment of land/ space shall 
be 30 years from the date of handing over of site. 
15.3    The other key measures taken by the Government to incentivise MROs in the country 
are:  
i. GST on MRO has been reduced from 18% to 5% with full Input Tax Credit from 1st 
April, 2020. 
ii. Transactions sub -contracted by foreign original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) / 
MRO to domestic MRO are treated as 'exports' with zero -rated GST from 1st April, 
2020 
iii. Exempted Customs Duty on tools and tool kits 
iv. Reduced Goods and Services Tax rates on various spare parts, accessories, and 
consumables 
v. Simplified clearance processing of parts 
vi. Relaxed restriction on utilization of duty-free parts from one year to three years 
vii. Extended stay in India of foreign aircraft for entire duration of MRO work or 6 
months, whichever is lesser 
viii. Revised the Notification to enable export of serviceable parts 
ix. 100% Foreign Direct Investment permitted via automatic route for MRO 
x. Liberalized policy for borrowing and lending in Foreign Currency and Rupees on 
competitive terms for MROs 

62 
 
xi. Modalities prescribed for concessional temporary imports of spare parts by  foreign 
airlines for repair of their aircraft in transit. 
15.4    As on date there are 150 (Operator + Standalone) AMOs/ MROs approved in India for 
Line/ Base maintenance. Since July, 2021, twenty seven (27) new AMO/ MROs have been 
approved by DGCA.  
15.5    Several rounds of discussions were held with the representatives of Safran at various 
levels regarding the proposed MRO facilities in India. Safran has evinced keen interest in 
making investment in MRO space and has committed to invest USD 150 million for setting 
up an aircraft engine MRO at Hyderabad. Further, HAL has aligned itself to achieve 
objectives of MoCA to make India a Global MRO hub. Various MRO services are planned at 
HAL Nasik for narrow body and general aviation aircraft.   In this regard H AL is 
collaborating with OEMs as well as Global MRO players. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation

Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) Services in the country. The Committee

facilities but Airports like Pasighat being very small and caterin g to smaller aircrafts and 
hence based on the requirement, ILS/IFR are not required and operated under Visual Flight 
Rule (VFR). 
21.5    Expansion and upgradation of airports is a continuous process which is done 
depending on various factors such as demand , availability of land, commercial viability, 
socio-economic considerations and traffic demand. Ministry of Civil Aviation is continuously 
monitoring the performance of the operational airports at the highest levels .Besides these 
projects are regularly monitored at various fora. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
21.6    The Committee is dismayed to note that the status of the Gondia Airport, an 
airport under the RCS , was changed from Scheduled Operations to Non -Scheduled 
Operations, within a year after it was operationalized. The Committee would like to 
know the reasons as to why the services were withdrawn by the Selected Airline 
Operator (SAO). The Committee, there fore, recommends that the Ministry should 
devise a policy and put in place a mechanism to maintain supervision and monitoring of 
the SAOs, as such unilateral withdrawal action  hampers the overall Civil Aviation 
operations resulting in losses and inconvenience to the public. 
  
21.7    The Committee also notes the Ministry’s reply regarding the installation of 
advanced landing systems like Instrument Landing System (ILS) and Night Landing 
facilities at various airports in the Country. The Committee, therefore , reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the Ministry should prioritize installation of latest landing 
systems at all the existing airports as well as the upcoming ones, so that the aircraft s are 
able to land/ takeoff at night and during adverse weathe r conditions, obviating the 
possibility of any risk of any untoward event.  
  
 

70 
 
Trans-Shipment Hubs 
 Recommendation/Observation 
22.      The Committee is of the opinion that given India's strategic geographical location 
between Europe and Southeast Asia, it  has the potential to become a leading air cargo 
transhipment hub. The National Civil Aviation Policy, 2016 also envisages un -tapping this 
trans-shipment opportunity and also proposes setting up of Free Trade and Warehousing 
Zones to facilitate trans -shipment cargo. The Committee notes that after the SEZ Act, 2005, 
only 8 FTWZs have been set up and out of these, 4 are non -operational. The Committee notes 
the low number of FTWZs set up since the Act was enacted in 2005 and desires to know the 
reasons for the obstacles and the steps taken by the Ministry to remove the bottlenecks. 
 (Para 185) 
Reply of the Ministry 
22.1   The Department of Commerce has informed that SEZs/ FTWZs being set up under the 
SEZ Act, 2005 and SEZ Rules, 2006 are primarily driven by private investment. No funds are 
sanctioned by the Central Government for setting up of SEZ and the infrastructure facilities 
of the SEZs are normally provided by the Developer/ Co-developer. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
22.2    The Committee is not satisfied with the reply given by the Ministry and urges the 
Ministry to exploit India’s strategic geographical location between Europe and 
Southeast Asia, which has the potential of becoming a leading air cargo trans  shipment 
hub. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to make concentrated efforts 
to augment Government interface to boost air cargo in the country instead of passing 
the buck to the private investor.    
 
Use of GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN) 
Recommendation/Observation 
23.      The Committee further notes that the Ministry has successfully tested GAGAN based 
approach procedures at the Kishangarh Airport, Rajasthan on 28th April, 2022. The 
Committee notes that NCAP, 2016 mandatorily prescribes that new aircrafts registered in 
India will have GAGAN onboard. But, it also notes that the major challenge for GAGAN is 
that the design changes required to be made in the aircraft has to be approved by the 
concerned regulator of that country, before importing the aircraft in India for regist ration. 
The Committee feels that this issue is a major obstacle to the complete implementation of 
GAGAN, as all the aircraft are presently imported. The Committee recommends that 
proactive steps may be taken by the Ministry to approach the foreign aircraft  manufacturer 
and the regulator to resolve this issue. 
 (Para 197) 

71 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
23.1    Following regulations are currently in place in the design certification regulatory 
mechanism for installation of Global positioning system Aided Geostationary  earth orbit 
Augmented Navigation (GAGAN) enabled GPS receivers: 
 As State of Registry (SoR), Recognition of Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) 
under the Rule 49G of the Aircraft Rules 1937. 
 As State of Design (SoD). Modification of change to the Type Cert ificate/Restricted 
Type Certificate under Subpart D of the CAR 21. 
23.2    Further, it is submitted that in the recent past, AED -DGCA type accepted FAA STC 
ST04436AT dated 13th December, 2018 vide IN23ASA035 dated 24 th March, 2023 to install 
Rockwell Colli ns GLU -2100 Multi -Mode Receiver (MM) for Boeing B737 -800 aircraft 
model to make the aircraft GAGAN enabled. The aircraft has been imported by M/s. Bluedart 
Aviation Limited for their operation. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
23.3    The Committee notes the reply and urges the Ministry to take corrective steps to 
ensure that all the operating aircrafts in the Country are GAGAN compliant. The 
Committee, further recommends that the Ministry should urge all aircraft 
manufacturers to provide for built in system to comply with GAGAN requirement and 
also disseminate the benefits of the GAGAN features to all the stakeholders.

Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee opines that there are various capacity constraints at the existing 
airports/ terminals. For instance, a fourth runway (29 ‘right’) at Terminal -1 of the Indira 
Gandhi International Airport, Delhi has not been operationalised due to some administrative 
reasons. The delay in operationalization of this runway is hampering the capacity of a 
critical airport as flights are being delayed affecting the operational cost of airl ines. The 
Committee recommends that this 4th runway (29 ‘right’) at the Delhi airport should be 
operationalised at the earliest and an Action Taken Report may be furnished to the 
Committee. The Committee would also like to know the details regarding the ai rcrafts of 
old/discontinued/non-operational airlines which are parked in the hangars/ on the runways 
of various airports. The details regarding the parking fee being charged by the respective 
airport operators and plans to remove these aircraft, may also be furnished. 
 (Para 161)

1.1       The 4th runway in Delhi (RWY11L/29R) has not been operational on account of the 
following:

(STAR): The DGCA approval  for the publication of AIP Supplement for 
commissioning 4th runway at Delhi Airport was received on 22nd May 2023 and the 
draft AIP Supplement was prepared by AAI and shared with DIAL for vetting of 
contents and comments on the draft.  The response was re ceived from DIAL on 24th 
May 2023. The AIP Supplements will be issued by 30th June2023 and will be 
effective from date 13th July 2023.

shipment problems from Russia n ports. ILS equipment has now reached the site on 
13th May 2023 and ILS installation is in process, flight calibration is planned on 6-7th 
June 2023.   
iv. AAI RED Building was one of the obstacles in operationalization of Runway 29, 
requiring lowering of its height, which has been completed recently.

CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
  
Regional Connectivity Scheme – UdeDeshkaAamNagrik (RCS-UDAN) 
The Committee notes the details of the 13 bids received and 04 routes awarded under 
the International Air Connectivity Scheme (IACS) – UDAN 4.0. The Committee  
appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry to boost air connectivity to international 
destinations, especially from the North-East Region. The Committee would like to know 
the status of the remaining nine bids and by when these routes would be awarded to  the 
Airline Operators. The Committee may also be apprised of the Ministry’s plans to 
initiate more bidding rounds under the Scheme, to enhance international air 
connectivity.      
(Para 1.5)  
  
The Committee notes that Regional Connectivity Scheme – Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik 
(RCS-UDAN) is the flagship Scheme of the Ministry of Civil Aviation with an aim to 
make air travel affordable and widespread. The Committee observes that the number of 
passengers availed this Scheme has reduced in 2022 -23 and only 20,26,8 00 passengers 
benefited till December, 2022. The Committee notes some of the contributory reasons 
for this scenario which include, among others, the delay in attaining scheduled 
commuter operators permit by the Airlines, non -availability of suitable aircra ft and 
leasing issues, The Committee recommends that before awarding the routes, all such 
issues, having potential to undermine the strength and efficacy of the scheme, may be 
looked into and appropriately resolved.  
(Para 2.3)  
 
The Committee observes that Kannur is a major international airport in the State of 
Kerala which became operational in 2018, however, till date, it does not have many 
flights operating from the airport. The Committee also notes that out of a total 32 
awarded routes under the UDAN Scheme connecting Kerala, 8 were cancelled and 6 are 
yet to commence. The Committee would like to know the reasons for cancellation/ non -
operationalization of these routes.    
(Para 3.7)  
 
 

75 
 
Further, the Committee notes that RCS flights on various sectors  were discontinued by 
the Selected Airline Operators (SAOs) after completion of 3 years tenure. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should look into the possibility of extending 
the stipulated tenure of contracts with the SAOs, to ensure that the fl ight operations are 
not affected and can continue without any interruption.  
(Para 3.8)  
NER Schemes: Providing Air Connectivity and Aviation Infrastructure in NER 
The Committee notes that to boost the air connectivity in the North -Eastern Region 
(NER), the Ministry has identified 13 Airports, 21 Heliports and 2 Water Aerodromes 
in the region. However, out of 13, only 10 Airports are operational as on date, whereas 
none of the identified Heliports and Water Aerodromes has been operationalized as yet. 
The Committee would like to be briefed about the reasons for non operationalization of 
remaining Airports, Heliports and Water Aerodromes and the expected timeline by 
when these will be made functional.  
(Para 4.6)  
The Committee also observes that as per the details provided by the Ministry, 142 RCS 
routes have been awarded in the NER. However, out of these, only 56 are operational 
and 16 have been cancelled. Further, the number of routes operationalised in other 
areas as compared to the awarded routes in NER,  are really low wherein only 38% and 
50% of the total awarded routes have been operationalised in Uttarakhand (Hilly area) 
and Himachal Pradesh (Hilly area), respectively. The Committee also notes that none of 
the RCS routes has been operationalised in Lak shadweep and Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands. The Committee would like to know the reasons for the non - operationalization 
of routes in all these areas which have immense tourism potential and urges the 
Ministry to take up the issues of air connectivity under RC S scheme to these areas with 
priority.     
(Para 4.7)  
Krishi Udaan Scheme 
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that Krishi Udaan is a convergence 
Scheme wherein various Ministries/ Departments, leverage their existing schemes to 
strengthen the lo gistics for transportation of Agri -produce, and hence, no specific 
budget allocation is made under Krishi Udaan Scheme, except a token provision. The 
Committee would like to know the plans of the Ministry of Civil Aviation in this regard 
and whether the Mi nistry is going to successfully implement the scheme only by way of 
token allocation. A list of 58 airports, covered under the Scheme, may also be provided 
to the Committee with the justification of their selection.   
(Para 5.6)

years and that the Ministry of Finance provided financial assistance amounting to Rs. 
64,026.40/- crore in the form of equity to Air India Assets Holding Lim ited (AIAHL). 
The Committee may be apprised of the details of the amount which has been invested 
by the Government of India in Air India over the years, since its Nationalization in 1953 
till the date of its strategic disinvestment.   
(Para 6.5)  
Disinvestment of Air India 
The Committee notes that Enterprise Valuation method was adopted for inviting bids 
for disinvestment of Air India which afforded the prospective bidders an opportunity to 
resize the balance sheet. The Committee would like to know as to ho w the enterprise 
valuation of Rs. 18,000/ - crore was arrived at. Further, the Committee may also be 
apprised of the assets of Air India including office buildings and whether all the assets 
were taken into consideration for valuation.   
(Para 7.7)  
The Com mittee notes the reply of the Ministry regarding the disinvestment of four 
subsidiaries of Air India (AI) viz., Alliance Air Aviation Limited (AAAL); AI Airport 
Services Limited (AIASL); AI Engineering Services Limited (AIESL); and Hotel 
Corporation of Ind ia Limited (HCI). The Committee would like to know the details of 
the disinvestment plans of these subsidiaries and the mechanisms put in place by the 
Ministry to oversee the disinvestment process in a time bound manner.  
(Para 8.3)  
Post Disinvestment Scenario 
The Committee commends the Ministry for taking considerate measures for providing 
medical facilities to the employees of Air India, especially the retired employees. The 
Committee would like to know the status of implementation of the pan India IPD 
facility for the AI retired employees.  
(Para 9.4)  
The Committee notes that an amount of Rs. 1,327.02 crore was provided to Air India by 
AIAHL for making payments of arrears to employees, based on the recommendations 
of Justice Dharmadhikari Committee. The Commi ttee would like to know the status of 
arrear payment and whether the entire liability has been paid off.    
(Para 9.5)

The Committee notes that the Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) 
produced a meagre 85 Commercial Pilot Licenses (CPLs) in financial year 2022 -23 as 
compares to pre covid pandemic years. The Committee would like to know the target 
the Ministry has set for the year 2023 -24. The Committee also notes that one of the 

77

IGRUA from 20 in financial year 2019 -20 to 15 in financial year 2022 -23, as a result of 
completion of their service life or total loss of aircraft in an accident. The Committee 
would like to know the action plan of the Ministry to procure more trainer aircrafts so 
that the number of commercial pilot licenses could be increased, making available 
adequate trained commercial pilots to the Airline operators. 
(Para 11.5)  
Surge in Air Fares and Rationalisation 
The Committee notes the significant variation between the demand placed and budget 
allocated for the Rajiv Gandhi National Aviation University (RGNAU) for  2023-24 
wherein an amount of only Rs. 7.00 crores was allocated which is merely 42% of the 
demand. The Committee feels that such a significant reduction in allocation may 
adversely impact the operations of the National University especially affecting the 
quality of the manpower produced by them. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry may reconsider the allocation for BE 2023 -24 and supplement the 
financial requirements of the RGNAU at the RE stage.

Brief note on GAGAN
(GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation)
GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN)is an Indian Satellite Based navigation
program, developed jointly by Airports Authority of India and Indian Space Research
Organization.
 ISRO provides Space Segment which includes 3 GEO Stationary Satellites.
 AAI provides all ground infrastructure and is responsible for Operation &
Maintenance of GAGAN system
Global Positioning System (GPS) alone does not meet the civil aviation requirements of
accuracy, integrity and availability. GAGAN enhances GPS Performance by providing better
horizontal and vertical accuracy, along with integrity information.
The ground segment of GAGAN architecture comprises of following components:
1. Indian Reference Stations (INRES): These are set of 15 reference stations strategically
located at precise locations within India to provide coverage over the required service
volume. INRES track all the GPS satellites and SBAS GEO in view and forward the
measurement data to Master control centre for further processing.
2. Indian Master Control Centres (INMCC):Master control centres use the real-time
measurement data from all the reference stations (INRES) and their precise known
positions to generate the correction and integrity messages for the designated service
volume. GAGAN consists of 3 INMCCs (Two INMCC at Bengaluru and one INMCC at
Delhi).
3. Indian Uplink Stations (INLUS): INLUS receives correction messages from the INMCC,
formats the messages for GPS compatibility and transmit them to GEO satellites.
GAGAN consists of 3 INLUS (Two INLUS at Bengaluru and one INLUS at Delhi).
The space segment of GAGAN comprises of three Indian GEO satellites (GSAT-8, GSAT-10 &
GSAT-15) with PRN codes 127, 128 &132 respectively. GAGAN system monitors the GPS
satellites & broadcast the correction messages to GPS signal through three Indian GEO
satellites and hence improves the accuracy and integrity compared to standalone GPS.
GAGAN was certified by Directorate General of Civil Aviation, India (DGCA) for operations of
RNP 0.1 services (enroute operations) in the year 2013 and for APV I services (approach
operations) in the year 2015. GAGAN can support operations for all phases of flight including
Oceanic, Approach, Terminal, Surface. Since May 2015, GAGAN Signal-In-Space is available.
National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP-2016) prescribes that new aircrafts being registered in
India from 1st January 2019 will mandatorily have GAGAN enabled GPS receivers onboard.
Accordingly,DGCA issued a public notice stating that “All aircraft being registered in India
from 1st January 2019 will mandatorily have to be GAGAN enabled.” (subsequently revised
to 1st July 2021).

B.E. 2023-24: Salient features and Projected Demand vs. Allocation 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that the Ministry has been awarded 85 per cent of its projected 
demand for BE 2023-24. The shortfall in demand versus allocation has increased from 11 per 
cent at BE stage in 2022 -23 to 15 per cent  in 2023 -24. Moreover, the allocation made to 
various Central Sector Schemes is much lower vis -à-vis the demand of the Ministry. This 
includes allocations under Support to Akademies (63.9% of demand), Support to Museums 
(76.1%), Support to Libraries (70%) and Buddhist Tibetan Institutions and Memorials 
(62.8%). These heads support the expenditure of various a utonomous bodies such as Sangeet 
Natak Akademi, Indian Museum (Kolkata), Delhi Public Library, Central Institute of 
Buddhist Studies. The Committee desires to be apprised of the broad impact of the shortfall on 
the activities of the various autonomous bodies under these heads. 
(Para 13) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The Ministry has been allocated Rs. 3399.65 crore for FY 2023 -24. In light of the deficit 
in the approved budget allocation for the fiscal year 2023-24 and after examining the expenditure 
pattern of the fiscal year 2022 -23, the ministry ensured an efficient allocation of funds among 
different sectors. Allocation under Other Central expenditure has seen a shortfall of Rs 435 crore 
when compared to the projected demand for FY 2023 -24. However, there i s an augmentation of 
Rs.93.19 Cr to the Ministry's 33 Autonomous Bodies as compared to FY 2022 -23. Adequate 
provisions are being made for the regular activities as well as some of the stand alone projects 
planned to be funded though this sector. It is anti cipated that deficiency in funds would be 
adequately addressed by MoF through an advance from contingency fund of India/at 
supplementary stage/ at Revised Estimate stage of FY 2023-24. 

4 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
      
2. The allocation of Rs. 3399 crore for BE 2023-24 is 13 per cent higher than BE 2022-23 
and 1 per cent higher than RE 2022 -23. However, the Committee notes that the increase of 1 
per cent  as compared to RE 2022 -23 is not sufficient to cover the impact of inflation. The 
spending power of the Ministry will actually decrease in 2023- 24. 
(Para 15) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
 
2.1 There was a significant increase in the Revised Estimate (RE) for the fiscal year 2022 -23

requirement under these projects have been considerabily reduced  and hence the augmented

ministry. However, if required,  the Ministry would request for enhancement of funds at RE 
2023-24 stage.    
Recommendation/Observation

of the Ministry. The budget of the Ministry has increased from ₹2169 crore in 2015-16 to ₹

Government in this period has risen from ₹17.77 lakh crore to ₹45.03 lakh crore, an increase

I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do

A. INTRODUCTION 
1. Niche tourism is a specialised segment of the tourism market, where specific tourism 
products are tailored to meet the needs of a particular section/market segment.  As opposed to 
the more conventional mass tourism which is characterised by large numbers of tourists 
visiting popular holiday destinations  on standardised tour packages, niche tourism caters to 
small groups of people sharing the same, often uncommon interests, and provides curated and 
personalised tour packages to appeal to  the customers‟ interests.  While mass tourism is 
homogenous in nature with a standardised product for a large market segment , niche tourism 
is defined by its heterogeneous nature with unique products/services meant for small market 
segments.   
2. Niche Tourism is an all encompassing  term covering a wide range of special ised 
tourism products like cultural, medical, rural, adventure, wi ldlife, historical, gastronomic  
tourism, etc. These niches offer travellers the right avenues to immerse themselves in 
particular aspects that align with their innate passions.  Once considered expensive and elitist, 
niche tourism is now gaining popularity and is one of the fastest growing sectors in tourism. 
The growing popularity of niche tourism  can be largely attributed to ch anges in consumer 
behaviour as an increasing number of tourists seek immersive and more fulfilling travel 
experiences, the effect of Covid-19 pandemic which changed the preferences of the travelling 
public, the rise in awareness of sustainable tourism and such other factors.   
3. India has great potential for niche tourism being b lessed with diverse geography  
from mountains and forests to deserts and beaches, rich tangible and intangible culture with 
majestic palaces, forts and historical monuments, rich traditions of music and dance , yoga 
and Ayurveda. Modern India also showcases world class medical facilities and resources for 
conventions, meetings and exhibitions for the corporate world. In short, India offers a wide 
range of all-year-round tourism options with tourism products for all reasons and seasons and 
something for every kind of tourist. These undeniable advantages notwithstanding, both mass 
tourism and niche tourism have still vast unrealised potential.  Meanwhile, Thailand is poised 
to become the top golf destin ation in the world ; Nepal has a thriving mountain tourism ; and 
Bhutan has a successful Sustainable Tourism Strategy.  India is a land of spirituality being the 
birthplace and home  of se veral major religions. Despite being a land of immense spiritual 
significance, the full potential of Spiritual Tourism is yet to be realised in India.  
4. The Committee decided to examine the reasons why India has not been able to fully 
tap its potential for mass tourism and niche tourism when even its much smaller neighbo urs 
have successfully done so. The Committee also decided to study the impact of the Thematic 
Circuits launched under the Swadesh Darshan 1.0 , the PRASHAD Scheme on Spiritual 
Tourism and the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 with its emphasis on  destination tourism. Since ease 
of obtaining v isas is a major factor impacting  foreign tourist arrivals, t he Committee also 
heard the representatives of the  MEA on the subject of issuance  of visas and promotion of

Indian Tourism abroad as the Indian Missions have the sole charge of promoting India abroad 
after the closure of the Overseas Tourist Offices of the Ministry of Tourism.

1. SUSTAINABLE TOURISM  
13. Sustainable Tourism is tourism that takes full account of its current and future 
economic, social and environmental impacts, and addresses the needs of visitors, the industry, 
and the  environment and host communities. The three basic principles of Sustainable 
Tourism are :- 
 Environmental Sustainability – Making optimal use of environmental resources and 
helping to conserve natural heritage and bio-diversity. 
 Socio-cultural Sustainability – Respecting the socio -cultural authenticity of host 
communities and conserving their built and living cultural heritage and traditional 
values. 
 Economic Sustainability – Ensuring viable, long -term economic operations, stable 
employment and social services to host communities and contributing to poverty 
alleviation.  
14. The Committee was informed that a  National Board for Sustainable Tourism and 
Eco-Tourism has been constituted under the Chairpersonship of  Secretary (Tourism) on 30 th 
June, 2022, comprising representatives from identified Central Ministries/organisations; State 
Governments/ UT Administrations and Industry Stakeholders. The Board shall guide the 

4 
 
operationalisation and implementation of various strategic initiatives as detailed below for 
development of sustainable tourism and eco-tourism in the country: 
(i) Detailed action plans and formulation of dedicated schemes  
(ii) Certification Schemes 
(iii) Capacity building, replication of national and global best practices  
(iv) Marketing and promotion 
(v) Private Sector Participation 
(vi) Destination and Product Development  
(vii) Specific strategies for sustainable and ecotourism 
(viii) Any other measures for growth of sustainable and ecotourism 
 
15. Three meetings of the Board have been organised till date. 
16. The Ministry apprised the Committee that sustainable tourism is not one part icular 
aspect of tourism but it  informs all segments of tourism, on how to make tourism more 
sustainable and responsible.  Since the formulation of the strategy, education and awareness 
have been the first course of action for which a National Summit and five regional workshops 
have been held.   The Travel for Li FE programme takes it to the next dimension of 
participation of the citizens or the tourist in promoting sustainable tourism.   
17. The Travel for LiFE Initiative  has been formulated on the philosophy of Mission 
Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE) which is a global mass movement against clim ate change 
led by Hon'ble Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi. The programme was launched during the 
third Tourism Working Group (TWG) meeting held in Srinagar, Jammu &  Kashmir. Travel 
for LiFE aims to promote sustainable tourism in the country in convergence with the National 
Strategy for Sustainable Tourism, through mindful and deliberate actions mobili sed toward 
tourists and tourism businesses in the consumption of tourism resources.

destinations and Responsible Traveller Campaign in association with Responsible

5

19. The Committee notes that India has be en ranked at 139, 134, and 128 in the 
years 2015, 2017 and 2019 , respectively  under Environmental Sustainability in  the 
World Travel and Tourism Competitiveness Ranking . While the new National Strategy 
and National Board for Sustainable Tourism have come into force in 2022, the Ministry 
had been promoting Sustainable Tourism in India for  nearly a decade after the launch 
of Sustainable To urism Criteria for India in 2014 . Not much progress has , however, 
been made in development of Sustainable Tourism in the last decade as substantiated by 
India‟s low rankings in this category . The Committee emphasizes that economic 
development should not be at the cost of the environment and recommends that the 
Ministry may ensure that the revised Sustainable Tourism Criteria  be scrupulously 

6 
 
implemented to minimize the adverse impact of tourism on the environment. While a 
Certification programme for tourism stakeholders, who have successfully implemented 
sustainable criteria, has been in existence for nearly a decade, only one Certification has 
been effected till date. The Committee desires to know the number of hotels surveyed 
for the Certification Programme and the strategy adopted for the survey. The 
Committee observes that while disbursement of monthly newsletters to stakeholders 
and workshops are useful for dissemination of information, the feedback from 
stakeholders like hoteliers and tour operators is equally important to comprehend the 
problems being faced while  implementing policies on the g round level. The Committee 
feels that the pace of the Ministry in promotion of sustainability in tourism is sluggish 
and recommends that the Ministry may step up its coordination efforts with both the 
stakeholders and the other Central Ministries for effective promotional campaigns.   
 
20. The Committee desires to know about the action taken on formulation of 
dedicated schemes, destination, and product development and other initiatives taken by 
the National Board for Promotion of Sustainable Tourism.     
 
2. RURAL TOURISM 
21. Rural Tourism is any form of tourism that showcases the rural life, art, culture, and 
heritage at rural locations, thereby benefiting the local community economically and socially as 
well as enabling interaction between the tourists and the locals for a mor e enriching tourism 
experience. 
22. The Committee was informed that a  Task Force for Development of Rural Tourism 
has been constituted  under the Chairpersonship of Secretary (Tourism) on 30 th June, 2022, 
comprising representatives from  identified Central Ministries/ organisations, State 
Governments/UT Administrations and Industry Stakeholders. The Task Force shall review 
progress on the implementation of the Strategy and coordinate action with all the 
stakeholders covering: 
 
(i) Preparation of detailed Action Plan for implementation of the Strategy for Rural 
Tourism and Rural Home stays 
(ii) Identifying national and global best practice and preparation of tool kits for their 
replication by the States and Rural Tourism Destinations  
(iii) Benchmarking State policies and standards and prepare model policies and minimum 
standards for rural tourism including B&B, Farm Stays, Home stays etc. 
(iv) Capacity Building measures including setting up of Resource Centres and Centres of 
Excellence  

7 
 
(v) Toolkits and guidelines for identification of clusters for rural tourism and preparation 
of development plans for the cluster, destination and product development  
(vi) Facilitating adoption of digital technologies for rural tourism 
(vii) Formulation of dedicated scheme to suppo rt development of rural tourism in the 
Country 
(viii) Private Sector Participation 
(ix) Any other measure, which can facilitate development of rural tourism in the Country. 
 
23. Two meetings of the Task Force have been organised till date.

8 
 
the Cluster Harshil – Bagori – Mukhwa – Dharali shall be undertaken. Also, the Ministry

25. The Committee is at a loss to note that the 2022 list of the United Nations World 
Tourism Organisation (UNWTO) featuring the 32 best tourism villages from 22 
countries,  does not contain a single village from India while several countries have two 
villages in the list, and Spain having even three villages. The Committee desires to be 
informed about the number of Indian villages which were nominated for the selection 
by the UNWTO.  The Committee notes that Khonoma in Nagaland has been selected for 
the “Upgrade” programme which would enable the village to receive the necessary 
support from the UNWTO to improve its conditions to meet the selection criteria.  The 
Committee wishes to know the e fforts being taken for the development of Khonoma 
after its inclusion in the upgrade list  of the UNWTO .  The Committee also desires to 
know as to how many Indian villages have so far been selected by the UNWTO in its 
best tourism villages list and the impact of such selection on the village tourism.  
26. The Committee observes that in a predominantly agrarian and rural economy 
like India, rural tourism has immense potential for boosting employment and income 
for villagers while offering opportunities to the city dwellers to take a break from the 
hectic pace of urban life to experience nature and local culture at a much slower pace. 
India is home to a diverse range of unique villages, each with its own cultural, 
architectural and historical significance. Unique villages such as „Mattur‟ in Karnataka 
where all the residents speak only Sanskrit and many others offer a glimpse into India‟s 
rich traditions and culture. The Committee, however, observes that the Rural Tourism 
website doe s not provide details as to how to travel to the unique villages nor details 
regarding rural homestays for most of the villages. Even the Khonoma village page does 
not provide any useful details for the tourists. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may ensure that the Rural Tourism website has all details of rural homestays, 
travel connectivity and tourist  spots in respect of every village featured for the 
convenience of the tourists.   
27. The Committee while appreciating the Best Village Competition initiated by the 
Ministry, is dismayed to note that in the past one year, only one Model Rural Cluster 
has been identified, without any action being taken on the ground. The Committee notes 
that the villages to be covered in the Vibrant Villages programme are located in far -
flung areas, and close to borders, often in difficult terrains. The Committee feels that 
the State of Uttarakhand has a number of border villages with rich traditions and local 
culture and recommends that the Ministry may make concerted efforts to develop the 
Model Rural Cluster in Uttarakhand within a targeted time schedule.
