proposes to develop River Amba (NW -10), Dabhol creek -Vashishti River (NW -28) 
and River Revadanda Creek -Kundalika River (NW -85). All these 3 NWs has been 
classified as Class -A Waterways from the point of view of development and Class -
VII waterways based on navigational requirement. In this line IWAI has appointed a

Assistance to Ship Building, Research and Development 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. The Committee further notes that the shipbuilding industry has the same impact as 
infrastructure sectors due to higher multiplier effects on investment and turnover and high 
employment potential. The shipbuilding industry is a strategically important industry. To ensure 
the safety of our vast coastline, naval requirement of so phisticated and modern vessels is 
growing rapidly. Maritime Vision 2030 envisions Indian shipbuilding to become competitive with 
reaching the threshold on volumes by 2025 and then building the momentum in high volumes to 
reach “Make in India Make for World ” levels and be one of the top 10 shipbuilding nations in 
the world. The Financial Assistance to Ship Building was one of the initiatives made by the 
government in furtherance of this objective. However, the funds under this head have never been 
fully utilised. The Committee desires that the Ministry should look into the reasons why sufficient 
proposals for Assistance to Ship Building, Research and Development were not received and 
take remedial steps. 
 (Para 125) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 Reasons for low off-take of the allocated budget under the Policy:- 
(i) Presently the shipyards that are registered under the policy (except Cochin Shipyard), 
are medium or small-scale shipyards; are building small ships / boats only. Hence the 
subsidy provided under the policy is relatively less. 
(ii) Private shipyard like, ABG Shipyard, Bharti Shipyard and Reliance Naval and 
Engineering Limited, Pipavav, which existed during the starting period of Policy has 
gone under NCLT and still remains non -operational. On the other  hand, the bigger 
government-owned shipyards like Hindustan Shipyard Limited  (Visakhapatnam), 
Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited  (Mumbai), Garden Reach Shipbuilders & 
Engineers (Kolkata) and Goa Shipyard Ltd . (Goa) are predominantly engaged with 
naval projects only, which is not eligible for subsidy under SBFA Policy. The newest 
bigger facility like L&T Shipbuilding, Kattupalli (Chennai) is also engaged with the 
construction of defence orders only. It is to be noted that while the Policy was being 

26 
 
conceptualised during 2014 -2015, the output capacity from these bigger shipyards 
had been factored in. 
(iii) The above facts along with the limitation to the number of bigger shipyards to 
construct bigger size vessels is one of the main reasons, as to why none of th e Indian 
Shipyards have secured shipbuilding orders from main fleet commercial vessel 
owners for shipbuilding contracts for large ships. 
(iv) Further, in view of the low off -take under the policy; a periodic review of the 
Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy (SBFAP) shall be carried out, every two 
years, in line with the Guidelines of the Policy.  SBFAP is being reviewed in 
consultation with DGS and stakeholders. 
 
13.2 The DGS is implementing the „Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy 2016 -2026‟ 
which is rolled out by Ministry of Shipping, as per the guideline issued vide file no. Sy -
16023/6/2015-SBR dated 27.10.2017, as amended in April, 2022 and further amended in 
November, 2020. 
 
13.3 Under the SBFA policy, the Ministry is providing Financial Assist ance of 20% of 
contract price, actual receipts, fair price (whichever is least) to Indian shipyards for contracts 
signed between April 1, 2016 to March 31, 2026, including the said dates, to promote the Indian 
shipbuilding industry. Under the policy, the f inancial Assistance extended would be reduced by 
3% every three years . Detailed guidelines of the policy are available on the website of the 
Ministry and that of the Directorate General of Shipping. 
 
13.4 The entire process, starting from one -time registra tion of shipyard, making application 
for in -principle approval by shipyards, application for release of Financial Assistance, 
submission of documents and processing the approval by Competent Authority etc., are done 
online on the web portal developed for t his purpose (www.shipbuilding.nic.in). This web -portal 
eliminates physical transactions related to application, submission of documents, scrutiny, 
approval and sanction of the financial assistance.

Coastal Shipping and IWT  
Recommendation/Observation 
15. The Committee observes that India‟s long coastline and the number of ports on both the 
east and west coasts grants a perfectly natural system for the country to build up a substantial 
coastal shipping industry. However this mode of transportation is relatively  undeveloped in 
India. The Committee appreciates that steps are being taken to develop coastal shipping and 
RORO ferries. The Committee observes that the discount given earlier in 2016 for port charges 
over foreign-going vessels was 80%. The Committee desi res to know why it has been reduced to 
40%. 
 (Para 134) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 The Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP) vide order dated 25.10.2016 to all Major 
Ports to grant 80% discount on vessels related charges and cargo related charges for coastal 
transportation of vehicles through Ro -Ro ship for a period of two years with effect from 20 th 
September, 2016. Accordingly, the Major Ports were directed to amend the Scale of Rates 
accordingly. 
 
15.2 Further on the direction of the Ministry, TAMP issued Order dated 3.2.2020 to all major 
ports conveying that with a view to promote a modal shift of transportation of automobiles from 

28 
 
road to coastal shipping to offer concessions to Ro - Ro vessels and Container vessels for coastal 
transportation of automobiles for two years as given under:- 
(i) Coastal Ro -Ro vessels or coastal Container vessels engaged in coastal movement of 
automobiles: 
 80% concession on both vessels related charges and cargo related charges 
(ii) Coastal Ro-Ro vessels or coastal Container vessels carrying both Export Import (EXIM) 
and coastal cargo of automobiles: 
 Or 
 Coastal Container vessels carrying both EXIM cargo and coastal cargo of automobiles 
and EXIM cargo and/or coastal cargo other than automobiles: 
 80% concession on vessel related charges and similar concession on cargo related 
charges be given for coastal cargo units of automobiles only and existing schedule of 
rates/ discount be made applicable for other cargoes. 
 
15.3 The Major Port Authorities (MPA) Act, 2021 came into force on 3 rd November, 2021. In 
pursuance of the new Act, the new Tariff Policy for Major Ports was also circulated by the 
Ministry on 3rd November, 2021paragraph 8.3 of which states as follows:- 
“Concessional tariff will be prescribed for costal cargoes/ containers, as per the policy directions 
of the Government. It is prescribed that the cargo/ container related charges for all coastal cargo/ 
containers, other than thermal coal and POL including crude oil, iron ore and iron ore pellets 
should not exceed 60% of the normal cargo/ container related charges. In case of cargo related 
charges, the concession should be allowed on all the relevant cargo handling charges for ship -
shore transfer and transfer from/ to quay to/from storage yard including wharfage.” 
 
15.4 Thus, it may be seen that Government is continuing to offer concessions to promote 
coastal cargo.

Recommendation/Observation 
18. The Committee feels that since Port Development and Modernizations is highly capital 
intensive, efforts of both the Public and Private sector are the need of the hour. The Landlord 
Model of Port Development maximizes the efficiency of port operations. The Committee 
appreciates the other initiatives taken for port development. The Committee  however feels that 
the policy of Land Management needs to be reviewed extensively as in the revised policy in 2014, 
the revisions were restricted to certain issues only.

Recommendation/Observation 
19. The Committee observes that the Vadhavan port with its natural draft of 20m is expected 
to handle large container ships of 16,000 -25,000 TEUs. In comparison, JNPT presently the 
largest container handling major port has can handle only mid size container sh ips as it has a 
draft of 15 m whereas modern deep draft ports require a draft of 18 -20m. The Committee 
observes that the size of Container ships is increasing and it is very important to have a deep 
draft port to accommodate such ships. Moreover, Container  traffic in the JNPT is expected to 
grow from 4.5 MTEUs currently to 10.1 MTEUs by 2022 -25 when JNPT's potential will be fully 
exhausted. The Committee desires that the Ministry may make more efforts to develop the 

31 
 
Vadhavan Port rapidly as nearly two years  have passed since the in principle approval of the 
port. 
 (Para 163)

19.1 The Government of India has accorded in -principle approval for the development of a 
modern deep draft all -weather port at Vadhavan in Dahanu T aluka in Maharashtra on 5.2.2020. 
Port limit for the project has been notified on 19.2.2020. Vadhavan Port will be developed on the 
“landlord model”. JNPA has entered into a joint venture agreement with Maharashtra Maritime 
Board (MMB) and have established a limite d liability company registered under the Companies 
Act, 2013 namely Vadhavan Port Projects Ltd. (VPPL), with 74% and 26% equity stake 
respectively to execute the Vadhavan Port Project. The SPV will develop the port infrastructure 
including reclamation, and  construction of breakwater, besides establishing connectivity to the 
hinterland. All the business activities would be undertaken under PPP mode by private 
developers. 
 
19.2 Project is currently in the process of getting Environment Clearance (EC). Applica tion 
was made to Dahanu Taluka Environment Protection Authority (DTEPA) on 12 th May, 2022 for 
obtaining NOC as compliance to approved ToR (Terms of Reference) for Environmental 
Clearance. Last hearing was held on 13.02.2023. DTEPA Committee has allowed opponents to 
raise queries within 15 days and JNPA to reply thereon within next 15 days. DTEPA Committee 
members have visited site on 28 th March, 2023. DTEPA will be fixing up next date of hearing in 
the matter. The matter is also pending in Hon‟ble Suprem e Court and next hearing is on 
25.04.2023. After getting clearance from DTEPA, JNPA will apply for CRZ clearance.

Shipping Corporation of India  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee feels that a strategic asset like Shipping Corporation of India ( SCI) is 
critical not only to its blue economy policy but also to its maritime security. SCI is not only 
India‟s largest merchant cargo carrier, it has also diversified into the Indian offshore marine 
business and has gained expertise in manning and operating h ighly specialised vessels. The 
Committee feels that the policy of disinvesting profitable and Core sector PSUs of the 
Government is irrational. There is justification in disinvestments of unviable PSUs. But PSUs 
performing well especially in core sectors should not be sacrificed for short term financial gains. 
While acknowledging that disinvestments enable the Government to check fiscal deficits, the 
Committee feels that a balance should be maintained to protect national strategic interests. The 
Committee r ecommends that the Government may rethink its policy of disinvesting profitable 
PSUs especially in core sectors. 
 (Para 83) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 Going forward, the strategic disinvestment policy will be guided by the New Public 
Sector Enterprise (“PSE”) Policy for Atmanirbhar Bharat, issued with the approval of Cabinet, 
which has been notified on 4 th February, 2021. As per the policy , public sector commercial 
enterprises have been classified as strategic and non-strategic sectors The policy mandates that in 
broad strategic sectors, there will be only bare minimum presence of the public sector enterprises 
with the remaining Central Public Sector Enterprises ( CPSEs) to be either pri vatized or merged 
or subsidiarized with other CPSEs or closed. In non - strategic sectors, CPSEs will be privatized, 
or closed. The policy, however, does not apply to certain entities which are non -profit in nature; 
or which deal with vulnerable sections or have development/promotional role. 
 
6.2 The objectives of the strate gic disinvestment policy have been articulated by the Finance 
Minister in the Budget speech 2021-22 which are as under:- 
a. Minimizing presence of Central Government Public Sector Enterprises including 
financial institutions and creating new investment space for private sector. 
b. Post disinvestment, economic growth of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs)/ 
financial institutions will be through infusion of private capital, technology and best 
management practices will contribute to economic growth and new jobs. 
c. Disinvestment proceeds to finance various social sector and developmental programs of 
the Government.

Policy” including minimizing the presence of t he Central Government PSEs in strategic 
sectors to create new investment space for private sectors and reiterate its recommendation 
that the Government may consider retaining profitable and well performing PSUs, 
especially in core sector instead of disinvesting for short term financial gains.

instance, the Average Turnaround Time for all Ships has decreased only marginally from 52.80

only 10 hours Singapore has 32 lakh TEUs per month and its port capacity is 65 lakh. In India it

(Para 156) 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee observes that none of India‟s major ports have as yet been ranked among 
the top 20 ports in the world on any performance index. India scores low on the Liner shipping 
bilateral connectivity index which aims at capturing a country‟s integration level into global 
liner shipping networks. A country‟s access to world markets depends largely on its transport 
connectivity. The turnaround time of the Major Ports of India has increased but still lags much 
behind the top international ports. The Maritime India Vision 2030 aims to reduce dwell time 
and turnaround time to 40 hours and 20 hours respectively. The Committee asked the Ministry to 
give details about the plans for future growth in port performance to achieve the goals of 
Maritime India Vision 2030.

Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways have been focusing on interventions across 
infrastructure development, process simplification and digitization to reduce pre -berthing time, 
dwell time and vessel turnaround time and to achieve the target of Maritime India Vision 2030: 
 Development of Integrated Centralized Parking Zone for parking of tractor trailers will 
reduce delay of export shipments arriving from hinterland. 
 Widening of roads connecting port/ terminals coupled with strict traffic regulation will 
lead to zero congestion, thus effecting quick clearance. 
 Deepening of navigational channel will ensure acceptance of deeper drafted vessels and 
ease of navigation. 
 E-Marketplace Transport solution will enable optimum utilization of trailers thereby 
saving fuel and reducing pollution. 
 RFID Based Terminal Gate transaction: RFID based port entry of trucks will reduce truck 
processing time at terminal gates to minimize formation of queues in front of terminal 
gates. 
 E Delivery Orders - Documentation clearance will reduce significantly. 
 Mechanization of berths will reduce the cargo handling time and hence reduce the Turn 
Around Time (TRT). 
 Direct Port Delivery (DPD) – DPD service will eliminate the need for CFS storage for 
OOC documents.

 Direct Port Entry (DPE) – Let Export Order (LEO) are  being issued in Central Parking 
Plaza to increase the efficiency. 
 National Logistic Portal -Marine (NLP -M) will bring all stakeholders on one common 
platform for simplification of processes and procedures which will reduce the cost and 
time in cargo handling. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation

Vizhinjam Transhipment Hub  
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee however observes that the International Container Transhipment 
Terminal (ICTT) at Kochi which was supposed to handle 5.5 million containers per annum has 
not lived up to expectations of becoming a transshipment terminal as envisaged. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry may a nalyse the reasons behind this and ensure that the other 
transshipment hubs proposed do not suffer from the same handicaps and take remedial 
measures. 
(Para 182) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 Cochin Port was chosen by the Government of India to be the transshipment port for 
India as Cochin was the Indian Major Port closest to the international trunk routes. The ICTT 
was to be in its final phase, a 3.0 Million TEU terminal with berth length of 1800m and draft of 
14.5m capable of handling 8000 TEU ships. In the first phase, it was to be, a 1.0 Million TEU 
terminal with 14.5m draft. The Government of India has invested about ₹1,700 Crore in the 
infrastructure for ICTT (NH & Rail connectivity, and Capital Dredging), while the BOT operator 
(DP World) has invested about ₹1100 Crore. The ICTT commissioned in February 2011 had the 
throughput of 7.36 Lakh TEUs of containers in 2021 -22 of which 1.56 Lakh TEUs were 
Transshipment containers. 
 
12.2 The ICTT was planned to attract transshipment back to India away from foreign 
terminals like Colombo; the competition was therefore, as much in infrastructure provision and 
offering competitive user charges at ports, as it was in providing trade -friendly procedures.  
Cochin Port allows up to 90% rebate on notified Vessel Rela ted Charges (VRC) to the Mainline 
Container Vessel Services and rebates up to 50% on the notified VRC to Feeder Container 
Vessel Services to be competitive in port charges with respect to Colombo and the neighbouring 
Indian Ports, towards promoting ICTT as  a Transshipment Hub. The Mainline Services have the 
potential to reduce the dependence of Indian ports on Colombo for transshipment and thereby 

53 
 
reduce logistics cost for the Indian containers, contributing to the economic growth of the 
country. 
 
12.3 However, still there are several deterrents for ICTT when it comes to competing with 
Colombo. Lighthouse Dues, now, designated as Marine Aids to Navigation Dues, recovered in 
India by the Customs on foreign ships is one of them, dissuading Mainline and Transsh ipment 
container vessels from considering a call at ICTT. The prevailing dues at Indian Ports for 
container ships is ₹85 per TEU plus GST of 18%, as revised in August, 2022. Colombo also 
levies Light Dues on ships at $4 per 100 GT or part thereof, which co mes to only about 30% of 
that applicable at Indian Ports.  Cochin Port Authority has now submitted an expansion plan for 
ICTT for deepening the channel to 16.0m. 
 
12.4 As regards the transshipment capacity at ICTT, Cochin, DP World has already lined up 
an expansion project (capacity to increase to 2 million TEUs) in view of the deepening of the 
channel to 16m. As per the traffic projection given by them, it is expected that by 2030 the total 
transshipment from ICTT Cochin would be 287000 TEUs and 725,000 TEUs by 2043. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.5 The Committee while examining  the functioning of Major Ports  had recommended 
that the Ministry may find ways and means to reduce Lighthouse Dues (LHD) to lower the 
logistics costs. Vessel Related Charges  (VRC) can be reduced only by reducing the 
operating expense which is practically not feasible in most Major Ports. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation and urges the Ministry to act on it.

The Committee is pleased that the Ministry has utilised almost its entire allocation under 
various heads during FY 2022 -23. However, under the head Central Plan Scheme for 
North-Eastern Areas (Major Head 2552), the utilization percentage is a mere 49.14%. The 
Committee desires to know the reasons for such under -utilization under such a crucial 
budget head and recommends the Ministry to make all out efforts to ensure maximum 
utilization of funds in FY 2023-24 as well.      
(Para 2.8) 
The Committee does not find the reasons for savings of ₹28 lakh very convincing, as the 
expenditure under the Budgetary H ead of Establishment has been only about half of the 
actual budgetary allocation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
should make advance assessment of the actual budgetary requirements keeping in mind 
the practical/ realistic projects, at the time of B.E. itself. Better planning of funds will 
minimize the instances of unjustifiable savings.   
(Para 3.4) 

59 
 
 
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry as regards the monitoring of ongoing 
Sagarmala projects. However, the Ministry has not provided an updated status of ongoing 
projects under the Sagarmala Scheme. The Comm ittee, therefore, desires to be informed 
about the status of the ongoing Sagarmala projects including the actual allocation and 
utilization of budget; physical progress; and expected date of completion.    
(Para 4.5) 
Proposed Initiatives under Sagarmala in 2023-24  
The Ministry has not given any information on the current status of the project. The 
Committee desires to be informed as to whether the project is likely to be completed as per 
the schedule.  
(Para 5.3) 
Shipping Corporation of India  
The Committee notes the objectives of the new “Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) Policy” 
including minimizing the presence of the Central Government PSEs in strategic sectors to 
create new investment space for private sectors and reiterate its recommendation that the 
Government may consider retaining profitable and well performing PSUs, especially in 
core sector instead of disinvesting for short term financial gains.  
(Para 6.3) 
Inland Water Transport  
The Committee has been informed that no action has been taken to remove the 
encroachments in the Buckingham Canal, despite the directions of the Madras High Court. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry and IWAI may resolve the issues by 
establishing n ecessary coordination mechanism with the State Government and local 
authorities to address State level issues.  
(Para 7.2) 
Coastal Shipping and IWT  
The Committee is concerned to know about the sluggish pace of progress as more than half 
of the 77 projects  under coastal shipping and IWT are still in development stage. The 
Committee notes that out of the 62 community jetties being developed under JMVP-II, only 
12 have been completed so far. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take 
appropriate steps to accelerate the pace of all the ongoing 77 projects under the Coastal 
Shipping & IWT and ensure their timely completion. 
 (Para 8.3) 
Analysis of Port Performance  

60 
 
The Committee while examining the functioning of Major Ports has observed that out of 
the 12 Major Ports, only 04 are functioning with acceptable performance. There has been 
only marginal improvement in the port performance parameters of the most ports, despite 
massive investments in technology, mechanization and infrastructure. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation that the Ministry may make all efforts for improvements of 
performance at all the Major Ports to realise the Maritime India Vision 2030.  
(Para 10.2) 
Development of Ports  
The Ministry has not furnished the replies to the query of the Committee on whether any 
other such centres are proposed to be established in other places in the country.  
(Para 11.3) 
Vizhinjam Transhipment Hub  
The Committee while examining the functioning of Major Ports had recommended that the 
Ministry may find ways and means to reduce Lighthouse Dues (LHD) to lower the logistics 
costs. Vessel Related Charges (VRC) can be reduced only by reducing the operating 
expense which is practically not feasible in most Major Ports. The Committee reiterates its 
recommendation and urges the Ministry to act on it. 
(Para 12.5) 
Mobile X-ray Container Scanners (MXCS)  
The Committee notes the Ministry‟s reply in this regard. The Committee is of the view that 
ports are the crucial exit points in the country, which can be used for illegal trade of goods 
including antiquities and other valuables. The Committee, therefore, r ecommends that the 
Ministry in consultation with the Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs, should 
ensure that container scanners are installed at all the Ports in the country (including both 
Major and Minor), especially the ports having maximum quantu m of trade. The 
Committee also would like to be informed of the progress made in this regard.   
(Para 13.4) 
Container Manufacture  
The Committee is aware of the fact that the Ministry was planning to announce a 
Production Linked Incentive Scheme for manufacturing of Shipping Containers to 
promote India as a container manufacturing hub, spread over a period of nine years. 
However, as p er the recent Media Reports, the Ministry is planning to shelve the Scheme, 
rework and announce it at a later date. In this regard, the Committee would like to 
reiterate its recommendation that necessary steps must be taken to initiate and promote 
shipping container manufacturing in the country including private participation. The

Committee may also be apprised of the current status of the PLI Scheme and whether the 
Ministry intends to introduce it soon.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
Review of awarded/ongoing projects 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee takes note of the ongoing NH projects in the States of Andhra 
Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar and Maharashtra and the various steps being taken by the 
Ministry to minimize delays in execution of the ongoing projects. The Committee 
recommends that all the ongoing NH projects may be monitored closely, the onset of any 
sort of deviation from the scheduled timeline for a NH project may immediately be looked 
into and necessary remedial action may be taken at the e arliest so as to avoid significant 
time and cost overruns. 
(Para 9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 All ongoing NH projects are monitored at different levels of Central and State 
Government apart from regular monitoring and supervision by executing agencies. Del ayed 
Projects are reviewed by Ministry with the executing agencies. Necessary actions as 
appropriate are taken to address the deviation from the scheduled completion period due to 
various site related issues. Moreover, the executing agencies of the Ministr y are directed to 
monitor the progress of the work closely and take urgent necessary action to resolve the issues 
hampering the progress of the projects. Further, the issues hampering the progress of the 
projects are also uploaded on PMG Portal  & these iss ues are reviewed by Secretary 
(Coordination), Cabinet Secretariat from time to time. The recommendation of the committee 
is noted for scrupulous compliance. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee recommends that due provisions for underpasses or flyover should 
be included at the DPR stage itself for all NH projects, for uninterrupted flow of both 
pedestrian and vehicular traffic for every village/town near the highway as well as on 
accident-prone junctions, to minimize accidents. 
   (Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The requirements of underpasses/flyovers are duly assessed during the preparation of 
DPR as per IRC guidelines/site requirements in consultation with stakeholders such as 
villagers/locals/public representatives/ local authorities etc. Further, additional crossing 
facilities, wherever required as per relevant IRC standards and site conditions are also 
provided even during the construction, Operation & Maintenance phase. Moreover, provisions 

3 
 
for grade separated structures such as flyovers / under passes/ over passes are invariably made 
as per IRC guidelines while preparing DPR for improvement and up-gradation of NHs. 
2.2 Steps are taken to conduct Pedestrian movement counts along/across the Highways 
invariably during preparation of DP Rs and based on the pedestrian volume count, required 
facilities are mentioned both in the DPRs and Technical Schedules. Accordingly, Foot Over 
Bridges (FoB), Pedestrian underpasses (PUP) and Pedestrian Subways (PSW) are constructed 
to ensure reduction in accidents involving pedestrians.

Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes that bituminous roads (flexible pavements) are common in use 
in India since it is relatively cheaper as compared to concrete roads. It is possible to 
construct relatively thin bituminous layers over existing pavements therefore the road can 
be strengthened by constructing bituminous pavement layers one after the other in stages in 
a certain period of time unlike the cement concrete or rigid pavement construction. Cement 
concrete pavement has a high initial investment but has excellent riding surface and longer 
life of 20 or so years in contrast with bitumen roads which have an average lifespan of 4 -5 
years. Cement con crete roads are prevalent in most developed nations. In India, Mumbai 
has switched to concrete roads. Flexible pavement failures are characterised by formation 
of potholes, ruts, cracks and localised depressions while the main defect developed in rigid 
pavements is structural cracks. Very little maintenance like maintenance of joints only is 
required in cement concrete roads. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry may carefully analyze the cost -benefit analysis of the bituminous roads and 
cement concrete roads. The Committee feels that the road condition often witnessed on 
National Highways points to the need for a holistic review of the policy for evaluation of 
materials to be used in order to ensure that best possible materials are being us ed and the 
National Highways being constructed are of best possible quality. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may take necessary steps to ensure that the choice 
of construction material used is made by factoring into account all long-term pros and cons 
of choosing one material over the other, given the specific needs of the particular NH 
project. 
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Type of pavement (flexible/rigid) is decided during DPR preparation based on the life 
cycle cost analysis of both flexible and rigid pavement options. 
3.2 The recommendation of the committee has been noted.

Recommendation/Observation 
14. Given the crucial role of service roads in improving road safety on the NH network, 
the Committee reiterates its following recommendation made in para 117 of its 317th 
Report on DFG (2022-23) of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways: 
The Committee observes that the lack of service roads alongside National Highways 
causes inconvenience to local residents and is, at times,  the cause of road accidents. The 
land required for development of National Highways is acquired from the local people 
and they should be given the benefits of service roads along National Highways. The 
Committee feels that service roads are an integral pa rt of National Highways and 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may make it mandatory to have service roads 
along NHs to the extent possible and provisions for the same may be included in the 
tender document for NH projects. 
(Para 62) 
Reply of the Ministry  
14.1 The requirement of Service Road along National Highways is broadly specified in 
IRC:SP:15 "Ribbon Development along Highways and its Prevention”. The concept of 
service roads is to limit the access to the main highway while simultaneously me eting the 
demands of the abutting land owners for ingress and egress. Thus, service roads are 
provided in urban/inhabitated sections along National Highways where ribbon development 
have already taken place to segregate the local traffic from long distance  traffic. Such 
service roads also prevent the congestion caused on the main highway due to purely local 
traffic and at the same time reduce the number of intersections which cause traffic hazards 
and reduce the capacity. Accordingly, the requirements of se rvice roads are assessed at 
DPR stage. Additional service roads are also provided on demand of villagers/locals/public 
representatives/ local authorities during construction and Operation & Maintenance phase 
of National Highways as per feasibility and viability.

16. The Committee notes that the majority of Indian roads face the most damage 
during the monsoon season.    Water logging in bitumen roads leads to potholes due to 
the eroding of the asphalt layer. To prevent water damage, most Indian roads do have a 
Camber which is the slope provided to the road surface to drain off water but lack s torm 
water drains which take the water which is drained to the side by a Camber and carry it 
off to a water body. Without drainage, a road will suffer during a monsoon even if it is 
well-constructed. In Tamil Nadu, rainwater harvesting was made compulsory some years 
back and since then there is less damage to the roads. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that drainage provisions should be made mandatory at the DPR stage itself, 
especially for NH projects in high -rainfall regions. The Committee further rec ommends 
that the Ministry may carry out thorough research in this regard in collaboration with 
expert research bodies and review its existing codes/guidelines, if any, for drainage 
provisions on NHs, based on the outcomes of the research. 
(Para 68) 
Reply of the Ministry  
16.1 Drainage study is included in the scope of DPR consultancy services and provisions 
for surface and subsurface drainages are taken in the scope of project as road side drains 
and CD works at DPR stage. NHAI has recently included draina ge expert as part of 
personnel of the consultant in the RFP for DPR Consultancy services so that drainage 
requirements are well addressed. Further, NHAI vide circular no. 18.48 dated 08.07.2020 
issued guidelines on drainage system adequacy & effectiveness which is already under 
implementation. However, the recommendation of the committee has been noted for 
compliance.

Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee takes note of the present mechanism for Maintenance and Repair 
(M&R) of National Highways in India. However, the Committee is deeply concerned to

note that the Ministry/NHAI is managing the maintenance and repair of NHs across the 
country with an allocation of just about 40% of the actual requirements estimated by the 
Ministry. The Committee feels that the shortfall of sufficient budgetary allocation is 
reflected in the sub -par quality of National Highways that is often witnessed across the 
country, especially in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar and Maharashtra. Maintena nce 
and Repair of the existing National Highways is of utmost importance in order to keep 
them in a safe, pliable condition and to permit good average traffic speeds. This should be 
given higher priority than construction of new National Highways. In this regard, the 
Committee notes that it has repeatedly recommended a much higher budgetary allocation 
for Maintenance and Repair of National Highways in its previous Reports viz., para 75 of

therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry must give  much more priority to M&R of

utilize the same to implement a robust monitoring mechanism to identify and meet the

world in terms of road accident deaths as per a 2021 World Bank Report 2 and this 
highlights the need  for much stronger, well -coordinated efforts to be put into minimizing 
the large number of road accidents taking place on Indian roads and highways. The loss of 
so many lives in road accidents every year has a severe detrimental effect on the lives of a 
large number of families as well as the overall Indian economy. The Committee, therefore,

coordination with State Governments and Union Ministries concerned in order to minimize

Recommendation/Observation 
14. The Committee takes note of the mechanism presently in place for arbitration and 
resolution of disputes between the authority and road contractors. The Committee 
observes that disputes between the concessionaire and the authority is one of the core 
reasons behind delays in road projects. Therefore, having an effective m echanism in 
place to minimize the delay resolution time to the extent possible is very important to 
avoid cost and time overruns in execution of NH projects. The Committee desires the 
Ministry to holistically examine the efficacy of the existing arbitratio n and dispute 
resolution mechanism in settling disputes between the involved parties and streamline the 
same so as to avoid litigations as far as possible. Further, it has come to the notice of the 
Committee that a significant portion of the amount of clai ms presently under arbitration 
pertain to a select few big concessionaires (details are placed at Annexure -III). The 
Committee notes that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has supplied the 
reasons for pending arbitration cases. The concessionaire s raised the claims on ground 
of delay in declaration of appointed date, delay in obtaining environment clearance, 
prolongation of project due to various reasons, termination payment, loss of toll revenue, 
delay in commencement of toll operation, loss of p roductivity of machinery, loss of 
revenue to the concessionaires envisaged in the financial model before accepting the 
project, etc.. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should study the reasons 
thoroughly to identify the veracity of the reasons and  ensure that such reasons should 
not become a reason in future for delay of projects or arbitrations. 
(Para 72)  
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 The settlement of disputes is being done through  Conciliation Committee of 
Independent Experts (CCIE)  constituted vide policy circular dated 01 -6-2017. It is an 
endeavor for faster settlement of claims through conciliation and reduce liabilities. National 
Highways Authority of India (NHAI)    has rigorously started the process of conciliation by 
constituting three Conciliation Committees of Independent Experts (CCIE) of three members 
each.  These Conciliation Committees are being headed by retired officials from the 
judiciary, senior experts from public administration, finance and from private sector. It is a 
measure to avoid litigations and is proving to be an effective system. Since the introduction 
of CCIE about 192 matters have been settled by NHAI through conciliation. 

27 
 
14.2 With respect to delay in arbitrations, it is submitted that vide Amendment Act 3 of 
2016, the  legislature has introduced Section 29A to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 
1996 (“the Act”). The aforesaid amendment came into force with effect from 23.10.2015. 
Section 29A of the Act was further amended in the year 2019. The effect of the above 
referred two amendments is that in the matter of arbitrations, other than International 
Commercial Arbitration, a time limit for conclusion of arbitration proceedings was 
introduced. Section 29A of the Act, as it stands today, provides that an arbitral tribun al has to 
publish the award within a period of twelve months from the date of completion of pleadings 
under Section 29A.

Quality of Roads  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes the existing mechanism to ensure that the road works are 
executed as per prescribed specifications and standards. However, in light of the sub -par 
quality of road construction often witnessed on NHs across the country, the Committee 

36 
 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorough review of the existing 
monitoring mechanism for road construction quality and come up with ways to plug the 
gaps in the same so as to ensure higher quality NHs in the future. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry may enact provisions for imposing severe financial penalty 
on the ind ividuals appointed as Authority‟ s Engineer/Supervision Consultants in cases 
where gross negligence of the prescribed specifications and standards is observed in roads  
approved by them. 
(Para 23)  
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Ministry is continuously making efforts  to strengthen the system of objective 
assessment of Quality of NH projects of all agencies (NHAI/NHIDCL/State PWDs/BRO).  
2.2 Mobile Quality Control Vans (MQCVs) have been engaged in 4 States, namely, 
Gujarat, Rajasthan, Odisha and Karnataka on a pilot basis. MQCVs are responsible for 
conducting Non -Destructive Testing (NDT) in 2000 Km of NH project length per quarter 
(about 670 Km per month). The NDT test results from MQCVs are being  shared with all 
Executing Agencies for taking up necessary follow -up actions through a Web Portal 
“National Highways Quality Monitoring Portal” under development by the Ministry. 
2.3 Retired Chief Engineers from Central and Sta te Government have been empanelled 
by NHAI and NHIDCL for conducting Third Party Quality Inspections of NH works in 
NHAI and NHIDCL respectively. The existing panels of NHAI & NHIDCL are utilized to 
conduct Third party quality inspections of projects under Roads Wing and BRO.  
2.4 As regards, imposition of severe financial penalty on the individuals appointed as 
Authority‟s Engineer/Supervision consultants in cases of their gross negligence is concerned, 
Ministry vide letter no. RW/NH -33044/76/2021-S&R (P&B) dated 6th October, 2021 issued 
SOPs to debar/penalize/declare as non -performer the   Authority‟s Engineer/Supervision 
consultants engaged in NH and other centrally sponsored road projects who are found to be 
providing deficient services. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee appreciates the recent initiative of the Ministry to strengthen the 
Quality Control set up of NH projects by engaging the services of Mobile Inspection Vans 
(MIVs) for Inspection and Quality assessment of NH projects. The Committee hopes that 
the pilot project for engaging the services of MIVs turns out to be a success so that the 
MIVs can be utilized across the country for better quality control of ongoing and future 
NH projects in the country. 
(Para 25) 
 
 
 

37 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 Mobile Inspection Vans (MIVs) (renamed to Mobile Quality Control Vans (MQCVs) 
for clarity) have been engaged in 4 States, namely, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Odisha and Karnataka 
on a pilot basis. Operations of MQCVs have already begun.  
3.2 Based on the efficacy of MQCV engaged, deployment of more MQCVs in other 
States of the country shall be taken up in phases.

3.3 The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take necessary steps for 
the deployment of MQCVs in the remaining States for better inspection and quality 
assessment of NH projects all over the country.

4. This Ministry and IRC have issued various codes and guidelines, from time to time, 
to implement various road safety measures so as to minimize accidents on National 
Highways. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may come up with 
provisions to make it mandatory to inst all street lights on the entire National Highways 
network in the country since poor lighting conditions lead to severe accidents. The regular 
maintenance of these street lights may also be suitably ensured in coordination with the 
concerned agencies.

4.1 There is provision in the contract agreement for providing lighting at specified 
locations of the project highway, using appropriate system and source of electric power as per

locations/intersections of NH with SH/MDR/ODR/Village roads for improving road safety

4.4 The recommendation of the committee has been noted. 
 
 
 

38 
 
Further recommendation 
4.5 The Committee notes that the Concessionaire is responsible for the provisions of 
lighting on the entire National Highways network. However, the contact details of these

4.6 The Committee also feels that the Ministry needs to come up with a better policy 
for illumination. In this regard, the Ministry must implement smart lighting systems

4.7 Further, measures should be taken to reduce light pollution, such as using 
shields and directing light downward to minimize glare and prevent unnecessary light

7. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may issue guidelines to limit the number 
of hours commercial drivers can drive in a day to a reasonable limit, say, 10 hours a day. If a 
suitable mechanism can be devised to implement this in earnest, this would ensure that 
commercial drivers are well rested, making the roads safer for all travellers. 
(Para 40) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Section 91(1) of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 states that “The hours of work of any 
person engaged for operating a transport vehicle shall be such as provided in the Motor 
Transport Workers Act, 1961 (27 of 1961).” 
7.2 Section 13 of Motor Transport Workers Act, 1961 (administered by Ministry of 
Labour and Employment) states that:- 
“No adult motor transport worker shall be required or allowed to work for more than eight 
hours in any day and forty-eight hours in any week: 
7.3 Provided that where any such motor transport worker is engaged in the running of any 
motor transport service on such long distance routes, or on such festive and other occasions 
as may be notified in the prescribed manner  by the prescribed authority, the employer may, 
with the approval of such authority, require or allow such motor transport worker to work for 
more than eight hours in any day or forty -eight hours in any week but in no case for more 
than ten hours in a day and fifty-four in hours in a week, as the case may be : 
7.4 Provided further that in the case of a breakdown or dislocation of a motor transport 
service or interruption of traffic or act of God, the employer may, subject to such conditions 
and limitations as may be prescribed, require or allow any such motor transport worker to 
work for more than eight hours in any day or more than forty-eight hours in any week” 
7.5 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted for compliance. 
 
Further recommendation 
7.6 The Committee notes the provision given in Section 13 of Motor Transport 
Workers Act, 1961. However, the Committee feels that there is laxity in implementation 
of this provision. It is therefore recommended that the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways and other stakeholders must come together to formulate a system for its 
proper implementation. Further, the Ministries must work in spreading awareness to 
common masses about this provision.

Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take immediate steps to ensure 
that the black spots on National Highways across the country are rectified on a war 
footing. Data pertaining to black spots may be analyzed to ascertain why the particular 
spots ended up causing so many road accidents and what steps could have been taken at 
the road design and construction stage to avoid the same from becoming black spots. The 
inferences drawn may be utilized in future NH projects across the country in order to 
minimize the development of black spots therein. 
             (Para 44)              
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 The Ministry vide OM no. RW/NH-29011/2/2015/P&M (RSCE) dated 7th December, 
2015 issued guidelines on “Preparation and submission of proposals for rectification of 
identified road accident black spots on National Highways”. Ministry vide letter No.  RW-
NH-29011 /08/2019 -S&R(P&B) dated 26.08.2019 also is sued guidelines regarding 
preparation of proposal and sanction & approval for rectification of Accident Black Spot. 
8.2 Regular review meetings are being conducted by senior officers of Ministry with the 
field officers of Ministry, NHAI and NHIDCL to formulate action plans for identification and 
rectification of Black Spots with a targeted Timeline. 
8.3 Road Safety Officer (RSO) has been designated at each Regional Office of road

Further recommendation 
8.4 The Committee further recommends that the contact information of Road Safety

8.6 The local administration must consider lowering speed limits in black spot areas, 
especially in residential or densely populated zones. 
8.7 Further, the Ministry must involve local communities in identifying and 
addressing black spots, as they often have valuable insights into local road safety issues. 
The Ministry should also establish key performance indicators (KPIs) to measure the 
success of black spot eradication efforts, such as accident rate reduction and traffic flow 
improvements.

affected road facilities as efficiently as possible. The operator runs 24x7 Route Patrols,

Focus Areas of the Ministry for the year 2023-24 
 
Recommendation/ Observation  
1. The Committee notes the various focus areas of t he Ministry for the year 2023-24. 
The Ministry has awarded 383 km of Expressway and A ccess-Controlled Corridors in the 
ongoing year. It will award 1667 km in the next 2 m onths and the remaining 1958 km in 
the next financial year. The Committee desires to b e apprised of the slow pace of award in 
the ongoing financial year. The Ministry may inform  how it plans to ensure that the 
remaining length is awarded by the next financial year.  
(Para 13) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Ministry has awarded 1,361 km of Expressway and Acc ess-Controlled Corridors in 
FY 2022-23. The Ministry is focusing on early finalization of the DPRs, and efforts are being 
made in consultation with State Governments for spe edy completion of land acquisition 
process to achieve the award target. In current yea r, Ministry has fixed an award target of 
13,290 km including Expressway and Access-Controlle d Corridors against the last year 
award target of 12,000 km.  
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2. The Committee feels that it is the responsibilit y of the Ministry to enable 
transportation access to the remotest areas of the country. The Ministry should work out a 
balance between the transportation needs of both re mote areas and tourist spots while 
planning projects under the Parvatmala programme. T he Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may lay due focus on enhancing connectivit y through ropeways as last mile 
connectivity to remote areas and hamlets in hilly r egions. This would help the local 
residents to contribute more to the local economy, besides improving their quality of life.   
(Para 15) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Considering transportation access to the remote st areas of the country as Ministry’s 
priority, “Parvatmala Pariyojana” was envisioned to  develop ecologically sustainable 
alternative mode of transport in hilly regions, rem ote areas and urban congested areas, which 
will help in improving connectivity and convenience  for commuters, besides promoting 
tourism.

Limited (NHLML) under Parvatmala Pariyojana in part nership with the State/ Union 
Territory (UT) Authority basis the proposals receiv ed from State Govt/UT. Projects have 
been prioritized for feasibility studies and develo pment based on various parameters such as 
Importance of the project, Demand Assessment, Acces sibility, Existing connectivity, Ease of 
implementation etc., which would help in improving tourism, economic activities and provide 
last-mile connectivity in remote areas of the country.  
2.3 Ropeway project at Varanasi has been awarded in  Dec’22 to decongest the streets of 
Varanasi and improve logistics efficiency. 6 projec ts are currently under bidding, viz. 
Kedarnath, Hemkund Sahib Ji, Bijli Mahadev, Shivkho ri, Gwalior and Dhosi Hill. Detailed 
feasibility study has also been initiated for 34 pr ojects and pre- feasibility study for 92 
ropeway projects.

made satisfactory utilisation of the available fund s. This is including the period wherein 
Coronavirus restrictions were in place. The Committ ee hopes that the Ministry may

Recommendation/ Observation

projects/ Corridors for a total tentative cost of R s. 6,78,505/- crore leveraging the PM Gati 
Shakti National Master Plan (GSNMP) Portal. The Com mittee feels that the GSNMP 
would help tackle long-standing issues in the infra structure sector in India, such as 
disjointed planning and lack of standardisation and  synergy among the various Ministries 
and Departments. The Committee would like to know t he present status of these 62 NHs in 
terms of progress percentage and expected date of completion. The Committee recommends 
that the remaining NHs out of the total 1,510 NHs p rojects may also be considered for 
examining through the PM GSNMP Portal. This will en sure smoother execution of the 
ongoing and upcoming road projects, in coordination  with other Ministries/ Departments/ 
State Governments under the GSNMP.

4.1 The 64 NH corridors were presented to the Natio nal Project Group (NPG) of the PM 
GatiShakti National Master Plan until the 49th NPG meeting on 8th June 2023 consist of 286 
project packages. Out of these 286 project packages , 42 packages have already been 
completed, 143 packages are currently under constru ction, 40 packages have been awarded 
but not yet appointed, and 61 packages are planned for award.  
4.2 Among the 143 packages that are under construct ion, 23 packages have achieved a 
physical progress greater than 80%, 32 packages hav e achieved a physical progress between 
50 to 80% while 88 packages have physical progress between 0% and 50%.  In regards to the 
expected date of completion, out of the 143 package s under construction, 75 packages are 
expected to be completed in the FY 2023-24, 54 pack ages have a projected completion date 
in the FY 2024-25, while 14 packages have a project ed completion date in the FY 2025-26 
and beyond. 
4.3 Ministry has issued fresh guidelines that all N H projects costing more than Rs. 500 
crore shall be routed through PMG of PM Gati Shakti . In addition, Ministry has also

Highways should co-ordinate with the Ministry of An imal Husbandry and Dairying to 
formulate a plan to prevent stray cattle and other animals from coming onto NHs. The 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should also  focus that the Cattle 
underpasses are built near the villages. Further, a  helpline number may be displayed so 
that the common people can inform the authorities about any cattle movement.  
(Para 19.3) 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should i nform the concerned State 
Government to take necessary action in the matter.  
(Para 20.2) 
The Committee notes that the network density and Hi gh Speed Corridor density per 
1000 sq.km is far less than the global benchmark. T he Committee feels that the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should ramp  up all its resources to increase 
the NH network density, particularly in respect of High Speed Corridor per 1,000 
sq.km.  
(Para 21.3) 
Driving Training Centres  
The Committee notes that the model Driving Training  facilities have not been set up in 
States like Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, etc. The Commit tee, therefore, recommends that 
all States should be covered under this project and  at least three centres should be 
developed in big states.  
(Para 22.2) 
The Committee recommends that the results of such s urveys must be placed in public 
domain so that the concerned private organisations/ NGOs can deduce required 
information from it.  

98 
 
(Para 23.4) 
DELAYS IN ROAD PROJECTS 
The Committee is of the view that the delayed proje cts should be taken up on priority 
for completion. Further, the issue of land acquisit ion must be streamlined as it is the 
main reason of delay in most of the cases. The Comm ittee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry should set up a hassle-free single win dow clearance/portal that includes all 
stakeholders involved in the process of land acquisition.  
(Para 25.3) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should e xpedite the creation of utility 
ducts at all the National Highways. Further, it is reiterated that the utility ducts may be 
developed at the construction stage in the expressways to be built in the future.  
(Para 26.2) 
Vehicle Fitness Certificate 
 
The Committee notes that the models Vehicle Inspect ion & Certificate Centres have 
been established only in 27 States/UTs. The Committ ee recommends that such Centres 
may be opened up in all States.

Chapter I  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY  
  
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee acknowledges the steps taken by AS I to retrace the monuments that 
were deemed to be missing by CAG in its 2013 Perfor mance Audit but feels that the same 
reflects at the questionable state of protection and preservation of monuments, with ASI being 
unaware of the physical untraceability of several o f the Centrally Protected Monuments 
under its ambit.  The Committee recommends that the  ASI immediately undertake a survey of 
the remaining CPMs which were not inspected in the CAG Audit survey and ascertain 
whether there are any other missing monuments in th e country apart from the 24 monuments 
of the original survey.  The Committee further reco mmends that a physical survey of all the 
Centrally Protected Monuments must mandatorily be c arried out by ASI from time to time as 
per a fixed time schedule. Digital log books may be  maintained which may contain textual 
and photographic/video record of the state of physi cal preservation of the monument, exact 
location coordinates and clearly demarcated prohibited and regulated areas in the vicinity of 
the monument. These digital records may be made eas ily accessible to the general public to 
avoid any ambiguities and details may also be published regarding the date on which the last 
survey was conducted, due date for the next survey and the contact details of the ASI officials 
in-charge of maintaining and protecting the monument.   
(Para 10)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 The monuments and the sites has been frequently  inspected at the circle, Regional and 
headquarter level by the officers of the ASI. The w ork of the survey through the Total station 
and Photogrammetric is under process.   
1.2 For keeping all the data of a monument in one p lace, ASI is in the process of 
preparing a “Heritage App” and “Health Card’. Herit age app would be meant for keeping 
monument's record in one place including its year o f notification, area, ownership, 
archaeological significance, internal and external status of the monument and the scope will 
be of adding inspection record in the App. It also will be accessible to the general public. 
 
Assessment of security requirements at Centrally Protected Monuments 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee is concerned to note that out of t he 3693 Centrally Protected 
Monuments, security guards are posted at only 248 C PMs/sites/museums i.e. less than about 
6.7 percent of the total number of CPMs. The Commit tee notes with dismay that out of the 
total requirement of 7000 personnel for protection of Monuments, the Government could 
provide only 2578 security personnel at 248 locatio ns due to budgetary constraints. The 

3 
 
Committee observes that budgetary constraints shoul d not be an excuse for not providing 
security guards to protect our rich cultural herita ge. It is the bounden duty of the 
Government of the day to protect our cultural herit age sites. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that budget may be provided by the Gover nment to appoint 7000 personnel for 
protection of the Monuments or as per the study con ducted by IIT, Delhi. In view of this 
worrying state of affairs, the Committee is of the strong view that the budgetary allocation 
available with the Ministry/ASI for safeguarding our Centrally Protected Monuments needs a 
serious relook. The Committee recommends that the M inistry/ASI may conduct an urgent 
thorough assessment of the security requirements an d budgetary allocation required for the 
same and a strong case may be made to the Ministry of Finance requesting allocation of 
additional funds for this purpose so as to ensure a  basic state of protection for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country to preserve them for generations to come. The 
Committee also recommends that the local Panchayats  and police may be involved in 
safeguarding the monuments and if necessary, the AM ASR Act may be amended in this 
regard.  
(Para 22)  
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 In 2022, ASI signed an MoU with the Indian Inst itute of Technology, Delhi on 
collaboration for providing expertise in the field of security and surveillance on monuments, 
sites, museums, and offices. A dedicated team of ex perts from the partnered institution will 
visit centrally protected monuments and will furnis h an analysis report containing short, 
medium and long terms security challenges along with solutions. Thereupon a comprehensive 
security policy to combat various identified issues  faced at the CPMS will be drafted. 
Subsequently, the requirement of the funds may be i dentified and accordingly, the 
requirement will duly be placed. The recommendation s of the committee are duly noted for 
exploring feasibility. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee takes note of the existing framewo rk and recommends that in the 
upcoming amendment of the AMASR Act being worked up on by the Ministry, strong 
provisions may be incorporated for fixing accountab ility of concerned Government officials 
to ensure that necessary steps are taken timely for  tackling encroachment of Centrally 
Protected Monuments. The concerned officials should  be liable to be prosecuted in case of 
gross negligence of their duties with regard to tac kling encroachment of CPMs. The 
Committee further recommends that the Ministry may examine the powers given to District 
Forest Officers (DFOs) under The Wildlife (Protecti on) Act, 1972 and consider granting 
similar powers to ASI officials in order to effecti vely curb the issue of encroachment of 
Centrally Protected Monuments.  
(Para 25)  
 

4 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 Amendment in the AMASR Act, 1958 is under consi deration. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee notes that no proposal exists at p resent with ASI for empowering local 
bodies to provide security guards to the unprotecte d monuments. The Committee feels that 
given their proximity and cultural ties with local monuments, local bodies are best suited to 
look after the protection of historical monuments especially those which are not under the list 
of Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs). Empowering  local bodies to provide security 
guards at such monuments for their protection can g o a long way in ensuring that these 
monuments are preserved in their present state for generations to come. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that provisions to e mpower the local bodies for the 
protection of historical monuments and to make them accountable may be incorporated in the 
amendment of the AMASR Act that is being worked upon by the Ministry.  
(Para 33)  
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 Noted for implementation. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee feels that there is a scope for us ing satellite imagery to monitor the 
Centrally Protected Monuments (CPMs) across the country for encroachment and any illegal 
construction activities in the prohibited and regul ated areas of the same. Satellite imagery 
should also be used to try and trace the monuments which are untraceable at present and to 
ensure that no existing CPMs become untraceable in the future. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that ASI may approach ISRO and, if feasi ble, sign a Memorandum of 
Understanding with ISRO to utilize ISRO satellite imagery for the above mentioned purposes.  
(Para 35)  
Reply of the Ministry  
5.1 Noted for implementation to monitor the central ly protected monuments for 
encroachment to trace the untraceable monuments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee may be apprised of detailed guidel ines, if any, issued by the 
Ministry/ASI under the AMASR Act in this regard.  
(Para 43.2.3)  
 

5 
 
Reply of the Ministry  
6.1 A policy for photographers to operate within th e premises of protected monuments 
has been notified in 2017. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The Committee is surprised to note the reply fur nished by the Ministry, after 9 years 
have passed since the CAG Report was laid before th e Parliament. The Committee may be 
apprised of the specific action taken by the Ministry in this regard, at the earliest.  
(Para 43.10.3)  
Reply of the Ministry  
7.1 In this context it is stated that Rule 8(d) of the AMASR Rules, 1959 specifies 
requirement of a licence from the ASI to undertake photography of a visitor by charging the 
fee. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee recommends that fixed timelines sh ould be put in place for carrying 
out effective action on-ground to tackle encroachme nts at the earliest and any delays may 
immediately be taken up at higher levels. Accountab ility may be fixed on both Central/State 
officials for time-bound action for removal of encr oachment at Centrally Protected 
Monuments.  
(Para 43.13.3)  
Reply of the Ministry  
8.1 For the effective implementation of the removal  of the encroachments and authorised 
constructions/activities in and around the monument s, the provision will be included in the 
amendment of the AMASR ACT and Rule.

 Chapter II  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee further notes that out of the 92 m onuments declared “missing” by the 
CAG, 42 monuments have been identified due to effor ts made by the ASI and out of the 
remaining 50 monuments, 14 are affected by rapid ur banisation, 12 are submerged by 
reservoir/dams while the location of the remaining 24 is untraceable.  The Committee feels 
that the distinction made by the Ministry regarding  the monuments lost to 
urbanisation/reservoirs and 24 monuments which are untraceable is an academic distinction 
since monuments lost to urbanisation/reservoirs are  as irrecoverable as the ones which are 
presently untraceable with scant hope of being foun d in future.  Moreover, the fact that the 
ASI had been unable to prevent the loss of the 14 m onuments to urbanisation and 12 to 
reservoirs/dams and only located them after the stu dy by CAG suggests that the ASI had no 
cognisance of these monuments prior to the study. The number of monuments lost from public 
viewing must therefore be held to be 50 taking into  account those lost to urbanisation or 
reservoirs.  The ASI has assured that the remaining  42 of the 92 monuments exist physically 
but the Committee would like to know whether these monuments exist in their entirety and 
undamaged or whether the ASI has only managed to lo cate some remains and ruins of such 
monuments.   
(Para 11)  
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 To ascertain the conservation status of these m onuments, they shall be again inspected 
through the field offices of ASI. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Ministry has stated that there is no term ca lled “Missing Monuments” in the 
AMASR Act and the term only came into existence as it was used by the Audit team on their 
Report. The Committee opines that the AMASR Act pro vides for the preservation and 
protection of ancient historical monuments and it would have been inconsistent to include the 
concept of “Missing Monuments” in the Act.  That th e situation warrants the use of such 
phrases only serves to underline the apathy of the Ministry and ASI regarding the 
preservation of our historical monuments.  The Mini stry has also stated that the exercise of 
removing the untraceable monuments under Section 35  of the AMASR Act has not been 
initiated by the ASI as there are chances that some  of these monuments shall be traced out in 
near future. The Committee observes that Section 35  of the AMASR Act, 1958 has the 
provision to issue notification only for such CPMs which have as per the opinion of the 
Central Government have ceased to be of national im portance. The monuments which have 
become “untraceable” have become so due to official  apathy and may not have ceased to be 

7 
 
of national importance had they been existing.  The  situation of a “Missing Monument” 
cannot be automatically equated with loss of its hi storical importance.  The Committee 
recommends that the Untraceable Monuments may not b e removed from the list of Centrally 
Protected Monuments by taking recourse to Section 3 5 as that Section provides the exclusion 
only of such monuments which have in the opinion of the Central Government ceased to be of 
national importance.  In fact, there is the danger that in case of such removal, there would be 
no imperative to find the untraceable monument and it would be well and truly lost to 
posterity. Since untraceable monuments also cannot continue to be on the Protected list, the 
Committee recommends that the list of Untraceable M onuments may be maintained as such 
and if necessary, the AMASR Act may be amended to include this terminology.   
(Para 12)  
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 The observation shall be taken into considerati on while amending the AMASR Act. 
  
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee feels that a thorough review of th e AMASR Act in consultation with all 
stakeholders and State Governments is the need of t he hour. The Committee, therefore, 
appreciates the process initiated by the Ministry o f Culture to amend the AMASR Act. The 
Committee agrees with the view that having the same  limits for all monuments for prohibited 
area and regulated area for restricting/regulating construction-related activities near the 
monument, is not a practical approach as the requir ement for such limitations could vary a 
lot depending on various factors specific to each m onument. The Committee, therefore, feels 
that the upcoming amendment which provides for such  monument-specific prohibited and 
regulated areas is much needed and hopes that once the amendment is passed, all necessary 
steps are taken to ensure that the monument-specifi c limits are decided upon for each 
Centrally Protected Monument at the earliest. The C ommittee notes that the ASI would be 
surveying all 3693 monuments while delineating monu ment specific protected and regulated 
limits and desires that a Report of the survey may be submitted to the Committee. However, 
the provisions of the Act may be strictly adhered t o in terms of the prohibited areas around 
the monument and even Government officials violating the provisions should be prosecuted.  
(Para 17)  
Reply of the Ministry  
3.1 For dealing with the NOCs cases in the circles and RD offices, the google and Bhuvan 
maps, wherever possible to delineate, were created for  showing protected, prohibited and 
regulated limit of the monuments. Since ASI is work ing on the amendment of the AMASR 
Act accordingly the marking of prohibited, regulated and prohibited limits on the Survey map 
would be initiated. 
 
 

8 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee reiterates the following recommend ation made in para 39 of its 311 th  
Report on ‘Creation of Regulatory Framework for pro tection of Historical Sites and 
Monuments’:  
The Committee fails to see why a person living in t he Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Comp etent Authority under the 
AMASR Rules for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of 
cracks, whitewashing, replacement of windows etc. T he Committee feels that such 
uncalled-for interference makes lives harder for pe ople living nearby the monuments 
and could slowly cause feelings of anguish towards the monument itself. Given the 
large number of monuments across the country and th e limited budgetary resources 
available with the Government, it is pertinent that  people residing near the 
monuments are encouraged to look after the monument s and protect them. Besides, 
placing such unnecessary curbs and implementing the m is a wastage of limited 
Government resources and turns the focus away from where it should be - actually 
protecting and preserving the monument itself. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorou gh review of the AMASR Act 
and Rules and omit any provisions that provide for seeking permissions for minor 
works where the same is not actually needed and str eamline the process for applying 
for permission in case where the same is actually needed. Steps may urgently be taken 
to make it possible for the entire process for seek ing permission for construction 
activities in prohibited and regulated areas, to be  completed online so as to not cause 
any hassle to bona fide residents living near the monuments.  
(Para 18)  
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 The Ministry of Culture in consultation with AS I is working on the amendment of the 
AMASR Act, and such issues shall be taken into consideration in the amendment of the act. 
  
Permitting Religious Activities in Religious Historical Monuments  
Recommendation/Observation

(Para 40)

The Committee also feels that the Ministry needs to  come up with a better policy for 
illumination. In this regard, the Ministry must imp lement smart lighting systems that 
can adjust the intensity of lights based on real-ti me traffic conditions and weather. This 
can help save energy and improve safety. 
(Para 4.6)  
Further, measures should be taken to reduce light p ollution, such as using shields and 
directing light downward to minimize glare and prev ent unnecessary light spillage into 
the night sky. 
(Para 4.7)  
In addition to it, the Ministry should consider int egrating emergency communication 
devices, such as emergency call boxes, into the lig hting infrastructure for the safety and 
assistance of motorists. 
(Para 4.8)  
  

22 
 
The Committee notes that the prices of items at res taurants, food courts, dhabas are 
exorbitantly high which should be kept in check for  all sections of the society. The 
Committee also noted that there is a need for imple mentation of strict cleanliness and 
maintenance standards to keep amenities in good con dition. Regular cleaning, pest 
control, and repairs are essential. 
(Para 5.2)  
Further, the Ministry must establish a feedback mec hanism for travellers to report 
issues or provide suggestions for improvement. The Ministry must act on this feedback 
promptly. 
 (Para 5.3)  
The Committee appreciates the measures taken by the  Ministry in respect of road 
safety. However, the Committee still notes that the re is a need for community training 
programmes for learning better road safety practice s like lane changing, helmets usage, 
etc. 
(Para 6.3)  
The Committee also suggests the introduction of ant i-sleep devices in automobiles that 
helps prevent accidents caused by drivers who fall asleep while driving. 
(Para 6.4)  
The Committee notes the provision given in Section 13 of Motor Transport Workers 
Act, 1961. However, the Committee feels that there is laxity in implementation of this 
provision. It is therefore recommended that the Min istry of Road Transport and 
Highways and other stakeholders must come together to formulate a system for its 
proper implementation. Further, the Ministries must  work in spreading awareness to 
common masses about this provision. 
(Para 7.6)  
Rectification of Black Spots  
The Committee further recommends that the contact i nformation of Road Safety 
Officers must be kept in public domain for better information regarding black spots. 
(Para 8.4)  
Further, there is a need to prioritize black spots based on the severity of accidents, 
traffic volume, and other relevant factors and the focus must be on the most critical 
locations first. 
(Para 8.5)  
The local administration must consider lowering spe ed limits in black spot areas, 
especially in residential or densely populated zones. 
(Para 8.6)  

23 
 
Further, the Ministry must involve local communitie s in identifying and addressing 
black spots, as they often have valuable insights i nto local road safety issues. The 
Ministry should also establish key performance indi cators (KPIs) to measure the 
success of black spot eradication efforts, such as accident rate reduction and traffic flow 
improvements. 
(Para 8.7)  
The Committee appreciates the measures taken by the  Ministry and directs the 
Ministry to approve the request regarding procurement of VIDS. 
(Para 9.2)  
The Committee further recommends that the implement ation of Incident Management 
Service should be expedited and extended to all the  National highways in the country 
with immediate effect. 
(Para 10.4)  
The Committee recommends that the Rajmarg Yatra App should be promoted on wider 
scale for the optimum utilization of Information, Communication and Technology (ICT) 
and for better dissemination of information regarding grievances of common public. 
(Para 11.2)  
The Committee reiterates that the funds should be a llocated to each State and Union 
Territory under the Scheme “Development, customizat ion, deployment and 
management of State-wise vehicle tracking platform”.  
(Para 12.2)  
Further, in order to ensure safety of women, police  patrols must be increased on 
highways, especially during night-time hours. It mu st also be ensured that female police 
officers are part of these patrols to make women travellers feel more secure. 
(Para 12.3)  
The Ministry should also encourage community polici ng initiatives, where local 
residents and volunteers work together with law enf orcement agencies to ensure the 
safety of women travellers. 
(Para 12.4)  
The Ministry should promote and support women-centr ic transport services, such as 
women-only buses or taxi services, especially during night-time hours. 
(Para 12.5)  
  

24 
 
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry sho uld design and maintain 
highways with gender-sensitive infrastructure, incl uding safe pedestrian crossings and 
waiting areas for women. 
(Para 12.6)  
Spur Road for linking Samastipur with NH-119D 
The Committee notes about the progress made in the spur road for linking Samastipur 
with NH-119D. However, the Committee is of the view  that the land acquisition process 
must be expedited and the project must be completed as early as possible. 
(Para 13.2)

on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundred Forty -Third Report 
on Demands for Grants (2023 -24) of Ministry of Tourism which was presented  to both the 
Houses of Parliament on 13th March, 2023.  
  
  
2.         The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 6 th October, 2023 in 
respect of all the observations/ recommendations contained in the Report. The replies have 
been categorized as follows:- 
  
Chapter-I: 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry:

view of the replies of the Ministry:

132, 133, 139, 140, 143, 151, 156, 168 and 174. 
Total: 26 
  
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not 
been accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.: 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 26, 39,  57, 62, 64, 75, 76, 88, 89, 96, 100, 114, 
115, 119, 127, 128, 129, 130, 131, 148 and 162.
