17. The Committee observes that while India has about 25% of the global 
market in ship recycling, its share of ship building is barely 1-2%. The 
Committee has been informed that the main reason for the low percentage 
share in ship building is the high cost of ship building in India which in turn 
is due to high cost of material and labour costs. Some of the other reasons are 
lack of strategic  guidance, level playing ﬁeld between private and public 
sector companies, funding, technology. The Committee has been informed 
that while India is very  competitive in normal steel an d even automative 
graded steel, the steel required  for ship building is more specialized.  Since 
the market for such specialized steels  is small in India, this further drives up 
the material costs. Since most Indian steel mills are located near to the mines, 
the rail transportation costs are also high and further push up the costs. Indian 
steel is therefore costlier by about 50 – 70 dollars a tonne. Further, the labour 
costs are also higher in India due to productivity  issues. Labour productivity 
in India is also low due to the fact that there is less automation  in India 
unlike Korea and China which have high levels of automation due to the 
investments made by these countries in this regard. 
18. Further, though Shipyards come under ‗Infrastructure‖, ships themselves 
do not come under Infrastructure and getting long -term ﬁnance at easy rates 
for ships is di ﬃcult. Shipbuilding payments is usually done in stage 
payments as per  deﬁned stages. If the owner defaults, he forfeits the money 
and the ship, the half built ship, belongs to the purchaser.  But then the 

 
12  
purchaser has to sell the ship in  the global market to recover his costs, so 
there is a risk involved.  The Committee was also informed that most of the 
leading maritime countries have got risk insurance cover given to banks or 
lending institutions. China has got Sinesure,  Korea has got K -sure and 
Netherlands has got Atradius. If India could get a scheme like that, the banks 
would be able to offer much lower rates of interest. 
19. The Committee observes that the high cost of steel, labour costs and high 
interest rates drive up the material costs of shipbuilding. The Ministry has 
informed that interests rates are as high as 10 -12 % in India while only 2 -
2.5% in China. Upon query of the Committee on whethe r the Ministry has

20. If India is to be positioned among the top 10 nations in Ship 
Building, then an ecosystem which would address the infrastructure, 
regulatory, ﬁscal issues and capability development is to be developed. 
The Committee observes that as per the Rangarajan Commission, six

(a) natural monopoly;  
(b) non-tradability of output;  
(c) bestowing externalities on society;

 (e) non-rivalness (up to congestion limits) in consumption; and,

37. The Committee was further informed that India has the following inherent 
advantages to become a major player  in the global ship repair market.   
Strengths of Indian ship repair industry 
(i) Geostrategic location of India 
India has a long coast line of around 7516 kilometre. There are a  number of all 
weather ports which are not subjected to severe weather conditions. The 
country's considerable coastal expanse, featuring numerous all -weather ports 
shielded from harsh weathe r conditions, stands as a significant advantage.  It is 
positioned strategically along major trade and shipping routes, with 7 to 9 % of 
the global trade passing within 300 NM nautical miles  of  its coastline. This 
represents increasing market potential fo r the ship -repair business, as ship 
owners prefer to repair their ships without deviating from their trade routes as 
much as possible. Additionally, India is poised well to offer repair services to 
Indian Navy and the ally US Navy for its 5th and 7th fleet  deployed in the 
Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. 
(ii) Abundance of labour 
Among   the resources required for the Ship Repair Units to function efficiently, 
labour market plays an important role and India has a huge untapped potential in 
terms of all segments of labour – from unskilled to highly skilled. Most of the 
existing and new ship repair yards in India concentrate on new building  and 
providing services to naval and coastal vessels. 
(iii) Competitive labour rates 
Apart from abundance of labour, the subcontract labour rates for steel work, 
pipe work, blasting and painting, mechanical and electrical works are  cheaper 
in India and are comparable to labour rates in Indonesia and Vietnam. In fact it 
is 10 to 15% lower than subcontract labour rates of Indonesia. 
38. With strategic location in the trade route of tanker/bulk carrier traffic on 
east & west and  availability of trained workforce, there are  opportunities for 
huge revenue generation in the ship repair market. Ship-repair service, a 

 
21  
supplementary service pr ovided by most of the shipyards, is also a labour -
intensive activity that utilizes the existing ship -building infrastructure to provide 
additional returns on the capital invested.  It is estimated that market size for ship 
repairs for domestic vessels is a round INR 4K crore, out of which nearly 800 
crores of ship repair market is under Government/PSU control.

(i) presence of competing international ship repair yards on major trade routes  
(ii) a capability gap of Indian yards in repairing certain kinds of vessels.  
(iii) One of the major deterrents in shi p repair has been GST which is an

(iv) Further, import of raw materials and parts for use in maintenance &

SHIP RECYCLING 
57. Ship recycling plays an integral role in the maritime  industry's life cycle, 
addressing the end -of-life phase of vessels. The ship recycling industry 
converts end-of-life ships into steel bars, billets, and rods for the construction 
industry, as  well as electronic equipment and tools for homes and small 
businesses. On the  one hand, such transformation of ships into new products 
positively affects the environment  as it avoids extracting iron ore – which is 
often associated with energy-intensive processes. In addition, the usage of 
ferrous scrap extracted from vessels promotes the use of Electric Arc Furnaces 
that usually emit lower amount of carbon -di-oxide per ton of steel produced  
compared to  Blast Furnaces/Basic Oxygen Furnaces.On the other hand, ship 
recycling poses  high risks to human health and the env ironment if it is not 
carried out in a proper and safe way, thereby leading to high levels of fatalities, 
injuries and work -related diseases. Ships contain many toxic substances, such 
as PCBs, PVCs, PAHs, TBT, mercury, lead, and asbestos, which can intoxicate 
workers and can have  signiﬁcant negative e ffects on the environment when 
dumped into the soil and coastal waters. Thus, while the practice can contribute 
to a circular economy by recycling valuable materials, if not carried out 
properly, it can pose si gniﬁcant environmental degradation as well as pose 
safety risks to the workers in the industry 
58. The history of modern ship breaking dates back to the 1960s and 1970s  
wherein ship breaking was largely carried out in large ship building yards of the 
developed countries such as United States of America and Europe. The 

 
30  
high costs involved in demolition of a ship in a safe and sound manner along 
with the development of stringent environmental regulations led to shifting of 
the ship recycling business, in the early 1990s, to South Asian countries such as 
Bangladesh, India, China, Pakistan and Turkey. 
59. Currently, these five leading ship recycling nations collectively account 
for nearly 97 percent of the world's ship recycled tonnage. However,  last 
decade witnessed China  slowing down their ship recycling business due to 
the domestic production of steel and change in their policy. Thus at present  
the ship recycling business rests with the rest of the 4 countries with major ship 
recycling in South East Asia in Bangladesh, India and Pakistan. As per 
UNCTAD report, in 2022, India (30.98%),  Bangladesh (38.13%), Pakistan 
(17.23%) and Turkey (6.33%) accounted for 92.66  per cent of known ship 
scrapping across the world. 
60. India, once the leader in the global ship recycling market with a substantial 
40 percent share, has now slipped to the second position, witnessing a decline in 
its market share to approximately 25 percent. In 2022, India recycled nearly 2.34 
million gross tons (GT), securing the second positi on behind Bangladesh, which 
recycled nearly 2.87 million GT during the same period. 
61. The Indian Government has set a goal to double its existing ship 
recycling capacity through the Maritime India Vision 2030 (MIV 2030) 
initiative. 
62. Regulatory framework for Sustainable Ship Recycling in India. 
(i) Ship Breaking Code in 2013: 
In 2013, the Government of India enacted the Ship Breaking Code , a 
comprehensive set of guidelines  that  encompasses various statutes and 
rules related to the management of  hazardous waste disposal, Factory 
Rules, Explosive Act, Petroleum Rules, Atomic Regulatory Board Act, 
Labour Laws, Employee State Insurance Corporation Act, Air Act, 
Water Act, etc. This code  was  formulated  in consultation  with 

 
31  
Directorate General of Shipping, Mu mbai,  ensuring alignment  with 
the stipulation   outlined in the Hong Kong Convention for Ship 
Recycling (HKC) 2009. Hong Kong Convention for Ship Recycling, 
2009 
63. The  growing demand for ship recycling has rightly led to an increase in  
regulatory pressure at both national and international levels. This regulatory 
demand resulted in the development of the Hong Kong International 
Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships 
(HKC) by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in 2009. This 
Convention aims to establish mandatory standards  for safety and 
environmental protection standards at ship recycling yards.  Despite its 
adoption in 2009, it is noteworthy that the Hong Kong Convention has not 
yet come into force. 
64. The Convention  becomes internationally effective 24 months after  
being ratified by 15 States, representing 40 per cent of world merchant 
shipping by gross tonnage and a combined maximum annual ship recycling 
volume not less than 3  per cent of their combined tonnage. Meeting these 
criteria, the Convention is set to enter into force on 25th June 2025, 
following accession by Bangladesh and Liberia on 26th June 2023. The  
Convention will provide a global standard for ship recycling,   promoting   
level-playing   ﬁeld   amongst   ship   recycling   facilities worldwide. The 
potential impact is  a reduction  in  incentives for ship-breaking in countries 
with lax environmental and safety regulations.   Currently, shipyards are 
investing between Rs. 5 cr ores to 10 crores each to meet international 
standards, creating a financial disparity of about 30 -50 dollars between India 
and Bangladesh. 
 
 65.  The implementation  of Hong Kong International Convention 
(HKC) in July 2025  opens up more opportunities to the Indian Ship 

 
32  
Recycling Industry.  Currently  India is having 114 Ship Recycling Yards  
that are in compliance  with HKC standards and  an additional 27 yards  are  
on the  verge of  being included in  to the European list of approved Ship 
Recycling yards as per European Union Ship Recycling Regulations 
(EUSRR). This number is  nearly 4 times the combined total  of HKC 
compliant yards in other major ship recycling states. 
66.  Flag Administrations and Shipping Companies will now have to 
partner with  HKC Comp laint yards in India to ensure that their ships are 
recycled in safe and  environmentally sound manner. Further, a Voluntary 
Resolution encouraging member states to recycle their ships in HKC 
complaint yards has been adopted at the Assembly  of the   International 
Maritime Organization (IMO), London, at the initiative of India. 
67.   Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 
The Recycling of Ships Act of 2019 places restrictions and 
prohibitions on the use and installation of hazardous materials on ships, 
regardless of  whether they are intended for recycling. New ships will be 
subject to immediate restrictions  or prohibitions on hazardous materials  
starting from the legislation's effective date., whereas existing ships will have 
ﬁve years to comply It's important to note that these restrictions or 
prohibitions regarding hazardous materials do not apply to government -
operated warships and non-commercial ships.

82.    The Committee was also informed about the status of the two main 
issues  due to which ship recycling has declined in India- 
(i) Regarding the Basel ban on export of hazardous material from 
OECD to non - OECD countries, in 2019, the European Union 
decided that any hazardous  waste, which is being produced in the 
OECD countries, will not be exported to  the non-OECD countries, 
and ship -breaking comes under haz ardous waste. That is why, the 
ships were stopped from being transferred from EU countries to  the 
non-OECD countries for recycling. The status on this issue is that a 
political agreement between the European Parliament and the 
European Council has  been reached in November, 2023. With this 
agreement, by April, 2024, the EU  will allow their ships to come to 

 
39  
India after Indian yards earn EU certification.  Further, Europe 
hardly has the capacity to recycle even 10% of their own ships  and 
would have to send 9 0% of their ships for recycling to India and 
other Asian countries. A ship has an average lifetime of 30 -35 years 
and many ships would  be completing this lifetime in the next few 
years. 
(ii) Regarding the  TMT bars issue, the Committee was informed that  
95% of a ship is made of steel and before the enforcement of the BIS 
standards, 60 per cent of  ship recycling plate was used as TMT bar. 
In 2012,  BIS deleted TMT bars of  over 6 mm diameter 
manufactured from recycled steel plates from its list of  approved 
products. After the quality control order has been implemented, the  
steel has to be sent to furnace plant to make ingots which are then 
used to make  the TMT bars. However, if the reclaimed steel plates 
can be rolled directly into  TMT bars, the melting cost of makin g 
steel into ingots can be avoided.  Many small industries in the 
Bhavnagar zone were selling the TMT bars made from  recycled ship 
steel. Because of this issue, many of the small industries have  closed 
down and thousands of workers have lost their jobs. 
83.   The representative of the Ship Recyling Industries Association 
informed the Committee that the ship steel plate   is as per the ASTM -A131 
brand, which is much above the BIS standards.  The Committee studying the 
issue had visited the plant and its report is awaited. 
84.    The Committee appreciates the steps taken by all agencies involved 
to resolve the issues arising out of the Basel Ban Agreement and that EU  
ships may start to arrive in India from April, 2024 which would restore  
much of the problems aff ecting the recycling industry.   Regarding the  
issue of TMT bars, the Committee has learnt from media reports that 
the Committee set up by the Steel Ministry to look into the issue of the 

 
40  
manufacturing TMT bars from ship steel has reportedly been unable to  
devise an SoP ( Standard Operating Procedure) for usage of ship plates  
without testing of chemical composition. Non-standardised offerings and 
the absence of wider data are seen as major reasons  for the rejection of  
using ship breaking steel plates for making TM T bars. The Committee 
studying the issue has also suggested that ship breakers can sell the  
plates along with grade certiﬁcate and chemistry. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry, GMB and Ship Recyclers may cooperate  
with the Committee and ensure that large size data is made available for 
long-term durability studies to settle the issue of use of TMT bars 
for structural purposes.  The Committee also recommends that the 
industry may explore the possibility of making other forms of steel, 
apart from TMT bars, from ship scraps, like grills, strips and other bars 
which may not require the same standards as TMT bars. 
85.   The Committee has been informed that due to the issue of the 
TMT bars, thousands of workers employed in small industries selling 
such bars have lost their jobs.  The Committee recommends that

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS - AT A GLANCE 
 
SHIP BUILDING 
The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Ministry for its efforts  
under the “Make In India” programme for promotion of shipbuilding activities . 
The Committee observes that Approved Standardized Tug Design and 
Speciﬁcations (ASTDS) have been issued by the Ministry to  assist the Major 
Ports in expeditious implementation of the Make in India Order. The Committee 
desires to know how many locally built Tugs have  been ordered by the Major 
Ports since the implementation of this Order in September, 2020. 
(Para 10) 
FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE POLICY 
The Committee observes that the earlier subsidy scheme of the Ministry of 5 
years offered shipbuilders 30% extra on building ocean-going merchant vessels 
that are more than 80 metres  in length, if they are manufactured for the 
domestic market. For export orders, however, ships of  all types and capacities 
were eligible for the subsidy. In the new ﬁnancial assistance scheme, assistance 
will be given for all types of ships irrespective of size.  In the new scheme, both 
state-owned and private yards  will get the assistance only after they construct and 
hand over to the ship to  the buyer to ensure timely delivery of ships. The new 
ﬁnancial assistance scheme was therefore for double the period of the earlier 
subsidy scheme, the focus extended for all ships and ensured timely delivery 
which had been a constraint in the earlier scheme. The Committee also observes 
that when commercial orders dried up in the wake of the 2008 ﬁnancial crisis, 
Indian shipyards were focusing mainly on defence orders to stay aﬂoat. The 
Government’s ﬁnancial assistance policy was meant to help bring in more and 
major commercial ship building orders. 
(Para 13.5) 
However, the Committee observes that in the nearly 8 years since the  launch 
of the scheme, only a paltry 6 -7% of the Rs. 4000 corpus has been  utilized. The 
target of Rs. 200 crores for the next ﬁnancial year appears to  be bit rather 
unrealistic considering the poor response of the past few years. Since there 
are only 2 years left for the Scheme, it appears that the  ﬁnancial beneﬁts under 
the Scheme have not been utilized to the extent  possible. The Commit tee 
disagrees with the Ministry’s contention that the  increase in ﬁnancial assistance 
availed over the years is signiﬁcant enough  to prove that the volume of ship 
building is increasing in India. The Committee desires to know how many of the 
31 Shipyards approved under the policy have actually utilized the beneﬁts of the 

 
43  
scheme and how many  ships have been built by individual shipyards under the 
Scheme. The Committee may also be informed of the type of vessels that have 
been built by the Shipyards which ha ve actually utilized the beneﬁts.  While CSL 
in the  government sector has been able to win orders from global clients, the  
Committee desires to know whether the private shipyards beneﬁtting under  the 
scheme have also been competitive enough to win global orders to build 
large container ships. The leading Ship Building nations of China, South 
Korea and Japan thrive on export orders to build their shipbuilding  expertise. 
The Committee while appreciating the Government’s efforts to  create an 
ecosystem for boosting shipbuilding recommends that the Ministry should 
evaluate the reasons for the poor utilization of the ﬁnancial  assistance scheme 
and whether technical reasons like high imports of material for shipbuilding, less 
automation in the shipbuilding proc esses are  affecting the competitiveness of 
Indian Ship yards. 
(Para 13.6) 
Promotion of tonnage under Indian Flag 
 If India is to be positioned among the top 10 nations in Ship Building,  then an 
ecosystem which would address the infrastructure, regulatory, ﬁscal issues and 
capability development is to be developed. The Committee observes that as per 
the Rangarajan Commission, six indicators  of sectors to be classiﬁed under 
Infrastructure were –  
(a) natural monopoly;  
(b) non-tradability of output;  
(c) bestowing externalities on society;  
(d) high- sunk costs or asset speciﬁcity; 
 (e) non-rivalness (up to congestion limits) in consumption; and,  
(f) possibility of price exclusion.  The Commission had  recommended the 
inclusion of Ships and other Vessel s on the basis of the  characteristics 
from (d) to (f).  
(Para 20) 
The Committee appreciates the grant of infrastructure status to Shipyards 
due to which the Ship Building industry  would be able to avail long term 
funding at lower rates and for various forms of ﬁnancial assistance, beneﬁts 
and concessions.  The Committee  also observes that the Government is 
planning to give infrastructure status  to coastal shipping.  The Committee 
recommends that the Government may  consider extending infrastructure 
status granted to Shipyards to all ships and Vessels, not only coastal shipping. 

 
44  
(Para 21) 
         The Committee recommends that the production of specialized steels 
domestically should be incentivized and strategic partnerships with global 
suppliers should be established to ensure a cost -effective supply chain to 
address the high costs of materials. The Committee recommends that se tting 
up a specialized ﬁnancing  institution/marine ﬁnance scheme could provide a 
much-needed boost to  the shipbuilding industry.  The Ministry may also 
explore the possibility of  getting a risk insurance cover scheme for ships in 
India on the lines of the  ones in Korea and China which would attract 
domestic and international investors to participate in financing maritime 
projects. The Committee observes that the private sector  ship building 
companies are mostly struggling with hardly any proﬁts, the  most recent 
casualties being Western India, Bharati and ABG Shipyards. The 
Committee recommends that the private sector must be considered as  much of 
a stakeholder in shipping as the public sector and a level playing  field for both 
sectors must be the concern of the Government. 
(Para 22) 
        The Committee observes that Skilled manpower is the most essential  
prerequisite in Ship Building industry. Ensuring proper education and 
training could bolster the effectiveness of the industry. The Committee 
observes that  as per studies  the labour productivity value for India is 
approximately 10 times lower than the major shipbuilding nations. All these 
translate to about 20 -25 per cent cost advantage for major shipbuilding 
nations vis -à-vis India. The Committee recommends  that investments in 
automation should be encouraged in order to improve labor productivity and 
reduce costs. 
(Para 23) 
One of the constraints of shipbuilding in India is the limited investment in 
R&D in ship  design and innovation.  The Committee recommends  that the 
Government focus on skill development and developing an R&D base to 
increase the competitiveness of the Indian shipbuilding industry. 
(Para 24) 
          The MIV document also advocates creation of a Maritime Development 
Fund to provide easy acce ss to working capital and long -term ﬁnance needs 
across marine sectors.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
implement the creation of the  Fund which can give access to Indian ship 
owners to improve their capacity   and shipyards to improve the infrastructure 
(Para 25) 
GREEN SHIP BUILDING 

 
45  
The Committee observes that ship engines and ship fuels are  undergoing 
rapid change and moving away from fossil fuels to new fuels  like green 
methanol, green ammonia etc. In the near future, every goods/service will 
have an identiﬁable carbon footprint and carbon neutral  products and 
services will have a competitive advantage. While the Committee appreciates 
the initiatives of CSL in constructing green vessels,  there does not appear to 
be the same efforts on the part of other shipyards.  The Committee 
recommends that the National Centre for Excellence in Green Ports and 
Shipping may act as a nodal entity for green shipping so  that there is a 
coordinated effort by all shipyards to position India as a  global hub for green 
shipping. 
(Para 32) 
Overall, the Committee observed that faced with high financial costs, the 
shipbuilders in India encounter difficulties in expanding their operations and 
providing competitive pricing to end -users. This predicament has led to low 
orders, diminished profits and a constrained capacity for reinvestment. 
(Para 33) 
As per a FICCI report, Indian shipyards require about 25 -35% of the 
ship's cost as working capital during construction, with interest rates 
averaging 10 -10.5%. In contrast, ov erseas shipbuilding yards enjoy 
significantly lower rates along with lower -interest export credit. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that measures to reduce interest rates on 
working capital for Indian shipyards be explored .  
(Para 34) 
The Committee feels that a potential Production Linked Incentive (PLI) 
scheme can go a long way to boost the shipbuilding industry. This 
multifaceted scheme could include output -based rewards, wherein 
shipbuilders stand to receive incentives commensurate with t he quantity and 
type of ships they manufacture. Additionally, the PLI scheme might introduce 
investment incentives tailored to encourage shipbuilders to modernize their 
facilities and integrate advanced manufacturing technologies. Shipbuilding 
entities mak ing investments in upgrading infrastructure and adopting state -
of-the-art manufacturing processes could qualify for these investment 
incentives. This dual approach of incentivizing both production and 
investment could create a dynamic environment that prop els the shipbuilding 
industry towards technological advancement, increased efficiency and global 
competitiveness. 
(Para 35)

SHIP REPAIR 
The Committee notes that India is suitably located to offer repair services for 
the Indian Navy as well as the US Navy for its 5 th and 7 th Fleet deployed in the 
Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. It has also been seen that many contracts of 
the US Navy have been awarded to either private Indian Shipyards or to other 
foreign shipyards.  Indian PSU Shipyards are not strong contenders for repair  
amidst global competition.  The Committee has also learnt from media reports 
that the US Navy and L&T have signed a 5 year Master Ship Repair Agreement 
(MSRA) which shows that the US is committed to utilize ship repair facilities on a 
regular basis at the  L&T shipyard in Katupalli in Tamil Nadu. The Committee 
understands that Mazagon Docks Shipbuilders have also concluded an agreement 
with an entity of the US Navy. While appreciating the above -said achievements, 
the Committee feels that while other Asian c ountries, notably Singapore and 
Japan have bagged many foreign ship repair orders, India has lagged behind due 
to inadequate infrastructural support services needed for ship repair. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may make efforts to improve the  
infrastructure to enable PSU shipyards to bag ship repair orders. 
(Para 53) 
The Committee notes that as per the Statistics of the Ministry placed at 
Annexure-II, 725 ships were repaired in private shipyards during the years from 
2019-20 to 2021 -22 whereas  448 ships were repaired in Government/PSU 
shipyards in the same period. Among Government/PSU shipyards, Cochin 
Shipyards handles the bulk of the ship repair market.  In 2021 -22 for example, out

repaired by CSL, 33 by Goa Shipyard and 14 by Hindustan Shipyard Ltd. That is,

Deendayal Port have 1 Dry Dock each but no ship repair activity has been 
undertaken by these Major Ports in the last few  years.  The Committee desires to

The Committee met at 11:00 A.M. on Friday, the 6th October, 2023, in Committee Room 
„1‟, First Floor, Parliament House Annexe Extension Building, New Delhi.

 Shri Madhu S. Nair, Chairman and Managing Director, Cochin Shipyard Limited  
     (Complete list of witnesses who attended the meeting is attached as Annexure)  
 
2.         At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and infor med them that the 
Committee has taken up the subject “ Status of Ship building, Ship Repair and Ship breaking 

66 
 
industries in the Country ” and has invited the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways, to 
deliberate on the said subject.  
 
 (After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
 
3.      The Chairman welcomed the Secretary , Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways; 
Chairman & Managing Director, Cochin Shipyard Limited; and other Senior Officers  of the 
Ministry. The Chairman informed that the Ministry has been invited to share their views and 
valuable suggestions on various aspects related to the subject  “Status of Ship building, Ship 
Repair and Ship breaking industries in the Country ”. He remarked that India, despite having a 
long coastline of over 7,500 km, favourable geographical location and  low labour costs,  has an 
insignificant share in the global shipbuilding and ship repair market. He also highlighted that  
India‟s share in Ship Breaking or Recycling market is  about 40% of the global market, perhaps 
due to the weak enforcement of environment and labor -related laws in India, as compared to 
developed countries. He further desired that the Committee may be appr ised on the following 
points:- 
i. Ministry‟s plans to promote and incentivise the shipbuilding and ship repair industries , to 
achieve the Maritime India Vision 2030 and be once again among the top ten nations in 
shipbuilding by 2030; 
ii. Impact of policies related to granting Infrastructure status and financial assistance , on the 
growth of shipbuilding industry; 
iii. Roadmap of the Ministry to further promote the Ship Recycling industry; and 
iv. Efforts to enforce stricter environmental and labour laws to ensure the safety of the 
workers in the Ship Breaking industry.  
 
4.         The Secretary, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) alongwith 
Chairman & Managing Director, Cochin Shipyard Limited  (CMD, CSL) made a detailed 
presentation on the subject and  highlighted the Ministry‟s Maritime India Vision, 2030 which 
envisages improving India's rankings in shipbuilding and ship repair; enhancing country‟s 
capabilities for shipbuilding with hybrid or green fuels; and positioning India as the global leader 
in s hip recycling industry.  The Secretary, MoPSW informed the Committee that there are 43 
shipyards in the country out of which 08 are in the Central Public Sector ; 02 with State 
Governments; and remaining 33 in the private sector. He informed the Committee that the cost of 

67 
 
ship building is higher in India primarily because of three factors viz., material cost; low labour 
productivity due to lack of automation ; and higher financing cost, in comparison with China, 
Korea and Japan. He also informed the Committee that while shipbuilding is declared as 
infrastructure, ships are not infrastructure , so they do not get long term financing and other 
advantages. Upon being queried by the Chairman, the Ministry clarified that while India is 
competitive in normal and automotive gr ade steels, steel for shipbuilding requires more 
specialization. Besides, the small market and high transportation costs further the cost of steel.  
 
5.         The Committee was informed that the present share  of India in Shipbuilding, Ship repair 
and Ship breaking/recycling in the global market is about less than 1 %, 1 -2% and 25%, 
respectively, and the Ministry is taking certain steps with regard to demand activation; ecosystem 
development; fiscal & regulatory  support; and capability development, to improve India‟s share 
and global rankings as well.  The Additional Secretary, MoPSW added that the Government has 
initiated several policy measures for the revival of the Shipbuilding industry viz., introducing 
Ship Building Financial Assistance  (SBFA) Policy, 2016 ; granting infrastructure status to 
shipbuilding in 2016; drafting Standard Operating Procedure for chartering/procurement of tugs; 
and effective implementation of the Atmanirbhar Bharat (Make in India) Policy for generation of 
employment. Under the SBFA Policy, 2016 , 14% of the cost of the ship is provided by the 
Government through an electronically driven scheme, implemented by the Directorate General of 
Shipping, from 2016 to 2026 . About  Rs. 58 crore were disbursed under this scheme in the 
previous year, while the budgetary allocation for 2023-24 stands at Rs. 102 crore. He also stated 
that under the SBFA Policy, 2016, assistance will be extended to vessels where propulsion is by 
means of 'green fuels' such as Methanol/ Ammonia / Hydrogen fuel cells and where propulsion is 
by 'electric and hybrid', at 30% and 20%, respectively, in order to incentivise green ship building. 
 
6. Further, the CMD, Cochin Shipyard Limited enumerated the various  types of ships/ 
ferries which are being developed in the country, as follows:- 
 Autonomous zero-emission ferry: a fully autonomous vessel and 100% export order by 
Norway; 
 Windfarm Service Vessels: equipped with Methanol engines to reduce emissions; 
 Zero Emission Shortsea Container Vessel: World‟s first hydrogen fuel cell powered 
vessel, for export order of Norway; 
 Future Proof Dry Cargo Vessel: with battery hybrid diesel-electric propulsion; 

68 
 
 Hybrid Electric Water Metro Ferry: already being used in the Kochi Water Metro and 
supported by the German funding; 
 Hydrogen Fuel Cell Ferry: India‟s first, being developed by CSL and after trials will be 
shifted to Varanasi for operation; and 
 Fully Electric Catamaran Ferry: fully electric, ordered by Inland Waterways Authority of 
India for NWs 1 & 2. 
  
7. The CMD, CSL highlighted the efforts being taken by private and small shipyards in the 
field of green shipbuilding including the development of energy -efficient electric hybrid vessel s 
by Chowgule shipyard in Goa and India‟s first solar -powered ferry named Aditya being 
developed by a Kerala based company called NavAlt. He informed the Committee about various 
other initiatives being taken by the Ministry for development of green shipping , including 
development of methanol or ammonia fueled vessels ; CSL‟s Maritime Startup Funding 
Programme with a corpus of Rs. 50 crore in collaboration with IIT, Madras and IIM, Kozhikode; 
and inauguration of National Centre of Excellence in Green Ports and Shipping in collaboration 
with TERI Institute, Gurugram.  
 
8. The Secretary, MoPSW also highlighted the roadmap for Green Shipping involving 
Green Tug Transition Programme; Special Finance Assistance for Green Ships; and Urban Water 
Transport Models, through which  the Ministry aims to achieve 02 green tugs at all major ports 
by 2026, and thereafter 75% green tugs by 2035 and 100% green tugs by 2040, at all the major 
ports.  
 
9. The Additional Secretary, MoPSW apprised the Committee about the ship repair industry 
in the country. He stated that the market size of ship repairs for domestic vessels is around Rs. 
4,000 crore, out of which nearly Rs. 800 crore is under the control of Government and PSUs. 
The main issues affecting the ship repair industry were the higher cost of procurement, lack of 
efficiency in the working processes, absence of modern tools and higher turnaround time. He 
added that in order to improve the status of ship repair industry, certain steps are being taken  
which includes reducing repair cost by at  least 40%; reduc ing turnaround time for repairs by at  
least 60%; optimis ing working processes; im proving utilization of ship repair facilities ; and 
focusing o n training &  skill development  and collaboration with foreign partners to adopt 
international best practices . He also mentioned that the Ministry is developing two major ship 

69 
 
repair clusters at Kochi & Vadinar and building an ancillary ecosystem to improve spares 
availability, which will enhance the ship repair capability in India.  
 
10. The representative of the Ministry also briefed the Committee about the Ship 
Breaking/Recycling industry in the country and stated that as per the UNCTAD Report, 2022, 
India is at number 02 among the ship recycling nations, having recycled 31% of the  World‟s 
total recycled tonnage. He added that ship recycling primarily concentrated at Alan g Sosiya Ship 
Recycling Yards in Bhavnagar, Gujarat and the process is governed by the Ship Breaking Code, 
2013. Further, he elaborated upon the Recycling yard at Alang which is owned by the Gujarat 
Maritime Board, having a 10 km long sea front and 131 ope rational plots which caters to 98% 
and 32% of ship recycling market in India and  World, respectively. Upon a query by the 
Chairman, the Ministry informed that the steel in the ships is recycled to make rods, grills etc., 
and the fixtures in the ship like chandelier, refrigerator etc. are sold in the retail and wholesale 
market at Alang.  
 
11. The Committee was also informed about the Hong Kong Convention (HKC) which is a 
convention of International Maritime Organisation and deals with the environmental and labour 
standards at the ship recycling yards. The representative of the Ministry stated that 103 plots  at 
the recycling yards at Alang are HKC compliant, and 27 of these have upgraded their compliance 
levels to meet the standards of the European Union (EU). He added that the EU Ship Recycling 
Regulation (EU -SRR) are very stringent and include downstream waste management system; 
concrete yard floors to prevent any material from going in to the water while recycling; 
development of social & health infrastructure  along with a 24X7 trauma centre ; and welfare & 
training of workers . He stated that to further the ship recycling industry, the Central and State 
Government of Gujarat has taken various initiatives including ratification of the “HKC for safe 
and environmentally sound ship recycling , 2009”; enactment of Recycling of Ships Act, 2019; 
amendment in ship recycling regulations, 2015; and master planning of Alang Recycling yard 
with development of new plots for capacity expansion.    
 
12. The representatives of the Ministry also highlighted two major issues being found i n ship 
recycling. The first being the regulation by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) of the steel 
recycled from ships which has prevented their use for reinforcement purposes. The issue is under 
study by a BIS Committee. The second issue is the non -arrival of ships from EU countries, due 

70 
 
to Basel Ban Agreement in 2019 which prohibits any hazardous material (like ships for 
recycling) of OECD countries from being taken to non -OECD countries. The hazardous content 
in ships is about 0.22 to 0.30 percent and include s oil, paint, insulation material, asbestos etc.  
However, the EU has very limited recycling capability and are dependent on India and other 
countries for ship recycling.  
  
13. The Chairman and Members also raised the following queries/ issues , some of which 
were replied to by the representatives of MoPSW and the CMD, CSL:- 
 Details of hazardous material being used for ship building; 
 Process being followed for inviting the foreign partner and what was their response of to 
invest money for the development of Cochin Shipyard; 
 Details of ship breaking units in India;  
 Initiatives being adopted for development of Cochin Shipyard; 
 Tentative Timeline for completion of initiatives taken by the Ministry including 
standardization of operations and increasing manpower in terms of ship repair industry;  
 Reasons for Alang Ship Breaking Yard prominence in ship recycling; 
 Proposal to operationalise Aditya – India‟s first solar powered ferry, in different parts of 
the country; 
 Timeline for completion of two ship repair clusters at Kochi and Vadinar; 
 Implementation of international regulations at the ship recycling yards for the safety and 
welfare of employees including medical facility, trauma care centre and waste 
management system; 
 Status of vegetation/tree plantation (Neem and Peepal)  around the Alang Ship Breaking 
Yard to minimize the impact of pollution;  
 Reasons for EU to select only two yards out of the eight ship breaking yards inspected at 
Alang; 
 Possibility of utilizing Ethanol instead of Methanol vessel operations; 
 Steps taken to reduce the time taken for turnaround operations; 
 Comparative study regarding the performance of Central Government, State Government 
and Private Sector shipyards; 
 Reasons for ship breaking units being concentrated in the Indian subcontinent; 
 Steps being taken to address the financial viability of Kochi Water Metro; and 
 Ministry‟s plans to give interest subsidy to encourage the ship building industry in India. 

71 
 
 
14.       The Secretary, MoPSW took note of all queries and suggestions made by the Members. 
The Chairman gave a list of ten questions on the subject to the Ministry and  directed that written 
replies to the se ten questions and also to the points which had not been adequately answered 
during the meeting, may be sent within one week.

74 
 
2.        The Chairman extended greetings to all the Members and informed that in the last 
meeting on 6 th October, 2023, the Committee heard the views of the Secretary, Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping &  Waterways on the subject of Ship Building, Repair and Recycling. Now, 
the Committee has invited the representatives of Gujarat Maritime Board, Ship Recycling 
Industries Association and the Directorate General of Shipping to provide valuable insights 
into the Ship Recycling Industry.  
(After the witnesses took their respective seats) 
3.        The Chairman welcomed the representatives of Gujarat Maritime Board, Ship 
Recycling Industries Association and the Directorate General of Shipping.  He observed that 
the Alang Ship Recycling Yard located in Bhavnagar, Gujarat, is one of the most preferred 
ship recycling destinations around the world and it caters to nearly 98 per cent of the 
recycling capacity in India. The Chairman asked the  Ship Recycling Association  to provide 
information regarding the safety and sanitary conditions of the workers and the welfare 
measures taken to ensure their well -being at the Alang Yard. Citing the ill effects of the 
recycling activity and weak enforcement of environment and labour-related laws in India, the 
Chairman enquired whether the ship yards in Alang are adhering rigorously to the 
regulations prescribed under the Hong Kong Convention (HKC).  He also sought information 
about the details of infrastructure development undertaken  by the Gujarat Maritime Board as 
well as the process of allotment of plots to ship breakers 
The Chairman observed that  India‟s current share in the ship breaking or recycling market is 
about 25 per cent of the global share, having decreased from about 40 % earlier.   The 
Chairman sought information on the present status, challenges faced, possible solutions and 
the scope of improvement in the area of ship recycling.  He observed that the Ministry in its 
earlier meeting had cited the following two reasons for  this decrease and desired to know the 
status of the same : 
 The policy change by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) due to which the TMT 
(Thermo-Mechanically Treated) steel bars made from recycled steel from ships are no 
longer recognized for reinforcement purposes, leading to significant revenue loss and 
reduction in turnover for the ship-breaking industries at Alang.  A Committee under 
the chairmanship of BIS was examining the issue and was due to give its report 
shortly.   

75 
 
 The second major issue was stated to be non-arrival of ships from EU countries due to 
the Basel Ban Agreement of 2019 which prohibits any hazardous material of OECD 
countries from being taken to non-OECD countries. 
5.        The Chairman asked Directorate General of Shipping (DGS)  about the latest measures 
and initiatives taken to enhance safety standards for shipping and prevent accidents at sea 
and addressing challenges related to piracy and security threats in maritime regions. 
6.       The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board, informed that  as of 2022, India is at second 
position with 32.28 per cent of the global share in ship recyling, after Bangladesh.   The 
Alang Ship Recycling yard has recycled almost 4.5 million LTD or more than 400 ships a 
year, accounting for 98% of India's total and 3 2% of the global ship volume. Out of 131 
operational plots, 101 are HKC -compliant, while 27 have applied for EU certification for 
ship recycling. He informed that this industry follows a circular economy and all items are 
reused or recycled. There are more  than 200 shops of retailers and wholesaler dealers in 
Alang for items recovered from ships which are sold there.   There are more than 60 -plus 
induction furnaces and 80 -plus re -rolling mills at Bhavnagar which re -rolls the steel 
recovered from the ships to  provide  TMT bars.   There is systematic disposal with TSDF 
(Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities), and environmentally and ecologically -
compliant method for ship recycling is being used. 
7.       He informed that the trend in ship recycling is fluct uating not only in India but all 
around the globe.  In 2021, all across the world, approximately 13,000 ships were recycled, 
and, in 2022, the figure came down to almost 6,500 due to reasons like increased transport 
costs and adverse impact of Covid -19. How ever, the following major reasons have been 
identified for substantial decline in Alang: 
 Decline in the business-cycle of the world economy;  
 Shortage of ships and increased freight rates;  
 Strong competition among nations and their need for steel;  
 Non-arrival of ship from EU countries; 
 Non-recognition by BIS standards; and 
 Rise in cost of recycling due to statute, environment and safety-compliance. 
 

76 
 
8.        He apprised the Committee that seven major initiatives that were required to be taken 
for HKC comp liance have been completed, namely, recycling facility management plan, 
ship-specific dismantling plan, oily waste reception facility, paint -chip removal plan, 
asbestos waste handling, hazardous waste management and water treatment plants.   He also 
informed that three conditions required for HKC to come into force have also been 
completed. Thereafter, he explained about the impact and benefits of Hong Kong 
International Convention. 
9.        It was informed that for compliance of EU certification, Medical f acilities at yards are 
also being developed and fifty -six per cent of the work of hospital facilities has been 
completed. For training purposes of workers, an advanced labour safety and training institute 
has been established. Since its inception in 2003, more than 1.5 lakh workers have been 
trained there. Free accommodation has been provided to more than one thousand workers.   
With reference to downstream waste management, it was informed that 99.95 per cent of the 
salvaged materials are dispatched to down stream industries and traders for use. However, 
less than 0.05 per cent is treated as hazardous waste. The facility to treat this waste will be 
upgraded to make it fully complied with EU norms. 
10.      Regarding the issue of non -arrival of ships from EU countries, tt was submitted 
that Ministry of External Affairs has informed that a political agreement, that is the EU's 
Waste Shipment Regulation has been reached between the European Parliament and the 
European Council in November, which signifies that the EU will agree to send their ships to 
Alang yards by next year after the certification. The Committee was also informed that the 
Government of India has taken following steps to support this industry: 
 Customs duty on ship recycling has been reduced from 2.5 per cent to zero, which has 
helped the yard owners. 
  Incentives of Rs.50 lakhs have been given to those yards which are HKC certified. 
 Annual charges have also been relaxed for the yards to the tune of Rs.52 crore in the 
financial year 2020-21, 2021-22 and Rs.28 crore in 2023-24. 
11.     The Committee was also informed about the short -term, medium-term and long -term 
initiatives for the development of the Alang yard.   It was informed that amen dments have 
been made in Ship Recycling Regulations, 2015 as a short -term measure.  As a mid -term 
measure, auctioning the vacant plots have been started and as a long -term measure, a Master 

77 
 
Plan of Alang -Sosiya Ship Recycling Yard to develop new plots and d ouble the capacity of 
the plots has been adopted.   The Committee was also informed that a 10 -kilometre long 
stretch along the coastline is also being developed, which will lead Alang to become the 
highest capacity ship recycling yard in the world. Further,  the plot sizes will also be 
expanded from 40-80 m to 200-300m. 
12.      The Chairman again raised the issue of non recognition of TMT steel bars for 
reinforcement purposes and asked about the difference between Basel Ban Agreement, Hong 
Kong Convention an d EU recognition. The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board explained that in 
2019, the European Union decided that any hazardous waste, produced in the OECD 
countries, will not be exported to the non -OECD countries. Since the ship -breaking 
industries come under the  hazardous waste category, the ships were stopped from being 
transferred from EU countries to the non-OECD countries for recycling.   
(Shri Dushyant Singh in the Chair) 
13.      A Member enquired about the development of Trauma centre and other facilities like 
library, cultural centres, etc. The CEO informed that fifty -six per cent of the work has been 
completed and the hospital with state -of-the-art technology and equipment will be ready 
within next few months. With reference to community centres, he informed that some centres 
have been built, however, they are not functional yet. He also noted the issue raised by the 
Member regarding provision of green spaces, libraries, etc for the psychological well -being 
of workers and assured that action would be taken on the same. 
14.      Upon a query by a Member about the impact on labour safety after application of rules 
and regulations of HKC, CEO apprised that it has led to increase in labour safety because the 
entire process of recycling is now systematic and more methodological. However, a  problem 
which is now occurring is due to the size of the plots because the size of the ships nowadays 
is quite huge and the yards are smaller.   
15.      Upon the query by the Acting Chairman regarding GST earnings and the nee d for 
development of tertiary industries, CEO informed that the major problem lies with the BIS 
standards as it does not allow recycled steel bars (more than 8 mm) to be used for building or 
other purposes. Earlier, before the enforcement of BIS standards, most of the small industries 

78 
 
were selling the bars made by recycling ship steel in Bhavnagar zone. However, now most of 
these industries have closed and thousand of workers have lost their jobs. The Acting 
Chairman also enquired about the financial struct ure, earning and taxation system. In the 
response, CEO stated that they have conducted research to expand their capacity and will 
submit a report for the information of the Committee. He also informed that in the coming 
ten years, more than 20000 ships wil l be recycled and since Europe has capacity to recycle 
only ten per cent of their ships, rest 90 per cent will be sent to India. 
16.      The Acting Chairman also enquired about the agreements with EU countries to create 
more shipbuilding areas and technol ogy exchange. The CEO, Gujarat Maritime Board 
(GMB) stated that once the Basel Ban hurdle is over, then agreement can be made with the 
countries for ship recycling. It was also informed that these days, the recycling plan of ship is 
made at the time of its  construction. GMB and the Ship Recycling Association have been in 
talks with ship owners to understand their requirements for recycling and accordingly 
enhancing the recycling facilities at Alang as per new technologies and methodologies. 
17.      Thereafter, Secretary, Ship Recycling Industries Association, gave a brief 
presentation. He informed that Ship Recycling in India began in 1912 in Kolkata and 
Mumbai. In 1983, a ship recycling yard was established on the western coast of Gulf of 
Cambay near Alang  Village due to its high intertidal gradient, allowing large ships to reach 
the shore.   He also informed that Alang Shipyard is eco -friendly, cost-efficient and follows 
Green Ship Recycling as it does not use any natural resources like iron ore or coal or  
electricity or water for production of steel. 
18.      With reference to reduction of Custom Duty on recycling to zero, the Acting 
Chairman enquired about the benefits and the beneficiaries. He also asked about the 
expansion of recycling facilities to oth er coastal areas. The representatives of GMB 
submitted that they would send a detailed note on this issue. The Secretary also informed that 
regular medical check -up for all workers in the recycling yards is conducted biannually and 
specific medical check-up is conducted for the workers involved in removal and handling of 
hazardous materials like asbestos, glass wood and hydrocarbons. In this connection, the 
Acting Chairman sought information about the common illness being faced by the workers. 
CEO, GMB informed that trade specific disease are not prevalent there. However, accidents 

79 
 
happen sometimes and a trauma centre is under construction to handle such cases. It was also 
informed that during Covid period only 20 people were found to be Covid positive out o f 
40000 people. There have been no casualty in Alang and workers are properly trained 
through mock drills, emergency preparedness. Workers are also equipped with PPE kits and 
helmets for their safety.  
19.      Secretary, Ship Recyling Association apprised  the Committee that the operation 
procedure is supervised by a certified safety officer, and key facility equipment includes fire 
fighting, water storage, breathing sets, gas meters, Co2, H2S, and oxygen meters for 
confidential work, ensuring safety in all  operations. Central Salt Research Organisation 
regularly conducts environmental impact analysis including monitoring of gas emission, sea 
water and soil water. It has been found till today there has been no instance of oil spilling in 
Alang. It was also i nformed by Chairman, GMB that training is a pre -requisite for any 
worker. There are three training modules free of cost – 12 days‟ comprehensive safety 
training programme, 3 days‟ refresher safety training only for workers who trained earlier 
and then 2 days‟ for gas cutter safety training. There is special training and drills for confined 
space, asbestos removal and evacuation in emergency. 
20.      The Committee was informed about the achievements of Alang yard like mandatory 
issuance coverage to all, AICC  Provident Fund and   other benefits; multispecialty hospital 
started from   March 2019, operated by Red Cross; upgradation to fulfil remaining facility 
i.e., trauma centre; fully equipped operation theatre is in progress; a housing colony, phase I, 
under operation from 2018. There is also a plan to develop housing colony in front of each 
yard equipped with fully operated TSDF site, which is available only in India.   
21.      The Acting Chairman also raised the issue of payment to labour when there is no 
work. However, it was informed that Government supports the plot owners. The Chairman 
further enquired about the fee for a plot. In response, CEO, GMB informed that the plot is 
available on lease basis which costs around  three hundred rupees per square metre.  There are 
different other charges like development charges, housing cess, etc and a subsidy is given 
when there is a recession. In 2021, around Rs. 54 crore worth of different charges was 
subsidized to ease the burden on plot owners. He also assured to se nd a note indicating plot 
fee, labour cost and other different charges. 

80 
 
22.      Upon a query on adherence to HCK norms, Secretary, Ship Recycling Associatio n 
informed that they are spending around Rs.5 crore to Rs.10 crore in each yard for meeting 
international standards.  There is a gap of around 30 to 50 dollars for Pakistan, Bangladesh 
and India. Around 15 dollars have been saved by reducing the duty of 2.5 percent and the 
remaining 15 -20 dollars will be saved once the HKC comes into force. With referenc e to 
expenses, it was informed that it varies from ship to ship. Reefer ships have higher costs as it 
has more hazardous waste and requires more labour and lengthy removal processes. 
Container and bulker ships have lower costs as there is no hazardous mate rial. Handling 
hazardous waste as per HKC certification, costs 15 -20 dollars per ship. Class N.K. ships 
charge 20 lakh rupees per annum for certification maintenance, unlike Pakistan and 
Bangladesh.  
23.     It was also reiterated that the steel in Pakista n is recycled and used in all construction 
works because there is shortage of steel. The cost for the plot owner to sell the steel turns out 
to be much more than what we get in India. However, in case of India, BIS Standard does not 
allow more than a certa in diameter of re -rolled steel for structural work. Before this quality 
control order, the ship recycling industry used 60 per cent of its ship recycling plate for 
manufacturing TMT bars. After implementing of this   quality control order, the industry 
became scrap-based, sending material to a furnace plant for ingot production. The industry is 
working on its ASTM -A131 steel plate, which exceeds BIS standards. The committee had 
already visited the plant and praised the plate's quality. If approved, the plate  will be used in 
a rolling mill for TMT bars. 
24.      Secretary, Ship Recycling Association apprised the Committee that they had a 
meeting with GMB and Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways in October and 
convinced EU to amend their hazardous waste la w, which will give an edge to India and EU 
ships may reach India by next year.    By voluntarily enforcing HKC 2009, Alang yards can 
establish a minimum three to four -year long -term association with selected 
ports/plots/facility. There are approximately 5000 owners in the world and 300 recycling 
yards and 111 HKC complied Indian yards, but only 15 -20 ship owners are sending their 
ships in India. Therefore, support from international community becomes important.  

81 
 
25.      CEO also clarified that, in the European Union, all the countries together have only 10 
per cent capacity to recycle the ships. GMB proved to EU that 90 per cent of the ships were 
going to non -EU compliant yards for recycling purposes and convinced them to certify 
Alang yards  which are complying with the regulations. With reference to flags of 
convenience, Chief surveyor, DGS informed that after the enforcement of HKC or SOLAS 
Convention, the era of flags of convenience will be over.   
26.      Secretary, Ship Recycl ing Association informed the Committee about the steps taken 
by Government of India to boost the ship recycling industry . The MoPSW has passed the 
Ship Recycling Act, 2019, removing 2.5 per cent Customs Duty, amending the Admiralty 
Act for smooth recycling , and providing Rs.50 lakh financial assistance to HKC -compliant 
plots in form of subsidy. He added that the Central Government provided financial assistance 
of Rs.11 crore for construction of labour housing colony, Rs.20 crore for hospital, Rs.49 
crore for obtaining the HKC -compliant plot and Rs.30 crore for providing training. It was 
also informed that GMB and Government of India participated in EUSR Summit to boost 
business.  Also, the MoPSW is supporting the industry by amending the Quality Control 
Order.  .  Ministry of Health is working on the affiliation of GMB multi-specialty hospital, its 
upgradation and work as per the EU requirement.   MoPSW is also working to amend a few 
clauses of Ship Recycling Code, 2013. Government has also resolved the issue pertaining to 
Customs, GPCB, ESIC and also some finance related issues. 
27.      He also gave brief overview of steps taken by GMB for boosting the industry by 
constructing a 25 crores labour housing colony, providing financial relief of 52 crores in 
2023-24 and 26 crores during Covid -19, amending the Ship Recycling Regulation, allotting 
free land, merging plots for larger ships, upgrading the multi -speciality hospital, and locating 
a new landfill site. He also added that the hospital run by GMB is providin g free -of-cost 
facilities not only to the Ship Recycling Yard's labour but also to the twenty surrounding 
villages. Thereafter, he showed some visuals of Alang Ship recycling Yard showcasing the 
work process at the site. He also made a point that GMB is pa ying ESIC for each and every 
labour, however, till today, the ESIC has not spent a single penny on recycling yard. 
 
 

82 
 
 
28.        The stakeholders assured to give the details in writing on the issues which could not 
be answered at that point of time. 
(The witnesses then withdrew)

30.       The meeting adjourned at 04.54 PM.

Capacity of Major Ports 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that of all the Major Ports, only the JNPA has achieved a 
world-class Turn Around time of 24 hours for Containers. The Committee commends the 
JNPA for this seminal achievement and exhorts the other Major Ports to follow the good 
practices of the JNPA to improve their respective Turn Around times. 
 (Para 22) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee also notes that the Average Ship Output Per Berth Day, like the TRT, 
shows only a marginal increase for many ports, and some ports have even shown a decline in 
output. Though the Paradip Port has crossed the threshold of 30,000 tones, yet unless all 
Major Ports project discernible increase in their performance parameters, the efforts of 
individual Ports would not help achieve the objectives. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry takes special efforts towards monitoring the ground situation at ports that impede 
the performance progress.. 
(Para 27) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. Several mechanization projects 
are currently underway at various stages in t he Ports. The completion of these mechanization 
projects will contribute significantly to the overall improvement of OSBD. These projects are 
monitored at both the port and ministry levels, ensuring effective oversight and successful 
implementation. Additionally, the Ministry is focusing on enhancing the OSBD through an 
increased share of Public -Private Partnership (PPP) berths, which will not only improve 
operational efficiency but also boost OSBD. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee observes that mechanization of berths, minimum dwell time, skilled 
labor, and port connectivity for reduction in evacuation time are essential to reduce the 

3 
 
Turnaround time and recommends that the Ministry may make efforts toBring in greater PPP 
partnerships for mechanization of berths. 
 (Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1      Noted. 
 
DRAFTS OF INDIAN PORTS VERSUS FOREIGN PORTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.        The Committee observes that the world over, the shipping industry is moving towards 
mega-size vessels with ships of 20,000 TEU and above. While a Capesize vessel requires 
upwards of 18m draft, the draft at Indian ports is in the range of 14 -16 metersonly, owing to 
siltation. The Committee observes that the geographical and topogra phical limitations being 
are identical for both the public and private ports inIndia, how but the private ports have 
been able to develop drafts matching with world class ports whereas the public ports have 
lagged behind. The Gujarat Pipavav port has a dra ft of 18.5 metres and plans to extend it to 
20.5 metres. The Committee, while acknowledging the high dredging costs, underscores that 
the ports drafts must be in sync with the growing size of the ships in the interest of 
maximizing the benefits of large ships in cargo handling. 
 (Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1      Most of the Major Ports have achieved a draft depth of 14 meters, while other Major 
Ports i.e. Kamarajar, Paradip, Deendayal, and Cochin, are working towards achieving even 
deeper drafts of up to 18 meters. Furthermore, the development of Vadhavan Port into a 
Mega Port, boasting an impressive draft depth of 20 meters, is a strategic move aimed at 
further bolstering the capabilities and competitiveness of maritime infrastructure. To make 
the major ports more competitive with Global Ports, the Ministry is exploring the possibility 
of treating the channel as a national asset and also examining the feasibility of funding the 
entire dredging cost, after studying the extant practices followed by the  other countries in the 
world. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
5.        Ports must increase draft according to the respective cargo profile. Indian container 
terminals must target an 18m+ draft. With the evolving ship types andIncreasing port parcel 
sizes, loading and discharge rates must be enhanced. The Committee also emphasizes that 
greater ship sizes and container loads need increased mechanization at Indian ports to 
improve the loading and unloading ecosystem. Dual cycle cranes and Automated Guided 
Vehicles (AGVs) may be introduced in ports to ensure incremental productivity. 

4 
 
 (Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1      The recommendation of the Committee is well noted.

VOC 
Recommendation/Observation 
13.      The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry but feels that the distance between two 
ports should be a matter of consideration as it impacts the overall productivity of both the old 
and also the upcoming ports. The Committee recommends that the distance between an 
upcoming port and another port in the region serving th e same hinterland should form a part 
of the study before establishing the need for a new port.  
 (Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1    In this regards, it is pertinent to mention that a new Major port i.e. Vadhavan port is 
under development stage and will be jointly implemented by JNPA and Maharashtra 
Maritime Board with a shareholding of 74% and 26% respectively. 
Further, the recommendations of the committee are well noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
14.      The Committee notes that one of the main  problems obstructing the development of 
Transshipment in India emanates from the lack of deep drafts of Indian ports, Especially 
those on the Eastern Coast and Southern coast. While dredging is necessary to deepen the 
drafts, the costs of dredging are charged to the shipping lines, adding to the cost of port calls 
in India compared to the foreign ports, thus, discouraging big ships from coming to Indian 
ports. The Committee has been informed that foreign ports do not bear the costs of dredging, 
which are borne by respective Government.  
 (Para 96) 
 
15.      Upon enquiry by the Committee, the Ministry acknowledged that the Syama Prasad 
Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, receives a dredging subsidy from the Government. But, the other 
Major Ports are responsible for their dredging expenditure, both capital and maintenance. 
The Committee desires to know why only the Kolkata port receives a dredging subsidy from 
the Government. The Committee would like the Ministry to give a comparative data on the 
number of foreign gov ernments which bear the cost of dredging and the number of foreign 
ports which bear the cost of dredging themselves without any government help. 
 (Para 97) 
 
16.      If the former is a practice worldwide, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
may explore the possibility of government support for dredging in Major Ports so that a 
globally uniform practice is followed so as to make our ports cost effective and competitive. 
 (Para 98) 

8 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1    Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, being a riverine port, is located in a unique and 
challenging environment. The Hooghly River on which it is located has a high rate of 
siltation. This means that the port needs to be dredged more frequently and at a higher cost 
than other ports. Therefore, dredgin g subsidy is given to the Port to maintain its draft and to 
continue to operate efficiently. 
 
16.2 To make the Major Ports more competitive with global ports, the Ministry is 
exploring the possibility of treating the channel as a national asset and also ex amining the 
feasibility of funding the entire dredging cost, after studying the extant practices followed by 
the other countries in the world. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
17.      The Committee also notes that solutions like Floating Cranes, which unload the cargo 
from Capesize Ships anchored in mid -sea into barges that take the cargo to the port, have 
helped ports like Kandla, a low draft port, to improve productivity and increase cargo 
volumes. The Committee desires to know if such solutions can be appli ed at other ports. In 
particular, it recommends that the Ministry looks into the solutions where dredging costs are 
prohibitive. 
 (Para 99) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1    The recommendation of the Committee is well noted. Ports like Deendayal and 
Mormugao currently use floating cranes for mid sea barge operations whereas ports such as 
JNPA, KPL, VPA and ChPA do not have a need for this service due to their cargo profile, 
draft availability and adequate berthing facilities. Some of the ports are exploring th e 
possibility of using floating cranes for mid sea barge operations in the future. 
 
DPA 
As far as DPA is concerned, yes the port users have the option of utilizing floating cranes 
available for mid sea barge operations at its port limits at O.T.B. (Outer Tuna Buoy), for 
handling Dry cargo ships. 
 
JNPA 
JNPA is predominantly a container port. Other than containers, JNPA handles small amount 
of Liquid and break bulk. JNPA do not handle bulk cargo. 
 
KPL 

9 
 
KPL is a deep draft Port which can handle larger vessels with a draft of 16m. 
KPL has initiated action for becoming the Cape Compliance Port to handle Cape size vessels. 
Hence, Barge operation at anchorage is not necessarily felt at this juncture. 
 
MoPA 
At Mormugao Port Floating cranes / Transhippers are used to unload/ load 
cape size vessels at outer anchorage through/into barges by taking advantage of natural deep 
water draft available at Outer anchorage. 
 
NMPA 
The Port  is  exploring  the  possibility  of  handling  cape  size  vessels  at 
Anchorage to handle iron ore. 
 
VOCPA 
Deploying floating crane for Anchorage operations & lightering from higher capacity vessels 
would augment the cargo handling potential of the Port. 
 
At VOC Port, floating crane was deployed from 15.02.2015 to 27.10.2016, for lightering at 
Anchorage using FC and barges and Subsequently handling the deeper draft vessel at berth. 
However, the Operator discontinued the services 
 
VPA 
At VPA there are adequate    berthing facilities in outer harbour  to accommodate cape size 
vessels with a permis sible draft of 18.10 mtrs. and LOA 390 mtrs. &in inner harbour to 
accommodate Babycape vessels with a permissible draft of 14.50 mtrs. and LOA 260 mtrs. 
 
As such the trade is not felt to handle cargo by floating cranes at ships anchored in mid sea by 
barges as the Port is equipped with international standards of Navigational and cargo 
handling facilities. 
 
MbPA 
Mumbai Port is also low draft port especially in the Dock Basin which cannot accommodate 
mother vessels. About 23.50 % of cargo of Mumbai Port is handled at anchorages where dry 
bulk cargo is discharged from Mother vessels to barges and these barges carry the cargo to 

10 
 
nearby ports like Dharamtar, PNP and Karanja. This cargo is discharged by Ships own 
cranes. 
 
ChPA 
There is no such requirement for deployment of floating cranes at ChennaiPort considering 
its cargo profile, volume and draft availability.

TRAFFIC HANDLED BY MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that the cargo handling of the Major Ports has been steadily 
increasing over the years, and only in the last year has there been an increase of 10%. On a 
query by the Committee, the Ministry replied that to augment the volume ofcargo handling, 
the Port Authorities have also explored the possibility of generating new cargo to reduce the 
gap between the actual traffic and the capacity. Major Ports also organize trade meets to 
attract traffic from their hinterland/region. Several steps have also been taken to boost 
coastal shipping.. 
 (Para 13) 
2.        The Committee also observes that the increase of 10% has come primarily due to 
JNPA’s impressive performance, followed by Paradip and Deendayal Port. There is only a 
marginal increase in the figures of the remaining Ports, while the Mormugao Port has 
witnessed a decline in traffic. The growth trend in the market share of cargo is, therefore, 
confined to only three of the Major Ports while the remaining show barely perceptible 
improvements. The Committee underscores the need for better performance by the rema ining 
nine Major Ports and recommends that the Ministry come out with a focused and calibrated 
strategy to raise the cargo handling performance of such MajorPorts. 
 (Para 14) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      FY 2022-23 has marked a positive trend in traffic growth across most of the Major 
Ports, surpassing the figures from FY 2021 -22. To capitalize on this growth and ensure a 
robust future, the Ministry has proactively identified a series of initiatives aimed at enhancing 
cargo handling capabilities at these ports. These initiatives include the addition of new berths 
for meeting the anticipated cargo profiles, upgrading existing berths to boost handling 
capacity, converting existing berths to accommodate new commodities, and exploring 
promising avenues such as  cruise shipping. All of these measures are aligned with the 
overarching Maritime India Vision -2030, charting a course towards a thriving maritime 
sector. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.        The Committee observes that India occupies the 11th position globally regarding 
container traffic handled. Massive Container Ships invariably require deep drafts, and the 

15 
 
ports must remain alive to their requirements. At present, most Indian Ports have dra fts of 
about 14 mts, with only a few having 16 mts drafts, while Container Ships require drafts of 
upto 18-20 mts..

 REVIEW PROVISIONS UNDER MAJOR CONCESSION ACT  
 
Recommendation/Observation

Reply of the Ministry 

47

46.      The Committee observes that while clauses relating to Amendments, Modifications etc 
are built into almost every agreement or contract, at the same time Agreements have a 
certain sanctity and adherence to its conditions is always expected. A Concession Agreement 
is signed, knowing fully well the duration of the contract, the market conditions and the risks 
involved and it is expected that the Concessionaire evaluated all costs and benefits at the 
time of the agreement.  
(Para 201) 
Reply of the Ministry 
46.1    Noted.

47.      As such, Private Public Partnerships require a framework that would enable the 
private sector partner to secure a reasonable return while enabling value addition for public 
resources. This can only be achieved by establishing clear and transparent norms for the 
PPP and by entering into unambiguous and specific contractual relationship. Concession 
Agreements are generally made for 30 years an d with the rapidly changing market scenario, 
every change cannot be anticipated at the bidding stage in contractsspanning three decades. 
In fact private players are now looking for even longer concession periods in the port sector. 
The Adani Ports and Spec ial Economic Zone (APSEZ) has won a bid to build a Greenfield 
port in Tajpur, West Bengal for aConcession period of 99 years. The MCA, 2021 also has 
provisions for 45 years Concession Period for multi -phase investments. The port sector is 
capital intensive and longer Concession periods which would lead to gestation for a larger 
Capital cycle may become the norm in future. It is unimaginable that the conditions 
prevailing at the time of the Agreement would remain the same in the next century.  
(Para 202) 
Reply of the Ministry 
47.1    Reply already given at para 200. 
  
Recommendation/Observation

audit/vigilance, the Committee observes that the issue of Royalty or revenue share raised 
above had, in fact been raised by the CAG in its 2015 Performance Audit Report o f Public 
Private Partnership Projects. The project under examination of the CAG was the agreement 

48 
 
of the JNPA with the Nhava Sheva International ContainerTerminal (NSICT) for operation of 
a Container Terminal where the JNPA had switched to the revenue shar ing model after 18 
years of operation from the earlier royalty model due to high royalty rate per TEU which 
increased progressively. The CAG had commented adversely on the design deficiencies of the 
model due to which the port had to migrate to the revenue  share mode after 18 years of 
operation. The CAG had also commented that a PPP Project would succeed only if the risks 
are uniformly apportioned between the two parties and that a Concession Agreement is 
unlikely to succeed if it has conditions which are harsh on the operator.  
(Para 203) 
Reply of the Ministry 
48.1    Noted. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
49.      In the considered opinion of the Committee, much of the issues arising from the 
Concession Agreements can be avoided by adopting the right models for the project from the 
beginning and ensuring that the Concessionaire Agreements retain an element of flexibility to 
incorporate necessary changes which would benefit both parties. Rigid Agreements have the 
potential to defeat the purpose of successful P PP partnerships. While the provisions of the 
Agreement should be largely adhered to, no purpose is served by an unyielding observance of

by the IPPTA in the light of the above position.  
(Para 204) 
Reply of the Ministry 
49.1    As time progresses, every policy requires revision. Scope of refinement always

ensuring that the Concessionaire Agreements retain an element of flexibility to incorporate 
necessary changes, which would balance the risk and benefit both parties i.e. Concessioning 
Authority and Concessionaire. In this regard, the Model Concession Agreement of 2018 was

INITIATIVES FOR LEGAL DISPUTES AND ARBITRATION 
Recommendation/Observation
