policy with all stakeholders and taking into consideration the viewpoints of the stakeholders 

49 
 
should be sufficient to make a policy which would address all the concernsof the stakeholders 
to the extent possible. It is understandable that once a policy is in place, the Government 
does not wish to make frequent changes in it. However, the success of the PPP pr ojects is 
essential for the achievement of the Maritime India Vision and the Ministry should make 
every effort to address the stakeholders’ concerns. The Committee recommends that in case 
of contentious issues emerging from the discussions with the stakeho lders, the Ministry may

50.1    Noted. MoPSW has announced the revised Model Concession Agreement (MCA) -

 a)            The parties shall first meet so as to disc uss and resolve the matter in mutual

b)            If above fails, the Concessionaire may agree to refer the matter to a conciliation and

50

CAPACITY OF MAJOR PORTS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.        The Committee observes that while port capacity is considered to be saturated at 70 -
75% of capacity, some of the Major Ports are functioning far below the mark. Mormugao 
operates at only 27% capacity, while Chennai and VoCA operate just at 32%.. 
 (Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1      The capacity of Major Ports has been re -rated with respect to global bench marks as 
per Berthing Policy 2016. The actual usable capacity of the ports is lower than the re -rated 
capacity. Hence, the utilization percentage against actual usable capa city is higher in these 
ports. However, a number of factors contribute to the low capacity utilization at these ports, 
including restrictions imposed by Goa State Pollution Control Board for handling cargo at 
Mooring Dolphins and other berths, single Railw ay line from Vasco to Tinaighat, challenges 
due to common hinterland and competition from other ports. The ports are taking steps to 
improve their capacity utilization, such as mechanizing berths, converting berths into 
container terminals, and promoting the use of oil jetties. 
1.2 Marmugao Port Authority (MoPA): Mormugao Port operates at 68% of its Usable 
Capacity, and 27% of its Re -rated capacity. The capacity as per CTO at Mooring Dolphins is 
only 4.75 as against re -rated capacity of 18.50 Milliontones. A lso seen from the table the 
rerated capacity of berth no 6, 7 and 8 is 17.40, 13.70 and 5.20 respectively as against usable 
capacity of 6.50, 5.20 and 1.00 Milliontones. Thus due to the restrictions imposed by Goa 
State Pollution Control Board for handling  cargo at Mooring Dolphins and other berths, Port 
is unable to handle cargo beyond the prescribed limit by GSPCB. Due to single Railway line 
from Vasco to Tinaighat, Mormugao Port is unable to evacuate cargo effectively through 
rakes. This affects the disc harge of vessel as it cannot discharge the cargo in stockyard, 
unless the cargo from the yard is evacuated. Details may be seen at Annexure-1. 
 
1.3 VO Chidambarnar Port Authority (VOCPA) 
VOC Port‟s has the rated capacity of 111.46 MMT and Usable Capacity o f81.47 MMT in FY 
2022-23. Against the Usable Capacity of 81.47 MMT, VOC Port has achieved the utilization 
of 46.7% in FY 2022 -23 by handling 38.04 MMT. Further, it is informed that 5 Port viz., 
Cochin, Chennai, Kattupalli, Ennore and Karaikal are competing  with VOC Port for the 
Common Hinterland Cargo Traffic. 

54 
 
 In-depth breakup of the Rated Capacity, Usable Capacity and its utilization are furnished at 
Annexure-2. 
a. Captive Berths are operated by Power plants and are functioning to its requirements and its  
coal needs / availability. 
b. Container terminals are operating at the Capacity of above 75% and to cater to the 
increasing container handling needs, action has been taken to convert the Port operated berth 
into an additional Container Terminal and Conces sion agreement in this regard was signed 
with M/s J M Baxi Ports & Logistics Limited on 03.09.2022. 
c. Tender for mechanization of the North Cargo Berth -III is in process. 
d. Oil jetty is being used for handling the defined cargoes and its promotion to im prove its 
utilization has been taken up. 
e.            One Berth, NCB II which was under PPP is presently non - operational and is under 
NCLT. 
f. Further, Berth Utilization was measured based on the tonnage basis. However, certain 
cargoes like Windmill Blades& Machinery, Iron and Steel, RoRo -Rock Boulders and other 
break bulk cargo have lesser handling rate and higher berth occupancy, which impacts the 
capacity utilization to a certain degree. Hence, based on the nature of cargo being handled at 
the Port, Berth Utilization and its occupancy differ across Ports. 
 
1.4 Chennai Port Authority (ChPA) 
The Capacity Utilization of Chennai Port during the last 3 years ending FY2022 -23 
has been 42%, 47% and 47% respectively at desired (ideal) occupancy level (85% f or 
Containerized Cargo & 70% for Other Cargoes). The national average of Capacity Utilization 
of Major Ports as observed in the report is only 49%. The marginal shortfall is only due to the 
common hinterland being shared by 3 major ports & 2 private ports operating in the state of 
Tamil Nadu and the ports in the adjacent states of Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.  
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
1.5      The Committee appreciates the steps being taken by ports to improve their 
capacity utilization, mechanization of berths, promotion of use of oil jetties etc and 
desires to know if any action has been taken to resolve the issue of  the single railway 
line from Vasco to Tinaighat which is hindering the evacuation of cargo and such other 
port specific issues which are contributing to the low capacity utilization of ports.  
  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.        The Committee observes that there is still much untapped potential to be harnessed so 
as to increase the capacity of most of the Maj or Ports. The Committee points out that the 
capacity utilization of the Non -Major Ports in India has remained at 64%, which is much 

55 
 
higher than the average capacity utilization in the Major Ports and recommends that the 
Major Ports may set targets to incre ase the utilization of their existing capabilities to an 
optimum level.  
 (Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1      Major ports have experienced remarkable traffic growth of approximately 10% during 
the fiscal year 2022 -23. Recognizing the importance of accommodating future demand in 
light of this substantial growth, it has become imperative to ensure spare capacity. To address 
this need, we are focusing on capacity expansion on two fronts: firstly, by introducing new 
berths, and secondly, by optimizing o ur existing infrastructure through the mechanization of 
berths, deepening of channels, and enhancing evacuation capacity. These strategic initiatives 
are vital for not only sustaining our current momentum but also for effectively meeting the 
increasing demands of the future. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.2      The Committee appreciates the capacity expansion initiatives taken by the 
Ministry and the Major Ports but the Ministry has not commented on the much higher 
capacity utilization in the Non -Major Ports, pointed out by the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may evaluate the reasons for the higher 
capacity utilization in Non -Major Ports and incorporate the same if possible, in their

Recommendation/Observation 
5.        The Committee had also been informed in its meetings that despite having the requisite 
infrastructure and land, the Jaigarh port could not handle containers due to lack of major 
rail connectivity. The Committee observes that one of the main factors for the low cap acity 
utilization of the Ports pertains to absence of road and rail connectivityto the hinterland to 
cater to the emerging demands. The need for good rail and road port connectivity for hassle -
free cargo transport must assume importance. It should be the p riority of the Ministry to 
ensure proper connectivity to all ports, which would driveup the cargo traffic and increase 
the revenues from this sector. The Committee is pleased to note that the PM Gati Shakti 
Programme is taking up 101 connectivity projects for both Major and Minor Ports, and the 
SagarmalaProgramme is also addressing the road and rail connectivity infrastructure gaps

Recommendation/Observation

and vehicles by 2030. This includes electrifying quay cranes, RTGCs, ITVs, grab unloaders,

operators to electrify their equipment.

8.3 Inputs received from Ports:  
KPL

in the Port are fully electrified. The grab unloaders used for coal unloading operations are

to Tank farms through pipeline. KPL has deployed 3 Nos. of Elec trically operated vehicles 
for Solid Waste Management within the Port. KPL is in the process of deploying 2 Nos. of E -
buses (14seater) for inter carting of manpower. Presently, the percentage of Port 
equipment/vehicle electrified is 5% and KPL will take efforts to reach the target.

date, 6 e-cars are in service at VOCPA. Tenders are under process for 14 Nos. of E-cars and 4

ISSUES ARISING OUT OF THE PROSPECTIVE APPLICATION OF THE 
NEWMODEL CONCESSION AGREEMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
9.        The Committee had requested the Ministry to give its comments on the issue of 
extending the benefits of the MCA, 2021 to both the existing as well as newConcessionaires. 
The Ministry has put forth the arguments that the PPP projects are executed through 
Concession Agreements which are legally binding and are governed by the policies that are 
applicable in that time period. Any post - bid changes in theConcession Agreement is open to 
litigation. The Ministry has also informed that a Committee consisting of the Chairmen of 
VoCPA, ChPA& JNPA was constituted in May, 2023 for deliberation on whether the 
provisions of MCA, 2021 can be made retrospective and the report of that Committee is 
awaited. 
 (Para 191) 
10.      The Committee observes that the within the past two decades, the Model 
Concessionaire Agreement has been changed thrice, in 2008, 2018 and 2021 
(Comparative statement of the provisions of the three MCAs placed at Annexure XIV). The 
first revision came after a decade and brought only minor changes in a few of the provisions. 
The second revision came within 03 years and brought about a major overhaul in existing 
regulations, with the introduction of market based tariff fixation, abolition of the authority of 
TAMP, provisions for change in cargo, etc. It is not surprising that the existing 
Concessionaires find themselves in a disadvantageous position vis -a-vis the new 
Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021.  
 (Para 192) 

62 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1    Noted. The proviso clause to Section 27(1) of the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, 
provides freedom to the Concessionaire to fix tariff based on the market conditions.  
10.2 The existing PPP concessions would be governed by the respective signed Concession 
Agreement and tariff provisions contained in respective signed Concession Agreement and 
tariff guidelines, if any, stipulated at the time of the Concession agreement. Government of 
India requires the Project sponsors (Major Ports) to award PPP projects through a transparent 
open competitive bidding process, due diligence through DPR, research and analysis for both 
short and long term business continuity during concession period are part of this process. 
This is also to ensure greater transparency and consistency to the bid process and terms of 
contract, level playing field to all players, throughout the project life cycle and market 
discovery of rates.  Hence, saying existing Concessionaires are in a disa dvantageous position 
vis-a-vis the new Concessionaires under the MCA, 2021 does not seem correct in full merit. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
10.3    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.   
  
Recommendation/Observation 
11.      The Committee also observes that the new Agreement was issued with the purpose of 
countering the lukewarm response of the private sector in PPP projects and to provide a 
framework to increase PPP participation to boost p ort performances. The Committee 
observes that in 2019, on the issue of periodic revision of SoR (Schedule of Rates) for land, it 
had been decided not to apply revision of SoR for land every 05 years for PPP projects as it 
may not be in the overall interest  of the Major Ports. TheCommittee feels that the 
retrospective application of the MCA, 2021 should be examined in the same spirit. The 
Concessions given to the private operators generally are passed on to exporters/importers by 
leveraging costs and therefo re the general public can only benefit by these measures. The 
Committee feels that the Ministry may take these concerns into account while examining the 
requests of the existingConcessionaires.  
 (Para 193) 
Reply of the Ministry 
11.1    In MCA 2021, the Concessionaire shall, as consideration for the use, in its capacity as 
a bare licensee of the Project Site and the equipment comprised in the Port‟s Assets, made 
available in accordance with Article 2.4, pay to the Concessioning Authority ₹ 1 (the 
“License Fee”). 
11.2 On the aspect of making enabling provisions to provide option to the existing PPP 
Concessionaires for migration to the market determined tariff regime, as has been done for 
the prospective bidders / concessionaires for new PPP projects, the majority of the  Major 

63 
 
Ports Chairpersons opined that such an arrangement would be desirable as it would provide a 
level playing field to the Concessionaires, presently being governed under different tariff 
norms, operating at a Port. However, considering the procedural c omplexities involved in 
drafting a workable solution within the framework of the existing rules and regulations, a 
detailed comprehensive study of the whole issue, including legal, financial and contractual 
aspects, would be advisable. 
11.3 Based on the vi ews expressed by Chairpersons of the Major Port Authorities during 
the meeting, the Ministry has decided to constitute a Committee of Chairpersons, to study the 
whole issue in a holistic manner. Report of the committee is yet to be received.. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
11.4   The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.    
  
Recommendation/Observation 
12.      The Committee notes that the issue is under examination by a Committee consisting of 
the Chairmen of various Major Ports and desires that the Ministry may update the Committee 
on its outcome. 
 (Para 194) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1    The Committee has not yet submitted its recommendations. 
  
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2    The Committee may be informed of the report of the Committee for deliberating 
on the issue.

REPORT
 
 
Demand No. 82 pertains to the Ministry of Tourism.  The Ministry of Tourism in their written note has informed that tourism is a major social phenomenon of the modern society with
 enormous economic consequences.  Its importance as an instrument for economic development and employment generation particularly in remote and backward areas has been now
 well recognised the world over. 
The provisions in this demand mainly include allocations for the Secretariat of the Ministry of Tourism, the expenditure on the headquarter establishment of the Directorate General of
 Tourism and the regional and field offices under it, expenditure on production and publicity material for the promotional programmes, both domestic and overseas; provisions for
 creation of infrastructural facilities like Tourist Bungalows, Yatri Niwas, Wayside Amenities etc. and Grants in Aid to the various Tourism Training Institutes of the Ministry of
 Tourism. The Director General of Tourism functions as the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and programmes and the coordination of activities of various Central
 Government agencies, State Governments and the Private Sector for the development and growth of Tourism in the country. 
Tourism is the world’s largest export industry.  According to the World Tourism Organisation, about 612.8 million tourists travel internationally in 1997 and spent about US$ 444
 billion.  It is estimated that tourism accounts for about 8% of the total world exports and more than 30% of international trade in services.  In 1997-98 travel and tourism was expected
 to provide direct and indirect employment for 212 million people and accounted for 10.7% of the global work force. 
The international tourist traffic to India during 1951 was just 16,829.  Over a period of 46 years, the arrivals increased to 2.37 million in 1997 and registered a compounded annual rate
 of growth of about 3.8%.  The foreign exchange earnings from tourism during 1997-98 was estimated to be about Rs.11,264 crores (US $ 3173 million).  The rate of growth in foreign
 exchange earning from tourism is exceptionally high.  The foreign exchange earnings for 1998-99 is projected to be Rs.12215.19 crores. During the Eighth Five Year Plan period, the
 foreign tourist arrivals including the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh recorded an annual growth of 5.6%.  The growth rate in arrivals, exclusive of nationals of Pakistan and
 Bangladesh, was 8.1%.  During the year 1997-98,  tourist arrivals were 23,70,985 inclusive of the nationals of Pakistan and Bangladesh as compared to 23,34,438 during 1996-97.  
The most significant feature of the tourism industry is its capacity to generate large scale employment opportunities particularly in remote and backward areas as it is a labour intensive
 industry.  It offers enormous potential for economically utilising the natural attractions like landscapes, mountains, beaches, rivers, etc. which would otherwise remain either idle or
 underutilised.  It also applies to a multitude of man-made attractions like monuments, palaces, forts and unique rural and city environments. 
The Ministry of Tourism has under its administrative control the following public sector undertakings/autonomous bodies:- 
India Tourism Development Corporation Limited
National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology
Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management
Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and Applied Nutrition at different locations in the country
Food Craft Institutes at different locations
Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering
National Institute of Water Sports

The Committee was informed that the budget estimate on plan side for year 1998-99 was Rs. 160.50 crores which was reduced to Rs.110.00 crores by Ministry of Finance at Revised
 stage.  An allocation of Rs.184.64 has been made for the Ministry of Tourism for 1999-2000, out of which Rs.160.50 crores are on the plan side.  The Budget estimates and revised
 estimates for 1998-99 were Rs. 182.55 crores and 134.24 crores respectively.
 The Committee expressed its deep concern to the fact that the budget estimates on plan side for year 1998-99 was Rs.160.50 crores which was reduced to Rs.110.00 crores by
 Ministry of Finance at Revised stage and expenditure was incurred accordingly.  The Committee further observed that tourism being a highly labour intensive industry holds a huge
 potential in providing employment in the country especially in the rural/backward areas and that it is also a third largest industry in terms of earning foreign exchange after export of
 garments and gems and jewellery. The Committee notes that on one side Government of India has declared tourism as an industry and converted the Department Of Tourism into the
 Ministry, however, on the other side the Government has decreased the plan allocation of the Ministry of Tourism at revised estimate stage.  This has been done not only this
 particular year but is being done during the last so many years.  This reduction in the budgetary allocations affected the growth and development of tourism in the country negatively. 
 The Committee was also informed that today tourism has become one of the major export industry of every country in the world and is playing a significant role in their economies. 
 Now a days, smallest countries i.e. Singapore etc. which have only some scenic beauties, beaches, resorts etc. are spending lot of money for the promotion of tourism and to attract
 tourist from all over the world.  They are trying to create their countries as major tourist destination points. Tourism industry, has now become number one industry of some of the
 countries which is helping in earning foreign exchange.  Today our country is celebrating 1999-2000 year as the ‘Explore India-Millennium Year’ to create public awareness about
 economic and social benefits of tourism amongst administrators, planners and masses;  improvement of the efficiency of the tourist facilitation; development of various tourism
 products in India as environmental friendly and sustainable destinations and encouraging the State Government and Private sector to create infrastructure facilities by providing
 incentives on a selective basis. The Committee has noted that during the last two years i.e. 1997-98 and 1998-99 the plan allocations were reduced to Rs.100 crores and Rs.110 crores
 from Rs.110.35 crores and Rs.160.50 crores.  The Committee was of the opinion that whatever amount is given in the plan side should not be reduced at R.E. stage in future.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should increase plan side allocations of the Ministry of Tourism proportionately or atleast 20% increase of the
 previous year’s budget allocation. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation mentioned in its 31
st Report on demands for Grant 1998-99 of the Ministry of Tourism
 that the involvement of private sector should be encouraged which will help in solving the problems of finance. The Committee also observed that since sufficient funds are not
 utilised in the beginning of the financial year major cuts are imposed by the Ministry of Finance at the time of revised estimates.  The Committee further recommends that instead of
 spending the amount in the last four or five months Ministry should try to incur the maximum expenditure in the beginning of each financial year i.e. in April, May and June on those
 projects/schemes which are already under progress.  In this way sufficient funds would be utilised and the Ministry may approach for more funds while sending their revised
 estimates.  
The Committee further recommends that tourism sector should be treated at par with the export industry and whatever incentives/facilities are available to export industry should also
 be made available to this sector keeping in view of vast potential and spin off benefits of tourism sector. 
 
11.            FACILITIES FOR FOREIGN TOURIST
 
It has been observed by the Committee that Airport is the first place where the tourist comes into contact with the local people and his interaction on arrival start with the various
 agencies viz. Custom, Visa, Immigration, Foreign Exchange, Transport, Shopping at duty free shops etc.  The Committee understands that the foreign tourist encounters lot of
 problems with all these agencies and besides it the airports in the country also lack adequate toilet/drinking water facility and other civic amenities.  The foreign tourist is also targeted
 by touts who fleece him to no end.  The tourists feels cheated and carries the impression that instead of getting welcome from India they are being harassed and neglected.  The
 Committee was of the view that first impression is the last impression and when tourist would not get proper treatment at the Airport itself their entire expectations towards the
 country would get negated and after getting back to their own country it is not known what sort of Indian picture they will depict to their own country men.  The Committee therefore
 recommends that there should be one high ranking Officer at all the Airports for maintaining efficient coordination amongst all the agencies like customs, immigration, visa, security,
 foreign exchange, operating at the Airport.  This power should preferably be vested with the Airport Director. The Ministry of Home Affairs may take necessary steps to provide
 better security to the tourists not only at the airports but within  the country as well.
 
     DOMESTIC CAMPAIGN

An important feature of the tourism is its contribution to national integration and environment of social and cultural lives of people.  Over 100 million domestic tourists visiting
 different parts of the country every year returned with a better understanding of the people living in the different regions of the country and the cultural diversity of India.  
The Committee, however, has observed that the Ministry of Tourism has given more attention on overseas campaign to attract foreign tourists and the needs of the domestic tourists
 has been somewhat neglected.  The special packages, which are offered to the foreign tourists so as to earn foreign exchange, are not made available to the domestic tourist.   The
 awareness about the tourism especially in the middle class families is increasing day by day due to which they are more interested to visit and know their country.  One school of
 thought is of the view that tourism may also act as a possible solution in tackling the tension prevailing in the society.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of
 Tourism should also prepare special packages in consultation with the State Governments and ITDC for the domestic tourist as well. The Committee also reiterates its earlier
 recommendations as contained in its 31st Report on demands of Grant 1998-99 of the Ministry of Tourism for giving proper attention and funds allocation to the domestic campaign.   
 
     OVERSEAS CAMPAIGN AND PROMOTION
 
The Department of Tourism performs its main marketing function through a network of 18 Government of India tourist offices located overseas with specific area demarcations under
 six distinct regions as given below: 
New York – Responsible for the entire North American and South American continent.
Frankfurt- Responsible for continental Europe
London – Responsible for U.K. and Ireland
Dubai – Responsible for West Asia and South Africa
Sydney – Responsible for Australia
Tokyo – Responsible for East Asia 
Under these offices, there are sub-offices located at Los Angeles, Toronto, Paris, Milan, Amsterdam, Madrid, Geneva, Stockholm, Bahrain, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, and Bangkok
 who work under the guidance of the above regions. 
 
The Committee was also informed that an allocation of Rs.67.80 crores has been made on plans

 receipts which was only 0.38% & 0.39% and 0.68% & 0.71% during 1996 and 1997 respectively.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that a thorough review is required of the
 overall functioning of the tourist offices abroad/overseas campaign and that this review should be done involving the India/foreign tour and travel operators, hoteliers and other
 connected organisations like domestic and foreign airlines, Indian embassies/missions abroad, voluntary organisations so that a coordinated effort may be evolved to make these
 campaigns more effective and result oriented in attracting foreign tourists to the country.
 
SURVEYS AND STUDIES CONDUCTED BY MINISTRY OF TOURISM 
 
The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Tourism has conducted following surveys and studies during the year 1997-98:- 
Tourism potential survey of Pachmari and Khajiar
International passenger survey 1996-97
Infrastructure development for Eco tourism in Orissa
Tourism potential study of Orissa
Feasibility study for setting up a convention centre at Leh
Preparation of a concept plan and design for the development of Chumukedima village in Nagaland. 
The Committee is of the view that a large amount of money has been spent on the above mentioned studies/surveys which were conducted to assist the Ministry of Tourism in chalking
 out policies/programmes for the development of the tourism in the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that findings of these surveys/studies particularly that of
 International Passenger Survey, 1996-97 should be taken into consideration while making planning of the Tourism Development in the particular tourist area.  Findings of these
 surveys/studies should be implemented strictly for future planning and should not be dumped  in the cold storage and that action taken notes may be furnished to the Committee within
 two months. 
 
     RAPID ACTION CELL
 
The Committee in its 31
st report recommended for the constitution of some sort of coordination Committee comprising of all the concerned Ministries/agencies so as to keep a check
 on the occurrence of incidents of harassment and atrocities and directed that the Ministry of Tourism should have its own ‘Rapid Action Cell’ under the officer of the rank of the Joint
 Secretary, so that it takes prompt action in such matters 
The Committee is happy to know and appreciates the initiative taken by the Ministry of Tourism for constitution of Rapid Action Cell headed by Additional Director General, Tourism

The Committee is of the view that the information regarding the Constitution of Rapid Action Cell for the benefit of the tourist has not been widely disseminated and publicised.  The

 created by the foreign media regarding our country.  The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Tourism should also have its own Public Relations Professional Agency
 which will help to create the positive image of India as a major tourist destination. 
 
TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE AND PRODUCT  DEVELOPMENT
 
The development of tourism infrastructure and improvement of tourism product during 1999-2000 would consist of integrated development of tourist/pilgrim centres, special tourism
 areas, major tourism projects, setting up of Prayatan Bhawan.  The budgetary allocations for this purpose is as under :
 
Proposed outlay                            50.00 crores
Approved outlay                           32.20 crores
 
In order to ensure integrated development of tourism infrastructure including basic amenities and other facilities, the Ministry of Tourism would provide assistance to State/Union
 Territory Governments for  the implementation of composite projects.  The assistance will be provided to selected tourist/pilgrim centres upto a maximum of Rs. One crore subject to
 matching contribution by the State/Union Territory Governments.  The Central Assistance will be provided over a period of two years at the rate of Rs.50 lakhs per year.
      The Committee noted that a provision of Rs.32.20crores
as grants-in-aid has been made for development of tourist centres/areas.  The Committee was informed by the Secretary that a new method of funding by way of grant-in-aid towards
 projects cost was introduced during 1992-93.  As per the scheme 28% of the project cost is provided by the Central Government and 12% is provided by the State Government.  The
 balance 60% has to be raised as loan from financial institutions or banks.  This method of funding is applicable to bankable projects requiring large investments.  It was expected that
 the State Governments would be able to mobilise  more resources from financial institutions for investment in tourism projects through this method .  The Committee noted that since
 the share of Central Government is 28% and State Government is 12% and from financial institutions/banks they have to take loans upto 60% which makes the share of State
 Governments to be 72% which is on a very high side.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to make this scheme more attractive the share of both Central and State
 Governments should be 50% each.   
 
     TRAINING OF OFFICERS AND GUIDES 
The Committee was informed that the availability of trained guides in tourist centres and monuments is a major requirement of tourism promotion.  The Ministry of Tourism is,
 therefore, giving considerable importance to train guides. An amount of Rs.0.30 crore has been provided under this programme. A three tier training programme at the national, state
 and local levels has recently been drawn up and is being implemented through Government of India Tourist Offices, State/UT Governments and others.  These courses include
 programmes for fresh tourist guides and language and refresher courses for those already engaged in guide services.  It is also proposed to provide training to the officers and staff in
 the field of information technology and tourism related courses.
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that an amount of Rs. 0.30 crores is not sufficient for the training of guides and officers.  The training should be given to the guides in such a
 way so that they could explain the importance of the Tourist places in India which would increase the knowledge of tourists towards Indian Culture and heritage. Accordingly, the
 Committee recommends that All India Training Course for travel guides should be introduced in order to develop tourism in the country and for this purpose Ministry should increase
 their budget proposals.

The Committee also observed that not much emphasis has been laid on the construction of budget accommodation for low priced tourists, the lack of which has not only led to the

 and provide more funds under this head.  It also further recommends that as an example one central assisted scheme may be undertaken in each State to develop a tourist place entirely

19.       CIVIC AMENITIES ON NATIONAL HIGHWAYS FOR TOURISTS
 
The Committee noted with concern that there are shortage of toilet/drinking water facility on the national highways.  The Committee was of the view that most of the tourists are of
 adventurous nature and they prefer to perform their journeys by roads, but since the above facilities are not commonly available on national highways they find it inconvenient to
 travel on those roads.  Sometimes the road sides are used for easing out which creates insanitary conditions.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that such facilities may be
 created on the national highways 100% funded by the Central Government and that a condition may be added in the licence/lease granted to the petrol pumps and restaurants on
 national highways to provide drinking water and toilet facility for the tourist and other travelling public.  The maintenance of toilet/drinking water facilities and other civic amenities
 so created under this scheme may be given to private parties/voluntary agencies.

th Plan the Ministry of Finance weeded out the scheme of Ministry of Tourism namely a Tourist Transport Scheme under which assistance

th Five Year Plan.

Election and Tenure of Heads of the National Akademis and Cultural Institutions 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that only the Chairman of Sahitya Akademi is elected. The process 
for appointment of the Chairman/President as also their tenure varies between the Akademis. 
The tenure of the Governing Body is also different for the different Akademis, ranging between 3 
years for Lalit Kala Akademi to 10 years for Kalakshetra Foundation. There are no fixed 
guidelines with regard to the number of me mbers of the Governing Council, the number of 
meetings to be held, etc. Also, there are no people's representatives in the Governing Council of 
the Akademis. 
 (Para 17) 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee observes that there are different parameter s for different Akademis. In 
Committee's view, this lack of uniformity is not desirable as it leads to administrative and 
organisational inconsistencies among the various Akademis and Institutions. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends Government to formula te a policy emphasizing uniformity among all the 
Akademis in terms of the tenure of the Chairman/President, representation and election of the 
General Council, and the minimum number of meetings to be held each year. If required, 
legislation governing the Akademis/ Institutions may be amended to ensure uniformity among the 
Akademis and their functionaries. 
 (Para 18) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 It is submitted that the Memorandum of Association (MoA)/Constitution of each 
Akademi has the set guidelines for app ointment of Chairman / President, tenure of the General 
Council, number of members of the General Council and number of meetings to be held. 
Ministry is making efforts to bring uniformity in appointment and governance structure across 
all the Akademis. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
2.2 The Committee notes the Ministry’s reply and reiterates its recommendation for 
establishing a uniform policy regarding appointment and governance structure across all 

 
28 
  
the Akademis. It believes that having fixed guideli nes will promote  parity and  effective 
functioning within the Akademis and will also aid the Ministry in exercising administrative 
control.  Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry to consider the inclusion of a  
Member of Parliament (MP) on the Governing Councils of each Institution.   
 
Regional Centres and Zonal Cultural Centre (ZCCs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee takes note of IGNCA's reply that the opening of Regional Centres in more 
number of States would be feasible subject to the a llocation of more funds for staff as well as 
establishment costs. The Committee takes note of the fund constraints faced by the Institutions. In 
this regard, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should seriously consider 
enhancing the budgetary allocation for the Akademis. The Committee also noted the suggestion 
from the National School of Drama, requesting Hon'ble MPs to contribute funds from MPLAD 
funds which could be used in the enhancement of art and culture education. 
(Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The total budget allocation to the Ministry for 2023 -24 is Rs. 3399.65 crore an d the 
allocation to the Akademis is Rs. 401.27 crore which is about 11.8% of the allocation.  In order 
to meet the additional requirement, if any, during the year, funds ar e made available to the 
Akademis through supplementary grants. It may kindly be appreciated that the grants allocated 
to the Ministry is decided by the Ministry of Finance. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
3.2 The Committee feels that sufficient budget is crucial for the Akademis growth. In 
the light of the repl y of IGNCA regarding establishing of new Regional Centres, the 
Committee  emphasizes that the Ministry should re assess the budgetary requirements  at 
the RE 2024-25 stage and at BE s tage in subsequent financial years. Also, Ministry should 
prepare a consolidated proposal for additional budget, keeping in view  the expansion 
requirements of each Akademi and the same may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance  
for approval.  
  
Administrative Staff and Vacancies 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee observes that the Government's Cultural Institutions are affected by 
vacancies and a lack of trained manpower. Lack of manpower not only affects the working of 

 
29 
  
these organizations but also hinders their efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry of Culture should urgently take measures to fill up the said vacancies at each level 
since manpower is the backbone of these organizations. The Committee also emphasizes that the 
Ministry must conduct the recruitment process in a fair and transparent manner, adhering to 
equal opportunity for all and non -discrimination principles. The Committee may be apprised of 
the recruitment process being followed in the Akademis and Cultural Institutions to fill in posts. 
(Para 37) 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee desires the Ministry to complete the recruitment process and fill up all the 
vacancies within a fixed period. The Ministry may also apprise the Committee of the status of the 
matter. 
(Para 38) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 As per Ministry of Finance guidelines dated 05.01.2024 regarding creation / revival / 
abolition of post s, all the p osts which are lying vacant for  more than five (05) years stand  
abolished, and to f ill these posts administrative M inistry needs to revive these posts by taking 
Ministry of Finance‟s approval. Ministry of Culture is making continuous efforts to revive these 
posts. Further, the posts which are lying vacant for less than 5 years, the recruitmen t process for 
these vacancies are undergoing expeditiously in all the academies. 
5.2 The current sanctioned / vacant strength of each Akademi is enclosed at Annexure III. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
5.3 The Committee is concerned about the  huge difference between the sanctioned and 
in-position strength across all  seven Central Akademis. Specifically, three Akademis viz., 
Sangeet Natak Akademi, CCRT,  and Lalit Kala Akademi, are functioning with less than 
40% of the ir sanctioned strength. National Sc hool of Drama has approximately 48%, and 
IGNCA has around 36% vacancies against their sanctioned strengths.   
5.4 The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for such meager working strength in 
the Akademis and urges the Ministry to make concentrated effo rts to streamline the 
processes and initiate the recruitment process at the earliest.   
 
Segregation of Functions 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that segregation of functions is also an important concept to 
internal control frameworks , financial reporting and regulatory compliance. The overall 

 
30 
  
effectiveness of the organization depends on an effective internal administration, adequate 
division of responsibilities, and the requirement of a sufficient number of staff who are 
adequately trained. Separation of functions is an important mechanism to help reduce the risk of 
fraud, error and other financial misconduct. In addition, it helps to promote accountability, 
transparency and ethical behaviour within the organization. The Committee, the refore, 
recommends segregation of the purchasing, provisioning, financing and policy -making functions 
within the Akademis. 
(Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 There are various verticals  under each A kademi to handle internal frameworks. As per 
the Memorandum of Associations / Constitutions of th ese Academies, the Governing Board / 
Society is the supreme authority in each Akademi which formulates policies as per the mandate. 
Further, General Financial Rules (GFR) is applicable to all Autonomous Bodies of the  Ministry 
and hence follows all purchasing, financial policies as per GFR. Administration Unit of each 
Akademi is responsible for hiring manpower as per approved RRs. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
6.2 The Committee is of the opinion that , given their distinct frameworks and mandate, 
each Akademi should have its own  dedicated functioning authority. The Committee notes 
the Ministry’s reply and reiterates that the administrative sections responsible  for tasks 
such as hiring manpower, purchasing, HR issues, and budget management  should be 
clearly defined in each Akademi and be empowered to ensure efficient functioning.  
 
Outreach and Inclusivity 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee feels that the National Akademis need to enhance its outreach, both  
within urban and rural areas, to make the arts more accessible and inclusive. Without effective 
outreach programmes, Akademis may struggle to reach a broader audience, beyond their 
immediate surroundings. A lack of outreach can reinforce existing cultural  hierarchies and 
exclude cultural practices that are not adequately represented or recognized. This exclusion can 
lead to marginalization of certain art forms, traditions or communities, thereby, limiting cultural 
diversity and stifling creativity. There i s also a risk of losing intangible cultural heritage, as 
there may be insufficient engagements with communities, artists and practitioners who are the 
custodians of these traditions. 
(Para 67) 
Reply of the Ministry 

 
31 
  
7.1 All the Akademi s through their  various regional centres try their  best to reach out to 
artists who are unaware of the functions and activities of t he Akademis. Also, some Akademis 
have project offices in different states for  particular art form. Further, Ministry of C ulture has 
set up seven Z onal Cultural Centres (ZCCs) in the country to protect, promote and preserve 
various forms of folk art & culture throughout the country and also to set up mechanism for 
development of the cultures of various regions. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2 The Committee feels that to enhance outreach and awareness, Ministry should issue 
directives to all the Akademis to implement specific measures.  Akademis could leverage  
social media platforms, radio stations, local newspapers , and other channels to enga ge 
communities, art practitioners and artists from across the country and tap into their full  
potential.  Additionally, t he Akademis should explore ways to publicize  their events, 
seminars and workshops through various platforms to reach a wider  audience a nd 
encourage greater participation.  
 
Infrastructure and Facilities  
Recommendation/Observation 
8. The Committee observes that investing in infrastructure for cultural Akademis is essential 
for supporting the growth, development, and sustainability of arti stic and cultural practices. 
Committee recommends that informal education may also be imparted through these Institutions. 
Ministry should provide the necessary funds and also promote synergy among the Institutions for 
sharing of infrastructural facilities. Committee also suggested Akademis to explore CSR funds to 
mobilise the resources for infrastructure developments including auditoriums, classrooms, 
studios, rehearsal halls and exhibition areas.  
(Para 82) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 This Ministry envisage s to  strengthen regional presence to facilitate the people of 
different region s and promote synergy among the Akademis for sharing of infrastructural 
facilities. All Akademis are autonomous in nature and they are free to obtain CSR funds. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.2 The Committee is of the opinion  that CSR funding could serve  as an additional 
budget source for the dev elopment and growth of Akademis.   The Committee may be 
apprised of the steps being taken by both the Ministry and the Akademis to secure and 

 
32 
  
utilize this funding.  The Committee also seeks information on the CSR funds received by 
each Akademi in the last three years and how these funds have been utilized.  
Returning of Awards  
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee notes the i nstances of recipients of awards, given by Akademis (such as 
Sahitya Akademi Awards), returning their awards in protest of certain political issues which are 
outside the ambit of the cultural realms and the autonomous functioning of the concerned 
Akademi. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of the other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. 
(Para 92) 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. A Member of the Committee opined agains t the view that artists, authors and other 
intellectuals and performers who have been recommended for awards must sign a commitment 
that they will not return the awards as a form of protest at any point in the future before they are 
able to receive it. He was of the view that India is a democratic country, and our Constitution 
has provided to every citizen the freedom of speech and expression and also the freedom to 
protest in any form. Returning of awards is only a form of protest. The Member added that th e 
Committee must strongly recommend to the Government to look into the actual issues in protest 
of which such awards have been returned and work towards resolving them. He was seconded by 
another Member. 
(Para 93) 
Recommendation/Observation 
11. The Committee questioned the re-engagement of such awardees who joined the Akademi 
after insulting it. Such inappropriate incidents involving the return of awards undermine the 
achievements of other awardees and also impact the overall prestige and reputation of the 
awards. The Member again submitted that the Akademis and the other Institutions should 
continue to work together with these artists and not shun them. 
(Para 94) 
Recommendation/Observation 
12. The Committee observes that the awards given by each Akademi con tinue to be top 
honors for an artist in India. The Committee emphasizes that Sahitya Akademi or other 
Akademis are apolitical organizations. There is no place for politics. The Committee, therefore, 
suggests that whenever an award is given, the consent of the recipient must be taken, so that 
he/she does not return it because of political reasons; as it is disgraceful to the country. The 
Committee recommends prior concurrence of short -listed candidates for awards before 

 
33 
  
finalization. A system may be put in p lace where an undertaking is taken from the proposed 
awardee citing acceptance of the award and that the awardees cannot dishonour the award at 
any point of time in future. Awards may not be given without such an undertaking. In the event 
that the awards a re returned, the awardee shall not be considered for such award in the award 
in the future. 
(Para 95) 
Reply of the Ministry 
12.1 The Ministry agrees with the Committee's perspective and would like to avoid 
controversies in all regards. However, obtaining a  signed commitment from the writer prior to 
the award announcement would unfortunately compromise the confidentiality surrounding the 
selection process. Additionally, the legal enforceability of such a pre -declaration commitment 
might be uncertain. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
12.2 The Committee acknowl edges the  Ministry’s reply  and understands its concern 
about confidentiality and legal implications related to obtaining signed commitment s. The 
Committee suggests that the commitment document should  include a non-disclosure clause 
to protect against  breach of confidentiality. Alternatively, the Ministry should explore 
other measures to prevent similar issues i n the future. A dditionally, a policy should be 
established to monitor  artists who have return ed their award s but remain affiliated with 
the Akademi.  
 
Youth Engagement 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. The Committee notes that the efforts are largely targeted at getting children to learn art 
forms - namely dance and music. The Committee feels that intervention is required to make them 
aware of what these traditions are; at least to a point where they can identify some very basic 
ideas of the performing and visual arts. While the Ministry of Culture set up the CCRT with 
somewhat a similar idea of reach ing out and creating opportunities for young children, 
especially from smaller cities, and all regions including the North -East, the program needs to be 
seriously reviewed and updated. Further, it should be linked with other ongoing efforts of the 
Ministry. 
(Para 121) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 The Sangeet Natak Akademi has two teaching institutions of dance and music , namely, 
Kathak Kendra in Delhi and Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy in Imphal. Akademi 

 
34 
  
through these institutions is imparting training of Kathak dance and Manipuri dance and music , 
respectively. These centres are also running Diploma Courses in their respective places. Sangeet 
Natak Akademi is also running various type of training programmes of local arts forms through 
its centres in Guwahati, Agartala, Chandankiyari and Thiruvananthapuram. 
13.2 In addition, internship programs are also provided by IGNCA to young artists and 
talented youth artists to provide them an opportunity for a direct learning in the field of art,

13.3 The Committee feels that  given the vast number of traditional dance and music

efforts to establish additional teaching institutions and centres, particularly in the North-
East Region, hilly areas, and islands, to create more opportunities for the young children.

Recommendation/Observation 
14. North East India is known for its geographical location, ecology and diverse culture . It is 
the homeland of large number of ethnic groups. Each ethnic community has its own distinct 
culture including food, music, dance, dress, language, etc. However, despite this, the North East 
has not been represented to the degree it deserves to be rep resented. Ministry must take 
measures in this direction and implement more schemes to preserve and promote various forms 
of art and culture in the NER. Ministry must extend all kinds of assistance including financial 
support to the individual artists and organizations in this region. 
(Para 129{ii}) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 Akademis through their region al centres established in North -East make  all possible 
efforts to preserve and promote various forms of art and culture in the NER. These centres also 
ensure the maximum participation of North-East in all their activities. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
14.2 The Committee notes the reply and urges  the Ministry to allocate a specific portion 
of the budget for each Akademi to the development and promotion  of the rich  culture of 

 
35 
  
the North -East Region. It also reiterates the need for special emphasis on providing 
assistance to NER to ensure maximum support and cultural growth in the region.  
 
Handling, preservation and digitization of Manuscripts 
Recommendation/Observation 
15. Manuscripts are the primary source of historic information. Manuscripts are diminishing 
along with time. Despite their best efforts, it is difficult to save manuscripts in a physical form 
beyond a time frame. Digital preservation of man uscripts restores them from damage, larceny 
and decay. The Ministry should evolve a well -designed digitization program that includes not 
just digital capture, but also appropriate care and repair of original materials, and long -term 
management of the digital files it produces. 
(Para 129{iii}) 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 National Mission on Manuscripts (NMM) since its inception in 2003 till today has 
contributed immensely to the preservation, documentation and dissemination of Ind ia's rich 
manuscript heritage . As of now, NMM has documented 5.2 million number of manuscripts, 
conserved 90 Million folios, digitized 3.30 lakhs number of manuscripts, organized  228 
preventive and 33 curative conservation workshops, published 114 books, organized  78 Basic 
level and  26 Advance level workshops on Manuscript logy  and Paleography,  1.28 lakh  
digitized manuscripts have been uploaded in the cloud server, out of which 70 Thousand 
manuscripts are available online for research purpose without download/ print facility. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
15.2 The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s reply and applauds the Ministry for its 
efforts in preserving, documenting and disseminating the country’s rich  manuscript 
heritage. The Committee  seeks information on  the numbe r of manuscripts still pending 
digitization and Ministry’s roadmap to achieve 100% digitization.   
 
Non-availability of information in Hindi or any other local language 
Recommendation/Observation 
16. Culture is encased in our languages. Art, in the form of  literature, plays, music films etc. 
cannot be fully appreciated without language. In order to preserve and promote our diverse 
culture, we need to preserve and promote a culture’s languages. Further, information on the art  
and culture must also be made available in Hindi and the local languages. 
(Para 129{vi}) 

 
36 
  
Reply of the Ministry 
 
16.1 The Ministry is continuously striving to disseminate information regarding the art and 
culture, in various languages. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
16.2 The Committ ee recommends the Ministry to take necessary steps to at least first 
make the various art forms available in Hindi and English languages in order to maximize 
reach and accessibility . Following this, t he Ministry, should work on making the 
information avail able in scheduled and other local languages, based on regional 
requirements, in a phased manner.

(Para 12.2) 

 
40 
  
 
Youth Engagement 
The Committee feels that given the vast number of traditional dance and music forms in 
the country, it is crucial to support and nurture the talents of the youth. A handful of 
institutions and centres may not  be adequate to address the diverge range of art forms. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry and concerned Akademis make dedicated 
efforts to establish additional teaching institutions and centres, particularly in the North -
East Region, hilly areas, and islands, to create more opportunities for the young children.  
(Para 13.3) 
 
Representation and promotion of culture of North East States of India  
The Committee notes the reply and urges  the Ministry to allocate a specific portion of the 
budget for eac h Akademi to the development and promotion of the rich culture of the 
North-East Region. It also reiterates the need for special emphasis on providing assistance 
to NER to ensure maximum support and cultural growth in the region.  
(Para 14.2) 
 
Handling, preservation and digitization of Manuscripts 
The Committee acknowledges the Ministry’s reply and applauds the Ministry for its efforts 
in preserving, documenting and disseminating the country’s rich manuscript heritage.  The 
Committee seeks information on  the number of manuscripts still pending digitization and 
Ministry’s roadmap to achieve 100% digitization.   
(Para 15.2) 
Non-availability of information in Hindi or any other local language 
The Committee recommends the Ministry to take necessary steps to at le ast first make the 
various art forms available in Hindi and English languages in order to maximize reach and 
accessibility. Following this, the Ministry, should work on making the information 
available in scheduled and other local languages, based on regio nal requirements, in a 
phased manner.  
(Para 16.2)

Construction of ROBs and RUBs 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee apprecia tes the increase in annual average progress in the number of 
Level Crossings (LCs) replaced with Road -Over-Bridges and Road -Under-Bridges. However, 
it also notes that the target of replacement of 1100 LCs set for 2023 -24 is lower than the 
annual average of  1207 progress achieved during 2014 -2023. The Committee is of the view 
that the target should be increased and the pace of replacement of LCs with ROBs/ RUBs 
should be expedited in the interest of greater safety and seamless mobility of the commuting 
public. 
(Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 As per the policy of the Ministry, all LCs on National Highways are to be replaced by 
ROB/RUB. Construction of ROBs/RUBs on NHs are taken up either on standalone basis or as part 
of improvement/ upgradation project of  a section of NH. The  recommendations of the Committee 
are noted and construction of ROBs/RUBs in replacement of existing LCs on NHs  will be 
expedited.

4. Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) should be used to penetrate the ground or structure, 
allowing for subsurface inspection of ROBs/RUBs. It can identify hidden defects, such as 
voids, delamination, or corrosion in concrete or steel elements. GPR can provide va luable 
information on the internal condition of the structure without the need for invasive 
investigations. 
Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) Systems should be adopted to involve the installation of 
sensors and monitoring devices on ROBs/RUBs to continuou sly monitor their structural 
behaviour. These sensors can measure parameters like vibrations, strains, and deflections, 
providing real-time data on the performance and health of the structure. SHM systems enable 
early detection of structural abnormalities and help in proactive maintenance and 
intervention. 
(Para 49) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Ground Penetrating Radar is being widely used to assess underground utilities. Foundation 
of ROBs/RUBs are generally not distressed as they are not located on river bed . Ministry has 
recently used guidelines for structural health monitoring on real time basis of bridges and structures 

4 
 
including ROBs and RUBs based on span length, location such as in coastal/highly polluted areas, 
age and history of previous rehabilitation/retrofitting measures using various kinds of sensors. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Techniques, such as ultrasonic testing, magnetic 
particle testing, and radiographic testing, can be employed for ROB/RUBs inspection. These  
techniques assess the integrity of structural components, detect cracks, weld defects, or 
corrosion, and identify potential failure points. NDT methods are typically used in 
combination with visual inspections to provide a comprehensive assessment of the structure's 
condition. 
(Para 50) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Schmidt Hammer Test, Ultrasonic Pulse Velocity Test and other NDTs are carried out for 
condition assessment of different components of bridges and structures including ROBs/RUBs. 
 
Environment clearances and land acquisition 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways in addressing the most important issue of land acquisition in fast tracking the 
ROB/RUB projects. The Bhoomira shi portal has undoubtedly expedited the process of land 
acquisition for National Highways. However, the Committee urges upon the Ministry and 
NHAI to accord continued priority to the land acquisition issue and fails to appreciate as to 
why huge Government  funds are parked with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition 
(CALAs). 
    (Para 55) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1  The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has launched Bhoomi Rashi Portal as a 
single point platform for online processing of Land Acquisit ion notification and payment of 
compensation to accelerate Highways infrastructure in India. The portal is a new mile stone in the 
nation’s journey towards digitization and transparency. The objective of the portal is to fast track the 
process of Land Acquisition notifications and to obviate the necessity of parking of huge amount of 
government fund with Competent Authority for Land Acquisition. 
6.2  The Ministry has made it mandatory for payment of compensation of Land Acquisition 

5 
 
through Bhoomi Rashi Port al for the projects of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highway and 
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The Ministry is continuously impressing upon the 
NHAI to make payment only through Bhoomi Rashi portal. The efforts has also been made for on -
boarding of National Highways Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited (NHIDCL) for 
payment of compensation through Portal. 
 6.3  The Present system of payment of compensation in respect of Ministry of Road Transport 
and Highways does not allow park ing of any fund with CALA. In case of NHAI, limit is 
created/fund is deposited for particular projects in CALA account up to which CALA can make 
payment through PFMS directly into account of the beneficiary. Therefore, the present system in 
NHAI inherently does not allow parking of Government funds with CALA. However, in some cases 
CALA could not be able to release compensation due to litigations in Courts, non -acceptance of 
award by beneficiaries, mismatch of beneficiaries’ details, arbitration awards etc. and the funds/limit 
remain parked/unpaid in CALAs Accounts.  
6.4  NHIDCL deposits the LA compensation amount with the concern CALA after passing of 
award under section 3G of National Highways Act, 1956 so as to enable them to distribute the 
compensation amount to beneficiary. No payment is deposited to concerned CALA’s account prior 
to 3G Award. In addition, NHIDCL has opened Zero balance accounts for the CALAs with only 
drawing rights so that money gets placed with the CALA for disbursement only. However,  in some 
cases, the CALAs are in the process of shifting to Zero balance accounts system.  
6.5  It is anticipated that once all the Implementing Agencies are completely on - boarded on 
Bhoomi Rashi Portal, there would be no parking of government funds with CALAs in any manner. 
 
Recommendation/Observation

8. The Railways should look for a cost -effective and durable solution to the problem o f 
water-logging by modifying embankment height, providing suitable cross and longitudinal 
drains, cutting off the ingress of water from the catchment area into the subway, etc. 
(Para 72) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Following steps are being taken to prevent water logging at various underpasses: 
 
i. Rain Water Harvesting (RWH) wells are provided to collect & dispose off rain water 
at LHS. 
ii. Fixed Pumps, Mobile Pumps & Heavy -duty pumps are arranged & deployed to 
discharge rain water from LHS. 
iii. Covering sheds are prov ided at critical LHS to prevent entry of rain water into the 
LHS. 
iv. Flood gauges are provided at LHS to indicate depth of water logging (More than 3 feet 
depth), during heavy rain. 
v. Caution boards are provided at LHS Not to enter in LHS if depth of water is b eyond 
dangerous level (more than 3 feet in depth). 
vi. Protection walls & Humps at the approach roads are provided to prevent entry of 
outside water into the LHS. 
vii. Dedicated team of Officer's & Supervisor's has been deputed to regularly inspect and 
monitor the water logging status in LHS. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation

Progress of projects under the Setu Bharatam Programme 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes  that only 25% of ROB/RUB projects have been completed since 
the inception of the Setu Bharatam scheme in March, 2016. The construction of the ROB/RUB 
projects indicates staggered growth. The majority of the projects are either in progress or 
have not been started as yet. The Committee recommends that the Ministry makes concerted 

26 
 
efforts to achieve the aims and targets of the Setu Bharatam Programme. If needed, Ministry 
should increase the allocation of funds under this programme for timely construction of 
ROBs/RUBs. Also, the Ministry should strive towards completing all the pending ROBs/RUBs 
projects in a time-bound manner to ensure safe and smooth flow of traffic besides minimising 
road fatalities. 
(Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Altogether 149 ROBs/R UBs are to be constructed under Setu Bharatam program. Till date 
45 nos have been completed, 55 nos are at different stages of implementation and 35   nos have been 
sanctioned which are to be commenced. Only 14 nos. are yet to be sanctioned. Progress of Set u 
Bharatam Programme is periodically monitored at several levels in Ministry to expedite progress. 
Co-ordination meetings are also held with Ministry of Railways to expedite various approvals from 
Railways. There are no fund constraints for construction of  ROBs/RUBs under Setu Bharatam 
Programme.  
Recommendation/Observation

should put up signboards along the service roads on the highway,  indicating that the traffic on

traffic on the service roads is one-way.  This creates hurdles for those coming from the opposite 
direction. Service roads should have painted arrows directing two-way traffic on the stretch.

2.1 Generally, Service Roads are designed for either two -way or one -way traffic movements

marking provided.

Use of technology for inspections 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. Modern technology for periodic inspection of ROBs/ RUBs can help in the early 
detection of damage, minimize human errors and lower maintenance costs.  The Committee, 
therefore, feels that more steps should be taken to adopt modern technology for inspection of 
ROBs/RUBs. Drones equipped with high -resolution cameras and sensors can be used to 
capture aerial imagery of ROBs/RUBs, providing a detailed visual assessment of th e 
structure's condition. The images can be analysed further to identify any signs of damage, 
deterioration, or structural weakness. Drones are particularly useful for accessing hard -to-
reach areas and can significantly reduce inspection time and costs. 
(Para 47) 
  

30 
 
8.1 Laser scanning technologies, such as LiDAR, can be used to generate accurate 3D 
models of ROBs/RUBs. LiDAR sensors emit laser pulses and measure the reflected light, 
creating precise point cloud data. This data can be used to assess the geomet ry, dimensions, 
and deformations of the structure, detecting any irregularities or deformations that may 
indicate structural deficiencies. 
(Para 48) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1.1. Visual as well as equipment based periodical inspection, evaluation and monito ring has been 
mandated for all bridges and structures including ROBs/RUBs. Close access to structural 
arrangements underneath bridge/structure deck is provided through use of mobile bridge inspection 
unit, where the bridge inspector closely examine condition of different components of bridges and if 
needed conduct different non-destructive tests. Drone and LiDAR are generally used for topographic 
surveys and can also be used for ROB/RUB condition assessment. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. Data Analysis and Visualization Software should be used to process and analyse the 
data collected from various inspection technologies. These tools facilitate the interpretation of 
data, enabling engineers and inspectors to identify anomalies, assess risks, and generate 
reports on the condition of ROBs/RUBs. Data Visualization software helps in presenting the 
raw inspection data in a clear and easily understandable format, which can be interpreted 
correctly to facilitate decisions. 
(Para 51) 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 Various software/analysis tool are used internationally for data analysis and       visualization 
to assess rehabilitation/retrofitting of different component(s) of bridges and structures including 
ROBs/RUBs or reconstruction. Under Indian Bridge Management System , software/analysis tool is 
being developed through consultant (civil and IT joint venture) for determining health index and 
prioritization of bridges and structures including ROBs and RUBs. Similar exercise is being done 
through IIT Madras for simply supp orted prestressed concrete box girder superstructure using real 
time data from different sensors for vibration, strain, corrosion, inclination, temperature, etc. Similar 
software/analysis tools are planned to be developed for other kinds of bridge topologies. 
 
Recommendation/Observation
